signals.title: [Model Runner][Multimodal] Add exact-budget encoder CUDA graphs for Cosmos3-Edge
signals.text: ## Purpose This PR adds image-encoder CUDA Graph support for the recently added `nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge` model. Cosmos3-Edge has a 27-layer SigLIP2 vision encoder. A 64-token image launches 281 CUDA kernels in eager mode on the RTX PRO 6000 setup below, making the encoder strongly launch-bound. The graph path precomputes dynamic metadata outside capture and records only the tensor-only vision forward: - patch projection and packed positional embeddings; - packed `cu_seqlens` and `max_seqlen`; - the 27-layer SigLIP2 encoder; - the patch-merge gather and Cosmos projector. Cosmos image shapes are highly dynamic. Padding an input into the next larger graph can be slower than eager and, depending on the platform and capture shape, can also change BF16 values. This PR therefore adds an opt-in per-path `require_exact_token_budget_match` policy to the generic encoder CUDA Graph manager. Cosmos enables it, defaults to one 64-token image per replay, and sends inputs between captured budgets through the existing eager fallback. Fixed-resolution deployments can add their exact merged-token counts with `encoder_cudagraph_token_budgets`. The graph path is intentionally limited to raw-pixel images and one image per replay. Video and precomputed image embeddings continue to use eager execution. ## Cross-platform validation The H20 validation supplements the RTX PRO 6000 results; it does not replace them. All comparisons are within one GPU and use identical inputs. The main performance and eager-regression benchmarks use balanced process order. The two platforms use the same model revision, BF16, FlashAttention 2, TP=1, `max_model_len=4096`, disabled prefix/MM processor caches, and `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` decoder graphs. | Setup | RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition | NVIDIA H20 | | --- | --- | --- | | Compute capability / visible SMs | SM120 / 188 | SM90 / 78 | | Driver / PyTorch | 580.159.03 / 2.11.0+cu130 | 535.161.08 / 2.11.0+cu130 | | PR source | clean final-head `a2f44889f` worktree | the four `a0ef3899` production files over the official `2e2ffd104` nightly wheel | | True pre-patch source | clean `2e2ffd104` worktree | untouched official `2e2ffd104` nightly wheel | | Model | `nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge` revision `9eff1178c4e6dcbed1e27c8113109a6cd6d3706e` | same | `a2f44889f` differs from `a0ef3899` only in the integration-test harness; the four production files used by the H20 run are identical. The RTX PRO 6000 runs used clean Python source trees with an identical runtime-only prebuilt-extension overlay for both arms. The H20 wheel overlay ran successfully for these experiments, but its PyTorch version differs from the wheel's declared dependency, so it is recorded as an experimental setup, not a general compatibility claim. FlashInfer autotuning was disabled on both platforms. ### Exact-64 performance Each process used 5 warmups and 30 measured requests with unique 256x256 images, one output token, and the palindrome schedule `pre-patch -> patched eager -> graph -> graph -> patched eager -> pre-patch`. Values are the midpoint of the two slot medians. The primary fast-path comparison is graph versus patched eager; graph versus true pre-patch is also shown separately. | GPU | Pre-patch encoder | Patched eager | Encoder graph | Graph vs pre-patch | Graph vs patched eager | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | RTX PRO 6000 | 5.697 ms | 5.841 ms | **2.952 ms** | **-48.19%, 1.930x** | **-49.47%, 1.979x** | | H20 | 8.760 ms | 8.970 ms | **3.548 ms** | **-59.50%, 2.469x** | **-60.45%, 2.528x** | | GPU | Pre-patch wall | Patched eager | Graph wall | Graph vs pre-patch | Graph vs patched eager | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | RTX PRO 6000 | 19.180 ms | 19.569 ms | **16.670 ms** | **-13.08%, 1.151x** | **-14.81%, 1.174x** | | H20 | 21.822 ms | 22.664 ms | **17.255 ms** | **-20.93%, 1.265x** | **-23.87%, 1.313x** | Both graph slots recorded 35 hits and 0 misses on each GPU. On the RTX PRO 6000, 60/60 paired encoder samples and 59/60 wall samples improved; one paired wall sample did not improve. On H20, all 60 paired encoder and wall samples improved. In the earlier memory-profile runs, reported CUDA Graph memory increased by about 0.03 GiB on the RTX PRO 6000 and 0.02 GiB on H20. The relative gain was larger in the measured H20 environment. I do not infer a cause from SM count: GPU architecture, host, driver, and installation method also differ. ### Correctness and dispatch All comparisons in this table are within the same GPU and use identical input images for the three source arms. | Validation | RTX PRO 6000 | H20 | | --- | --- | --- | | Natural greedy generation | pre-patch = patched eager = graph for **960/960** token positions and all decoded text | same: **960/960** token positions and all text | | Output diversity | 149 distinct token IDs / 25 distinct sequences | 76 distinct token IDs / 26 distinct sequences | | Encoder tensors | **31/31 bitwise exact** across all three arms | **31/31 bitwise exact** across all three arms | | Exact `[64, 256]` dispatch, 5 measured requests/shape | 64: 5 hits; 100: 5 eager fallbacks; 256: 5 hits | same | | Forced-padding control for 64/100/256 | 15/15 one-token outputs and encoder tensors exact | same | | Exact replay 256 -> 64 -> 256 | 3 measured hits, all tensors/tokens exact; repeated 256-token output bitwise exact | same | | `max_vision_items=2` guard | expected actionable `ValueError` | same | | `enable_mm_embeds=True` guard | manager disabled (`modalities=[]`), eager request still generated 8 tokens | same | The MM-embeds guard check verifies that enabling that configuration disables the graph manager and preserves eager execution; it is not a claim that the test payload itself was a precomputed embedding tensor. ### Why exact budget matching is conservative The following controls deliberately disabled the exact-match policy and forced smaller inputs into larger captured graphs. `Exact policy` is graph-enabled but records misses and executes eager fallback. Times are measured-request medians. | GPU | Actual -> capture | Eager encoder | Exact policy (hit/miss) | Forced padding (hit/miss) | Forced/eager | Wall ratio | One-token outputs changed | Encoder tensor vs eager | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | | RTX PRO 6000 | 176 -> 256 | 5.740 ms | 5.947 ms (0/30) | 6.397 ms (30/0) | **1.115x** | 1.040x | **1/30** | **0/30 exact**, max abs 1.061 | | H20 | 176 -> 256 | 8.960 ms | 8.932 ms (0/30) | 9.409 ms (30/0) | **1.050x** | 1.031x | **0/30** | **30/30 exact** | | RTX PRO 6000 | 64 -> 4096 | 5.919 ms | 5.781 ms (0/15) | 51.933 ms (15/0) | **8.775x** | 3.297x | **2/15** | **0/15 exact**, max abs 0.461 | | H20 | 64 -> 4096 | 8.839 ms | 8.667 ms (0/15) | 112.319 ms (15/0) | **12.708x** | 5.826x | **0/15** | **15/15 exact** | An earlier exploratory RTX PRO 6000 image set changed 6/30 one-token outputs for 176 -> 256; the matched diverse-image rerun above changed 1/30. H20 stayed bitwise exact even under the 4096-token control, while the RTX PRO 6000 did not. Thus numerical sensitivity is platform- and shape-dependent: zero-length `cu_seqlens` padding prevents padded tokens from participating in varlen attention, but it does not guarantee bitwise equivalence for every differently shaped GEMM/MLP capture. The exact policy is therefore a conservative cross-platform performance and numerical-consistency choice. Padding is not claimed to be slower in every small case; for example, the five-sample 100 -> 256 control had opposite directions on the two GPUs. The policy avoids relying on that variability. ### Eager-path regression audit An independent `pre-patch -> patched eager -> patched eager -> pre-patch` schedule used 60 measured requests per slot. These median deltas are much smaller than the graph benefit; no material eager-path regression was observed, and the deltas were within slot drift and run-to-run noise. | GPU | Pre-patch encoder | Patched encoder | Delta | Pre-patch wall | Patched wall | Delta | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | RTX PRO 6000 | 5.7503 ms | 5.7418 ms | -0.147% | 19.3401 ms | 19.3697 ms | +0.153% | | H20 | 8.812 ms | 8.697 ms | -1.31% | 21.974 ms | 21.785 ms | -0.86% | ## Correctness and testing - `tests/v1/cudagraph/test_encoder_cudagraph.py`: **58 passed** on both platforms. - `tests/models/multimodal/test_cosmos3_edge.py`: **4 passed** on both platforms. - H20 in-process Cosmos image/video encoder-CG integration: **2 passed**. - The H20 run exposed that the new graph-hit assertion accessed an in-process private object and failed under default V1 multiprocessing. The follow-up commit `a2f44889f` reads worker-local counters through `collective_rpc`. On the final RTX PRO 6000 head, the default-multiprocessing image/video run passed both cases. - Final-head RTX PRO 6000 tests: 58 passed, 4 passed, and the default multiprocessing image/video integration 2 passed. - All relevant pre-commit hooks passed locally, including ruff, mypy, typos, markdownlint, SPDX, forbidden imports, and configuration validation. Final-head local commands from the source-overlay validation environment: ```bash env PYTHONPATH=/root/r22/runtime_overlay:/root/r22/vllm-main \ /root/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/v1/cudagraph/test_encoder_cudagraph.py env PYTHONPATH=/root/r22/runtime_overlay:/root/r22/vllm-main \ /root/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/models/multimodal/test_cosmos3_edge.py env PYTHONPATH=/root/r22/runtime_overlay:/root/r22/vllm-main \ /root/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_vit_cudagraph.py -k cosmos3_edge /root/vllm/.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ $(git diff --name-only 2e2ffd104..HEAD) ``` ## Duplicate-work check I searched open and recently merged PRs for Cosmos3-Edge encoder CUDA Graphs, exact encoder token budgets, and padding-sensitive graph fallback, and found no duplicate implementation. Related work is complementary: - #42796 reduces excessive Qwen2.5-VL metadata padding; - #43403 falls back when inputs exceed capture capacity; - #42785 adds a secondary capture axis for inputs with the same token count but different shapes; - #49852 adds MRV2 encoder CUDA Graph support; - #51221 and #51949 touch Cosmos video pruning and LoRA, respectively. The exact-token policy here handles inputs whose token count falls between captured budgets and is orthogonal to #42785's secondary shape axis. ## AI assistance OpenAI Codex assisted with code analysis, implementation, validation and benchmark scripting, duplicate-work review, and drafting this PR description.

signals.title: [Feature] Support batch invariance on ROCm
signals.text: ## Purpose This PR enables broad-based batch invariant inference on ROCm, keyed by `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. The benefits of this PR are however not limited to ROCm. 1. All-reduce and reduce-scatter are supported via `CustomAllReduce` and `CustomReduceScatter`. The 1stage algorithm is already batch-invariant, and the 2stage algorithm can be made batch-invariant by a one-line change. **This makes the entirety of custom all-reduce/reduce-scatter batch-invariant, including on CUDA**, which likely can lead to performance improvements there. However, this code path is disabled on CUDA pending tuning in a follow-up PR. - A corresponding fallback via all-gather and fixed-order sum is added that supports all platforms. - On ROCm gfx950, custom all-reduce / reduce-scatter have been measured to be on par with if not faster than the RCCL implementations. 2. Triton kernels have been added for batch-invariant softmax / scaled FP8 GEMM. 3. Fixes a longstanding bug where `torch.mm`/`torch.bmm`/`torch.addmm` were not batch-invariant under Inductor (because Inductor lowers to the `.out` variants) has been fixed. ## Testing Numerous E2E runs were carried out on a variety of models (DeepSeek R1, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-OSS-120B, including quantized variants) across a variety of parallelism strategies (TP, PP, DP, EP, DCP) and logprobs examined to confirm batch invariance. The E2E runs also confirm that gsm8k accuracy is not degraded by batch invariance. The batch-invariance test groups on AMD CI (both gfx942 and gfx950) pass. New tests have been added to the aforementioned test groups: | module | GPUs | covers | |---|---|---| | `test_mx_linear_batch_invariant.py` | 1 (gfx950) | the native MX linear kernels, including the four AITER MXFP4 entry points | | `test_moe_row_permutation_batch_invariant.py` | 1 | the fused-MoE expert GEMM against row order within an expert | | `test_tp_all_reduce_batch_invariant.py` | 4 | all-reduce across token counts spanning the protocol thresholds | | `test_tp_reduce_scatter_batch_invariant.py` | 4 | the same for reduce-scatter | The four upstream modules the first commit un-skips — `test_batch_invariance`, `test_rms_norm_batch_invariant`, `test_matmul_batch_invariant`, `test_online_batch_invariance` — cover the rest of what this touches and now actually run on ROCm. Run on 8x gfx950 (MI355), ROCm 7.2, `VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn`, from `tests/`: | command | result | |---|---| | `pytest v1/determinism/test_matmul_batch_invariant.py` | 26 passed, 17s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_rms_norm_batch_invariant.py` | 475 passed, 2m35s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_mx_linear_batch_invariant.py` | 21 passed, 17s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_moe_row_permutation_batch_invariant.py` | 23 passed, 13s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_tp_all_reduce_batch_invariant.py -m 'distributed(num_gpus=4)'` | 6 passed, 4m00s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_tp_reduce_scatter_batch_invariant.py -m 'distributed(num_gpus=4)'` | 6 passed, 3m59s | | `pytest v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py` | 6 passed, 1 skipped, 5m03s | ## AI assistance Written with AI assistance (Claude). Every line has been reviewed by the submitter, who can defend the change end to end. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [Bugfix][NIXL] Fail closed on HMA receive errors
signals.text: ## Summary NIXL receive failures are currently propagated through flat block IDs. That works for uniform KV caches, but HMA block IDs are scoped to independent pools, so the worker intentionally omits them. The failed request is then reported as finished receiving without any failure signal, allowing decode to continue with invalid KV. This change: - propagates unrecoverable HMA receive failures by request ID; - aggregates that signal across workers until the receive is complete; - applies the same aggregation to uniprocess execution so failure and completion notifications cannot be split across scheduler steps; and - fails the request before consuming any sampled tokens, regardless of the block-recovery policy. Uniform-cache failures keep the existing block-level fail/recompute behavior. ## Duplicate-work check This is not duplicated by an open PR: - #40364 fixed handshake-failure recovery through `invalid_block_ids`, but explicitly left HMA failure handling as a TODO because its block IDs are not group-qualified. - #50754 reports push-side write-posting failures to the decode worker; it still relies on the downstream receive-failure path fixed here. - #50494 and #48263 extend supported HMA layouts rather than propagating failed receives to the scheduler. ## Tests ```text .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_error_propagation.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_output_aggregator.py -q # 8 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py::test_handshake_failure_returns_finished -q # 2 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector_hma.py::test_hma_failed_transfer_reports_request_error -q # 1 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/executor/test_executor.py \ -k uniproc_executor_pairs_receive_failure_with_completion -v # 2 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_output_aggregator.py -v # 3 passed pre-commit run --files \ vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py \ tests/v1/executor/test_executor.py # all file-scoped hooks passed ``` Linux validation used a vllm-development-platform environment on the `vllm-envs` PVC and Kueue-managed Jobs: ```text .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_error_propagation.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_output_aggregator.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector_hma.py::test_hma_failed_transfer_reports_request_error -q # 9 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py::test_handshake_failure_returns_finished -q # 2 passed (B200) ``` The serving regression was reproduced with Gemma-4-26B FP8, NIXL HMA, prefill block size 128, and decode block size 64. Both runs used the same Manifesto-rendered PD topology and EPP always-disaggregated routing: - current main `71b0da7c4e`: the compatibility hash passed, the NIXL handshake then raised the heterogeneous-block-size assertion, and the API returned HTTP 200 with 64 tokens of gibberish despite zero successful KV transfers; - this change `9e80dac9eb`: the identical handshake failure logged `Failing 1 request(s) due to unrecoverable KV receive failure` and the API returned HTTP 500 with only an error object—no choices, content, usage, or generated tokens. No model-quality evaluation is applicable: successful KV transfer and model output paths are unchanged. The serving validation targets the changed failure path and asserts that no generated tokens escape. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate, implement, and test this change. The human submitter reviewed the changed lines before marking the PR ready.

signals.title: [Quantization] Clarify MXFP4 MoE W13 layout requirement from backends
signals.text: ## Background GPT-OSS checkpoints store fused gate/up weights in interleaved row order [g0, u0, g1, u1, ...], while standard MoE checkpoints (DeepSeek, Kimi-K3, and most of the ckpts from different quantizers etc.) store them contiguously [gate; up]. In the beginning when mxfp4 oracle was initially created, this interleaved weight format is overlooked. Some backends accepts interleaved format while others accepts contiguous format. They are all mixed together in the same `convert_weight_*` and `select_mxfp4_moe_backend` call. Later when DSV4 was added, two parallel functions (convert_gpt_oss_weight_* and convert_weight_*) were created. The original `convert_weight_*` was renamed `convert_gpt_oss_weight_*`, despite it handles more models than just gpt-oss. Now several backends shared identical code between them, meaning they silently accepted either layout without converting, which is incorrect for backends that assume a specific layout. ## Audit DeepDive This PR starts a complete, deepdive audit to the existing state of all the backends. **NOTE:** The audit is produced by Claude Code, and verified carefully by the author. There could be mistakes. ### Terminology - **Contiguous [w1;w3]** = `[gate_0..gate_N; up_0..up_N]` (standard vLLM checkpoint layout) - **Contiguous [w3;w1]** = `[up_0..up_N; gate_0..gate_N]` (FlashInfer CUTLASS convention, halves swapped) - **Interleaved [g,u]** = `[gate_0, up_0, gate_1, up_1, ...]` (GPT-OSS checkpoint layout) - **Interleaved [u,g]** = `[up_0, gate_0, up_1, gate_1, ...]` (TRTLLM convention, w1/w3 swapped within pairs) ### w13 Layout Expected by Backend x Activation | Backend | Activation | w13 Layout | Proof | |---|---|---|---| | **DEEPGEMM_MXFP4** | SILU | **Contiguous [w1;w3]** | [`fp8_utils.py:143`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py#L143): `hidden_size: tl.constexpr = N // 2`; [`fp8_utils.py:165-178`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py#L165): loads gate from `input_ptr + offset`, up from `input_ptr + hidden_size + offset` | | | SWIGLUSTEP | **Contiguous [w1;w3]** | [`layers/activation.py:37-38`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/activation.py#L37): `gate = tl.load(x_row_ptr + offsets)`, `up = tl.load(x_row_ptr + offsets + d)` with `d = n // 2` at [line 55](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/activation.py#L55) | | | SITU | **Contiguous [w1;w3]** | [`activation_kernels.cu:483-484`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/csrc/libtorch_stable/activation_kernels.cu#L483): `gate_ptr = input + row * 2 * d`, `up_ptr = gate_ptr + d` | | **TRTLLM** | SWIGLUOAI, SILU, SITU | **Interleaved [u,g]** | [`mxfp4.py:1310-1317`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/mxfp4.py#L1310): comment "TRTLLM kernel expects interleaved [w3_0, w1_0, ...]"; `torch.stack([w3_weight, w1_weight], dim=2).reshape()` produces `[up_0, gate_0, up_1, gate_1, ...]` | | | | | [`trtllm_mxfp4_moe.py:139-146`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/4be4e9a580/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/trtllm_mxfp4_moe.py#L139): SITU support gated behind `has_flashinfer_situ_activation()` | | **FLASHINFER_CUTLASS** | SILU, GELU_TANH, SWIGLUOAI, SWIGLUOAI_UNINTERLEAVE, RELU2_NO_MUL | **Contiguous [w3;w1]** (swapped halves) | signals.title: [Bugfix][V1] Restore hybrid GDN prefix-cache hits under MTP spec decoding
signals.text: ## Purpose On **Qwen3.5-122B-A10B** with MTP speculative decoding, a replay of a cached prompt never reaches the depth the prefix cache could give it, and prompts whose length is a multiple of the hash unit get **no hit at all**. Measured live before this change, with a 1072-token GDN page and `--prefix-match-unit 67`: | prompt | cached tokens on replay | ceiling | |---|---|---| | 1072 | **0** | 938 | | 2000 | **0** | 1876 | | 2144 | **0** | 2010 | | 3000 | 1072 | 2881 | | 3500 | 2144 | 3417 | ### Root cause Three rules compose badly. A lookup caps at `prompt_len - 1`, because the last token must be recomputed for logits. The MTP/EAGLE drafter then rewinds the hit one hash unit (67) further. But the producer publishes the GDN state at the prompt's own tail boundary, `prompt_len // 67 * 67`, which is at or above the cap — so the recurrent group cannot resume where the rewind lands, and the coordinator intersects the two groups down to the previous full page (or to zero). The same cap breaks the full-attention side whenever `prompt_len` is a multiple of 67 — and every page multiple is, since `1072 = 16 × 67`. Its partial-tail entry is registered at `prompt_len // 67 * 67 == prompt_len`, which the `- 1` cap excludes, so full attention itself matches nothing below the page boundary and the hybrid hit collapses to 0. That is the `1072 → 0`, `2144 → 0` row above. ### Fix Write-side only, all of it gated on MTP/EAGLE plus fine-grained hashing being active: - `mamba_state_cache_position(num_tokens, block_size, hash_block_size)` in `kv_cache_utils.py`: `unit = min(hash_block_size, block_size)`, returns `(num_tokens - 1 - unit) // unit * unit` — the position a replay actually lands on. - `Scheduler._mamba_block_aligned_split` stops a prefill chunk there, so that state exists to be published. It is an **extra** stop; the existing block-aligned stops stay. Replacing them lets intermediate chunks end off-grid and re-triggers the state poisoning of #43559 (14 tests in `test_mamba_align_chunk_split.py` fail that way). - `MambaManager._cache_partial_tail_block` publishes the GDN state there instead of at the prompt tail. - `FullAttentionManager._cache_partial_tail_block` additionally publishes `(prompt_len - 1) // 67 * 67`, the deepest tail a replay can reach. The unshifted tail is kept, because requests that *extend* this prompt have a higher cap and can still match it. - `MambaManager` reports a block-aligned prompt end as unreachable through a new `reachable_block_mask()` argument, so that state is not cached in any retention mode: no lookup can land at or past a prompt's own end, and the rewound state below it is where consumers land. Guarded on the latter being cached. The rewound position is read from one `MambaManager` helper rather than recomputed per caller, and keys off whether the engine runs a drafter rather than the per-group `use_eagle` bit, which is only set on groups that take the drop. Without the last item the page multiples stay at 0 no matter where the GDN state sits: the producer had the state at 938 / 2010 / 3082, but full attention offered nothing below 1072 / 2144 / 3216 for the intersection to meet. ## Test Plan ```bash # unit pytest tests/v1/core -q # e2e: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, 4x B200, MTP 3 tokens, sub-page hashing vllm serve $QWEN35_122B --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-chunked-prefill \ --spec-method mtp --spec-tokens 3 --prefix-match-unit 67 --port 8110 ``` Hit depth is read from the `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` delta of a replay: a token-id prompt of an exact length is sent three times and the second and third deltas are the cached length. 132 lengths from 1 to 15k were swept — every page multiple with its `+1`, `+unit-1`, `+unit`, `+unit+1` neighbours, plus scattered lengths. Two further passes cover the configurations where the patch must do nothing, and quality was checked on top of real hits. ## Test Result (1) Hit Length Boundary All 132 lengths land exactly on the replay ceiling `(P - 1 - 67) // 67 * 67`. Page-boundary neighbourhoods, where the old code either missed entirely or fell back a full page: | prompt | position | before | after | replay ceiling | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1072 | k*1072 | 0 | 938 | 938 | | 1073 | k*1072 + 1 | 0 | 1005 | 1005 | | 1138 | k*1072 + unit - 1 | 0 | 1005 | 1005 | | 1139 | k*1072 + unit | 0 | 1005 | 1005 | | 1140 | k*1072 + unit + 1 | 0 | 1072 | 1072 | | 2144 | k*1072 | 0 | 2010 | 2010 | | 2145 | k*1072 + 1 | 1072 | 2077 | 2077 | | 2210 | k*1072 + unit - 1 | 1072 | 2077 | 2077 | | 2211 | k*1072 + unit | 1072 | 2077 | 2077 | | 2212 | k*1072 + unit + 1 | 1072 | 2144 | 2144 | | 3216 | k*1072 | 0 | 3082 | 3082 | | 3217 | k*1072 + 1 | 2144 | 3149 | 3149 | | 3282 | k*1072 + unit - 1 | 2144 | 3149 | 3149 | | 3283 | k*1072 + unit | 2144 | 3149 | 3149 | | 3284 | k*1072 + unit + 1 | 2144 | 3216 | 3216 | | 5360 | k*1072 | 0 | 5226 | 5226 | | 5361 | k*1072 + 1 | 4288 | 5293 | 5293 | | 5426 | k*1072 + unit - 1 | 4288 | 5293 | 5293 | | 5427 | k*1072 + unit | 4288 | 5293 | 5293 | | 5428 | k*1072 + unit + 1 | 4288 | 5360 | 5360 | | 10720 | k*1072 | 7504 | 10586 | 10586 | | 10721 | k*1072 + 1 | 9648 | 10653 | 10653 | | 10786 | k*1072 + unit - 1 | 9648 | 10653 | 10653 | | 10787 | k*1072 + unit | 9648 | 10653 | 10653 | | 10788 | k*1072 + unit + 1 | 9648 | 10720 | 10720 | Other lengths: | prompt | before | after | ceiling | |---|---|---|---| | 500 | 0 | 402 | 402 | | 999 | 0 | 871 | 871 | | 2000 | 0 | 1876 | 1876 | | 3000 | 1072 | 2881 | 2881 | | 3500 | 2144 | 3417 | 3417 | | 5000 | 3216 | 4891 | 4891 | | 7777 | 6432 | 7705 | 7705 | | 12345 | 10720 | 12261 | 12261 | | 14999 | 12864 | 14874 | 14874 | `before` comes from a CPU replica driving the real splitter and the real managers on the base commit; on the patched build that replica reproduces the end-to-end numbers length by length, so the two columns are comparable. Configurations where the patch must be inert: re-running the same 132 lengths without `--prefix-match-unit` (both groups sit at 1072, so `hash_block_size == block_size` and sub-page hashing is off) gives `((P - 1) // 1072) * 1072 - 1072` on every length, and the CPU replica shows this build and the base commit agreeing on all 132. `mamba_cache_mode=all` cannot be exercised on this model — it is not in `SupportsMambaPrefixCaching`, so vLLM falls back to `align`. Unit tests: `tests/v1/core` 492 passed. The one failure and two errors are GPU-exclusive e2e cases (`Free memory on device cuda:0 ... less than desired`) blocked by the serving process on the same box, and reproduce without this change. `tests/v1/core/test_mamba_align_chunk_split.py` is updated so the replay landing position counts as a legal intermediate chunk end alongside the partial-tail boundary. (2) Model Quality Test GPQA Diamond Score for Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B : 85.9% (match official score 86.6%) GSM8K 5-shot, 300 questions: 0.890 / 0.853 with 0.0% / 1.3% invalid on this build, against 0.847 / 0.830 with 1.7% / 2.7% invalid on the base commit. Run-to-run spread is larger than the gap, so this is "no regression", not an accuracy claim. Output quality on top of a real hit: an English passage of 700 / 1500 / 2400 / 3500 words, sent cold and then replayed (hits of 670 / 1608 / 2613 / 3819 tokens), returns byte-identical text at `temperature=0` in all four, twice over — no truncation, no repetition, no garbling. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details> ## Reproduce Low KVCache Hit Length with Qwen3.5 (1) Launch ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 \ PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \ vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B \ --served-model-name Qwen3.5-122B-A10B \ --trust-remote-code \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --spec-method mtp \ --spec-tokens 3 \ --prefix-match-unit 67 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8110 ``` (2) Send the same prompt twice ```bash python3 - <<'EOF' import json, random, re, urllib.request N = 2144 BASE = "http://localhost:8110" def hits_total(): metrics = urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BASE}/metrics").read().decode() return float( re.search(r"^vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total\{[^}]*\} (\S+)", metrics, re.M).group(1) ) random.seed(N) body = json.dumps({ "model": "Qwen3.5-122B-A10B", "prompt": [random.randint(1000, 100000) for _ in range(N)], "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, }).encode() for attempt in (1, 2): before = hits_total() urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request( f"{BASE}/v1/completions", body, {"Content-Type": "application/json"})) print(attempt, int(hits_total() - before)) EOF ``` (3) Check the second request's cache length Before the fix it is 0, after the fix it is 2010.

signals.title: [ROCm][Quantization] Support AMD Quark per-block FP8 for fused MoE layers
signals.text: ## Purpose `QuarkConfig._is_fp8_w8a8` already accepts per-block (128x128) FP8 weights, and #47972 added `QuarkW8A8Fp8PerBlock` so that **linear** layers can consume them. `QuarkW8A8Fp8MoEMethod` was never updated, so it still rejects the `per_block` qscheme: ``` ValueError: For FP8 Fused MoE layers, only per-tensor and per-channel scales for weights and activations are supported. Found per_block, per_group ``` The result is an asymmetry: for a Quark checkpoint whose routed experts are quantized per-block, every linear layer loads fine but the MoE layers cannot be built at all. ### Concrete case: the MTP layer of an MoE model Models that ship an MTP (multi-token prediction) draft layer make this asymmetry easy to see, because vLLM builds the MTP layer from the *same* decoder-layer class as the main model. For `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`, `Qwen3_5MultiTokenPredictor` instantiates `Qwen3_5DecoderLayer(layer_type="full_attention")`, which for an MoE config contains a complete `Qwen3NextSparseMoeBlock` with all 512 routed experts. Broken down by quantization path (`{i}` runs over `mtp_num_hidden_layers`, default 1): | Module | vLLM layer | Quant path | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `mtp.embed_tokens` | `VocabParallelEmbedding` | — | not quantized | | `mtp.fc` | `ColumnParallelLinear` | linear | supported (#47972) | | `mtp.norm`, `mtp.pre_fc_norm_hidden`, `mtp.pre_fc_norm_embedding` | `Qwen3_5RMSNorm` | — | not quantized | | `mtp.layers.{i}.self_attn.qkv_proj` | `QKVParallelLinear` | linear | supported (#47972) | | `mtp.layers.{i}.self_attn.o_proj` | `RowParallelLinear` | linear | supported (#47972) | | `mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.gate` | `ReplicatedLinear`, built with `quant_config=None` | — | never quantized | | `mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.shared_expert_gate` | `ReplicatedLinear`, built with `quant_config=None` | — | never quantized | | `mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.shared_expert.gate_up_proj` | `MergedColumnParallelLinear` | linear | supported (#47972) | | `mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.shared_expert.down_proj` | `RowParallelLinear` | linear | supported (#47972) | | **`mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.experts`** | **`RoutedExperts`** | **fused MoE** | **rejected — fixed by this PR** | `mtp.layers.{i}.mlp.experts` is the only module in the MTP stack that takes the fused-MoE path, and it is the only one that fails. It is also not a small module: with `hidden_size=4096`, `moe_intermediate_size=1024` and 512 experts it holds roughly 6.4B parameters, so leaving it unquantized is not a practical workaround. Two related details worth noting: - `mlp.gate` and `mlp.shared_expert_gate` are constructed with a hardcoded `quant_config=None`, so they are never quantized regardless of the Quark config. - When `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS` is enabled and the shared expert is not excluded from quantization, `Qwen3NextSparseMoeBlock` sets `shared_expert = None` and folds the shared expert into the routed-expert tensors, which moves those weights onto the fused-MoE path as well. ## Changes All changes are inside the existing `QuarkW8A8Fp8MoEMethod`, following the `BLOCK` strategy of `CompressedTensorsW8A8Fp8MoEMethod` rather than adding a new class: the weight, bias, input-scale and kernel-setup code is shared with the per-tensor and per-channel paths, and only the scale layout, the scale parameter name and a few flags differ. - `__init__`: accept `per_block`; read `block_size` from the weight config; use `kFp8Static128BlockSym` / `kFp8Dynamic128Sym` for backend selection; require dynamic activation quantization for per-block weights; select the scale parameter name (`weight_scale_inv` for per-block, `weight_scale` otherwise) the way `Fp8MoEMethod` already does. - `create_weights`: propagate `layer.weight_block_size`; validate that `intermediate_size_per_partition` is divisible by `block_n` (and by `block_k` when TP > 1) so misalignment fails at weight-creation time rather than silently producing wrong results in the kernel; allocate block-grid weight scales, register them as `w13_weight_scale_inv` / `w2_weight_scale_inv`, and tag them with `FusedMoeWeightScaleSupported.BLOCK` so `RoutedExperts.weight_loader` shards them on the block grid instead of per row. - `process_weights_after_loading`, `_setup_kernel` and `get_fused_moe_quant_config`: look the weight scales up through the selected name, and pass `block_shape` through to `make_fp8_moe_quant_config`. The per-tensor requantization loop and the per-channel `unsqueeze` in `process_weights_after_loading` remain guarded on `weight_qscheme`, and per-block weights require dynamic activations so the static input-scale branch is skipped. The only per-block change there is routing the fnuz normalization through the selected scale name, so per-block also works on MI300. The per-tensor and per-channel paths are unchanged: `block_shape` stays `None`, the scale parameters keep the `weight_scale` name, and the scale shapes are identical to before. ### Why the per-block scales are named `weight_scale_inv` Block-quantized checkpoints store their per-block scales as `weight_scale_inv` (the deepseek-v3 convention Quark follows), and `RoutedExperts.load_weights` derives the parameter name from the checkpoint tensor name by replacing only the module-path portion and carrying the suffix over verbatim — `...experts.0.down_proj.weight_scale_inv` resolves to `w2_weight_scale_inv`, with no aliasing step in between. Registering the scales under `w2_weight_scale` therefore made every per-block checkpoint fail to load: ``` AttributeError: Layer mtp.layers.0.mlp.experts has no parameter 'w2_weight_scale_inv' for checkpoint weight 'mtp.layers.0.mlp.experts.0.down_proj.weight_scale_inv' ``` Both names hold the same quantity (a dequantization multiplier, multiplied into the block-scaled GEMM), so this is purely a lookup-key mismatch and it always fails loudly. ## Test Plan Added to `tests/quantization/test_quark.py`: - `test_quark_w8a8_fp8_moe_per_block_requires_block_size` — a per-block weight config without `block_size` is rejected. - `test_quark_w8a8_fp8_moe_rejects_per_block_static_input` — static activations are rejected for per-block weights. - `test_quark_w8a8_fp8_moe_per_block_weight_shapes` — `w13`/`w2` weight and scale shapes, that the scales are registered under the `weight_scale_inv` name and not under `weight_scale`, and that both scales carry the `BLOCK` loader attribute. - `test_quark_w8a8_fp8_moe_per_block_rejects_misaligned_partition` — a partition size that is not a multiple of `block_n` fails during `create_weights`. ```bash pytest tests/quantization/test_quark.py -k per_block ``` ## Test Result Hardware: 1x MI355X (gfx950), ROCm. Checkpoint: `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` re-quantized with AMD Quark from `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8` into an NVFP4 backbone plus a per-block FP8 MTP layer (775 MTP modules per-block FP8, 10 kept in BF16 through `exclude`). This reproduces the asymmetry described above: the MTP `mlp.experts` module is per-block FP8 while the main model is NVFP4. ### Load and module routing TP=1, `speculative_config={"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 1}`: | Model | Module | Bound method | | --- | --- | --- | | target | 40 MoE layers | `QuarkNvfp4MoEMethod` | | drafter (MTP) | `mlp.experts.routed_experts` | `QuarkW8A8Fp8MoEMethod` | | drafter (MTP) | `self_attn.qkv_proj`, `self_attn.o_proj`, `shared_expert.{gate_up,down}_proj` | `QuarkLinearMethod` / `QuarkW8A8Fp8PerBlock` | | drafter (MTP) | `fc`, `mlp.gate`, `mlp.shared_expert_gate` | `UnquantizedLinearMethod` | Backends selected, with no fallbacks reported: ``` Selected TritonFp8BlockScaledMMKernel for QuarkW8A8Fp8PerBlock Using TRITON Fp8 MoE backend Using 'EMULATION' NvFp4 MoE backend ``` ### MTP acceptance `Draft acceptance rate: 94.7%-95.9%`, acceptance length 1.96 out of a maximum of 2 for `num_speculative_tokens=1`. This is the most direct evidence that the per-block expert weights and scales are loaded correctly: a scale mismatch drives acceptance towards 0. ### GSM8K `lm_eval` 5-shot over the full 1319 questions, chat template with thinking disabled: | Filter | exact_match | | --- | --- | | flexible-extract | 0.9629 ± 0.0052 | | strict-match | 0.9636 ± 0.0052 | ### Unit tests ``` pytest tests/quantization/test_quark.py -k per_block 8 passed, 35 deselected ``` This covers the four new MoE tests above together with the pre-existing per-block linear tests from #47972, which still pass.

signals.title: [CI][AMD] Improve Kubernetes failure diagnostics
signals.text: Collect Kubernetes-scoped AMD CI failure evidence while keeping the failing test log concise and immediately visible. - Resolve the current cgroup-v2 directory through `/proc/self/cgroup` and mountinfo instead of assuming node-level resource paths. - Capture pod, namespace, node, process limits, PID/RSS state, checkout/workspace/tmp/shared-memory mounts, device-node permissions, GPU health, and network timing. - Keep infrastructure diagnostics for CPU-only AMD jobs while skipping only GPU probes. - Write detailed evidence to `artifacts/amd-gpu-diagnostics/<job-id>/diagnostics.log` without duplicating it into the terminal log. - Reject artifact paths that escape the checkout or resolve through symlinks. - Print a dependency-free two-column Bash summary at the end, with no emoji shortcode or separate Buildkite diagnostics group. - Preserve `--- Test log` so the pytest failure and infrastructure summary remain in the same last-expanded section. - Let Buildkite perform the upload after the command exits; there is no custom uploader or upload timeout in the runner. Depends on [vllm-project/ci-infra#475](https://github.com/vllm-project/ci-infra/pull/475), which configures the exact `artifact_paths` pattern and should merge first.

signals.title: [ROCm] Give EngineCore cleanup grace after request abort
signals.text: AMD CI exposed a shutdown race where `shutdown_timeout=0` aborted requests as intended but also gave EngineCore no time to release ROCm resources before SIGKILL. This change preserves immediate request abort while giving the ROCm EngineCore process manager a bounded 60-second cleanup grace when both the configured and remaining process timeouts are zero. It keeps exhausted budgets for positive shutdown timeouts unchanged and extends the DP supervisor's outer deadline to cover the cleanup window. - The motivating failure is [AMD CI build 12007](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/12007/list?sid=019ffc53-a1ab-472f-8b77-7c52a7d6edc0&tab=output). - The final request completed successfully, but EngineCore was force-killed immediately and GPU memory remained at 11.72 GB for the full 120-second release wait. - The `LLM()` to `vllm_runner()` migration does not cover this path because these tests launch a real out-of-process `vllm serve` server. - Add a ROCm-only 60-second EngineCore process cleanup grace when both the configured request timeout and remaining process timeout are zero. - Keep `shutdown_timeout=0` inside EngineCore so in-flight requests are still aborted immediately. - Preserve exhausted positive shutdown deadlines instead of accidentally granting them a fresh cleanup window. - Extend the DP supervisor's outer wait budget so it does not kill the process tree before EngineCore cleanup can finish. - Add manager and DP supervisor regression coverage in the existing test files.
signals.author: AndreasKaratzas

signals.title: [CI] Harden RemoteVLLMServer GPU cleanup checks
signals.text: This PR is stacked on `akaratza_enginecore_shutdown` and hardens `RemoteVLLMServer` cleanup after a server exits. GPU baselines and cleanup waits are tracked per child-visible physical device, including overlapping multi-server scopes, so one leaked allocation cannot be hidden by a later aggregate baseline. Unavailable telemetry and timed-out cleanup now fail closed and retain affected-scope state until recovery can be verified. The test server's outer termination window also covers the EngineCore cleanup grace introduced by the first PR. - Prevent a teardown failure from ratcheting leaked VRAM into the next server's `_pre_server_gpu_memory` baseline. - Measure the physical devices selected by each child server's visibility environment on ROCm and CUDA. - Preserve parent-logical ordinal measurement on XPU, where `torch.xpu.mem_get_info` cannot consume physical or tile mask IDs. - Retain cleanup poison while intentionally concurrent servers make recovery unverifiable, and fail closed for unsafe partial coverage. - Merge partially overlapping scopes and use the earliest per-device baseline so a broader server cannot hide a leak behind an earlier sibling's allocation. - Keep GPU-less render-server tests outside GPU release accounting.

signals.title: [Bugfix][MRV2] Apply thinking budget to greedy requests
signals.text: ## Summary - Ensure Model Runner V2 does not take the no-logits-processing fast path when a scheduled request has an active thinking token budget. - Add focused GPU regression coverage for greedy sampling. ## Problem The Model Runner V2 sampler returns logits unchanged when `_requires_logits_processing()` is false. The predicate covered penalties, bad words, and non-default sampling, but did not cover `ThinkingBudgetState`. As a result, a greedy request with only `thinking_token_budget` enabled could bypass `apply_thinking_budget()` entirely. This made the budget ineffective even though the request state was configured correctly. This change includes active thinking-budget rows in the predicate. Requests without a thinking budget keep the existing fast path. ## Why this is not a duplicate The thinking-budget implementation was added in #46727, while the logits-processing fast path was introduced in #47711. This PR fixes the interaction between those changes. Immediately before submission, open-PR searches for `thinking_token_budget greedy` and `_requires_logits_processing` returned no matches. Broader sampler searches only returned speculative-decoding and frontend changes that do not modify this predicate. ## Tests - `uv run ruff check vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/sampler.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_thinking_budget.py` - Passed - `uv run ruff format --check vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/sampler.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_thinking_budget.py` - Passed - `uv run pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/sampler.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_thinking_budget.py` - Passed - `python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_thinking_budget.py -v` in the CUDA validation container - Baseline plus the new regression test: failed as expected because the end-reasoning logit remained `0.0` instead of `1.0e9` - Patched source: `13 passed` ## Model validation Validated on a task-owned GPU with ModelScope Qwen3.5-9B: - Greedy request without thinking returned the exact expected response. - Greedy request with `thinking_token_budget=5` stopped reasoning and produced the final answer successfully. - Existing service workloads on the other GPU were not modified. The GPU source-overlay baseline was `ac7509e2`. The submitted base is `8e6d8e4f`; the intervening upstream change only touches XPU/release files and does not overlap this sampler or test. Static checks were rerun on the submitted base. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used. The human submitter reviewed every changed line and the validation evidence and can defend the change end-to-end.

signals.title: [Bugfix] Fall back when zentorch import fails
signals.text: ## Purpose Fixes #52238. On AMD Zen CPU builds, a non-`ImportError` raised while importing zentorch currently escapes `cpu_platform_plugin`. Platform discovery then silently drops the CPU plugin and selects `UnspecifiedPlatform`. This change logs the underlying zentorch import failure and falls back to the standard `CpuPlatform`. A CPU-only regression test covers an incompatible shared library represented by `OSError`. I reviewed the issue comments and searched open PRs for both `#52238` and the zentorch CPU-platform import path. No overlapping open PR was found. AI assistance was used to develop and test this change. I reviewed every changed line of code and the regression test, and I understand and can defend the change end-to-end. ## Test Plan ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_zen_cpu_platform_detection.py -q .venv/bin/ruff check --ignore ISC004 vllm/platforms/__init__.py tests/test_zen_cpu_platform_detection.py .venv/bin/ruff format --check vllm/platforms/__init__.py tests/test_zen_cpu_platform_detection.py ``` The repository pre-commit hooks also ran during commit. ## Test Result - Before the implementation, the new regression test failed with the simulated `OSError: incompatible shared library` escaping platform detection. - After rebasing onto the latest `upstream/main`: `6 passed in 0.75s`. - Ruff check and format check passed. - All commit-time pre-commit hooks passed, including mypy and repository policy checks. - An additional platform-plugin test was attempted with its required dummy plugin installed. Its platform assertion passed, but the process later segfaulted in the existing macOS PyTorch global cleanup path at `torch.accelerator.memory.empty_host_cache`; this is outside the changed code. - Model evaluations were not run because this change does not affect model outputs, accuracy, or serving behavior. No documentation update is needed.

signals.title: [Model][Generative Recommendation] Add HSTU model support to vLLM
signals.text: ## Purpose This PR adds HSTU-based generative recommendation model support to vLLM. HSTU is a ranking model architecture designed for generative recommendation. Unlike traditional language models, HSTU does not autoregressively generate text tokens. Instead, it synchronously computes ranking scores for all candidate items in a request. The goal of this change is to enable generative recommendation models to reuse the existing vLLM and large-model serving ecosystem, including: - Hugging Face model and configuration loading. - vLLM model registration. - GPU model execution. - Attention backend selection. - Optimized CUDA operators. - Request batching and scheduling. - Asynchronous output handling. - CUDA Graph execution. - Future distributed inference and online serving infrastructure. Generative recommendation and large language models have several common characteristics. Both can be represented as sequence models, use embedding layers and transformer-style computation, and benefit from optimized attention kernels, GPU batching, asynchronous execution, and production-level model serving infrastructure. By integrating HSTU into vLLM, generative recommendation models can reuse the existing large-model ecosystem instead of maintaining an independent inference stack. ## Inference Paradigm Although HSTU and large language models share several model and runtime components, their inference semantics are different. | Aspect | Large language model | Generative recommendation model | | --- | --- | --- | | Decode behavior | Autoregressively generates one token at a time | Synchronously computes scores for all candidates in a request | | Model output | Vocabulary logits for the next token | One ranking score for each candidate item | | Sampling | Requires token sampling and token ID generation | Does not generate a sampled token | | Request progress | Continues until the requested number of tokens is generated | Completes after all candidate scores are returned | | Output format | Usually `[num_tokens, vocab_size]` | Packed candidate-score output | | Scheduler signal | Uses sampled token IDs to update request state | Uses candidate scores to complete the request | The default vLLM generation path is designed around language-model execution: 1. Run the model forward pass. 2. Produce vocabulary logits. 3. Invoke the token sampler. 4. Generate token IDs. 5. Update the request state. 6. Continue decoding until the request is finished. This flow cannot be directly reused for HSTU because HSTU produces candidate ranking scores rather than vocabulary logits. Passing HSTU outputs through the normal sampler would incorrectly interpret candidate scores as vocabulary logits and could produce invalid token IDs. Therefore, this PR adds a score-only execution path: 1. Run the HSTU forward pass. 2. Extract the score corresponding to each candidate item. 3. Convert candidate IDs and scores into `LogprobsTensors`. 4. Return the scores through `prompt_logprobs_dict`. 5. Skip the standard token sampler. 6. Skip generated-token state updates. 7. Complete the request after all candidate scores are returned. The scheduler is also updated to support score-only recommendation requests. A request can be completed after candidate scores are produced even when no `new_token_ids` are returned. ## Implementation Overview This PR contains five main categories of changes. ### 1. Model Structure and Model Registration Files: - `vllm/model_executor/models/hstu.py` - `vllm/model_executor/models/registry.py` - `tests/models/registry.py` Changes: - Add the HSTU model implementation. - Add HSTU embedding layers, transformer blocks, normalization layers, and prediction heads. - Register the HSTU model with vLLM. - Support Hugging Face HSTU model loading. - Add HSTU to the model registry test data. - Add model registration and model import coverage. ### 2. Model Configuration and Configuration Registration Files: - `vllm/transformers_utils/config.py` - `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/__init__.py` - `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/hstu.py` Changes: - Add HSTU-specific configuration classes. - Support HSTU model and task configuration fields. - Support `model_type = "hstu"`. - Convert HSTU configuration data from Hugging Face configuration files into the vLLM configuration representation. - Preserve compatibility with the existing vLLM configuration loading flow. ### 3. Model Operators and Operator Registration Files: - `vllm/v1/attention/backends/hstu_attn.py` - `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py` - `vllm/v1/attention/selector.py` Changes: - Add the HSTU attention backend. - Integrate the external HSTU variable-length attention operator. - Register the HSTU attention backend with vLLM. - Automatically select `HSTU_ATTN` for HSTU or generative recommendation models when no explicit backend is configured. - Preserve explicit attention backend configuration as the highest-priority option. - Validate unsupported attention combinations and return clear errors. - Pass per-request context and candidate metadata to the HSTU attention implementation. Automatic backend selection is only applied when the user has not explicitly selected an attention backend. This preserves the existing backend override behavior. ### 4. Model Runner V1 Adaptation File: - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` Changes: - Add generative recommendation metadata collection. - Add HSTU candidate score extraction. - Pass HSTU metadata through the forward context. - Bypass the standard token sampler for HSTU requests. - Return candidate scores through the prompt-logprobs output path. - Add recommendation-specific request completion handling. - Preserve the existing execution path for non-HSTU models. ### 5. Model Runner V2 Adaptation Files: - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/gr_state.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/async_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` Changes: - Add `GRState` for request-scoped generative recommendation state. - Store user IDs, candidate count, prompt token IDs, and request stage. - Move candidate score extraction from the Model Runner into `GRState`. - Convert packed HSTU outputs into `LogprobsTensors`. - Add asynchronous score output handling. - Return candidate scores through `prompt_logprobs_dict`. - Skip token sampling and token-state updates for HSTU requests. - Complete score-only requests in the scheduler when candidate scores are available. - Preserve the one-token early-return behavior required by generative recommendation inputs. ## Test Plan ### 1. Environment Setup The operator is installed inside the following NVIDIA PyTorch container:`nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.06-py3` Install the required system dependency:`apt update && apt install -y libxcb1` ### 2.HSTU Operator Installation and Validation The HSTU attention operator is provided by the NVIDIA `recsys-examples` repository. Clone the recsys-examples repository:`git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/recsys-examples.git && cd recsys-examples/corelib/hstu` For H20 and other Hopper-based devices, enter the corresponding device directory before compiling: `cd hopper` Install the HSTU operator:`Install the HSTU operator:` After the compilation completes successfully, validate the operator installation with: `python vllm/tests/models/generativemodel/test_hstu_op.py` ### 3.vLLM Installation Clone the vLLM repository:`git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git && cd vllm` Install the current vLLM source with CUDA support:`VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cuda pip install -v -e .` ### 4. HSTU Model Inference: After the HSTU changes are included in vLLM, run:`python vllm/tests/models/generativemodel/test_hstu.py` This test validates: * HSTU model loading. * HSTU configuration loading. * HSTU model registration. * HSTU attention backend initialization. * HSTU forward execution. * Candidate score extraction. * Candidate ID and score formatting. * Score-only execution without token sampling. * Recommendation request completion. * Model Runner integration. * CUDA Graph execution. ### 5. Model Registry and Hugging Face Loading Run the model registry tests:`pytest -q tests/models/test_registry.py -k HSTUForCausalLM` This validates that: * HSTUForCausalLM is registered. * The HSTU model class can be imported. * Hugging Face model metadata is available. * The HSTU configuration can be loaded. * The vLLM model registry can resolve the HSTU model. ## Test Result ### HSTU Operator The test returned like: ```text Input q shape: torch.Size([40, 4096]) Output shape: torch.Size([40, 4096]) Run success ``` ### HSTU Model Inference The test returned candidate IDs and their corresponding ranking scores. A truncated example of the output is: ```text Request 0: 12676:0.6602 47052:0.5078 45082:0.4336 79131:0.3984 34671:0.4844 5695:0.4570 95647:0.1777 60217:0.5273 70284:0.4258 16361:0.4238 Request 1: 8023:0.4863 24460:0.6094 ... ``` Each line follows the format:`Each line follows the format:` The output confirms that HSTU synchronously computes the scores of all candidates for a request and returns the scores through the generative recommendation output path. The test also confirms that: * HSTU outputs are not passed through the standard vocabulary sampler. * No artificial generated token IDs are produced. * Requests complete after candidate scores are returned. * Candidate scores are returned through prompt_logprobs_dict. * Both Model Runner V1 and Model Runner V2 execution paths are supported. * The HSTU attention backend is initialized and executed successfully. * CUDA Graph execution works in the validated CUDA environment. ### Model Registration and Hugging Face Loading The model registration and Hugging Face loading tests passed. HSTUForCausalLM can be resolved and imported through the vLLM model registry, and the HSTU configuration can be loaded from the Hugging Face model configuration. ### Scheduler and Score-Only Execution The scheduler validation passed for score-only recommendation requests. A recommendation request is correctly completed after candidate scores are produced, even when no new_token_ids are returned. The standard token sampling path is skipped for HSTU requests, and no regular language-model token state update is performed. ### Attention Backend Selection When no explicit attention backend is configured, the HSTU model automatically selects HSTU_ATTN. When an explicit attention backend is configured, the user-provided backend remains authoritative and is not overridden by the HSTU automatic selection logic. ### Current Scope and Limitations This initial integration focuses on bringing HSTU into the vLLM model and serving ecosystem. The current implementation assumes: * Prompt lengths are consistent across users. * Candidate lengths are consistent across users. * HSTU and non-HSTU requests are not mixed in the same batch. * Candidate scores are produced during an unchunked prefill. * Pipeline parallelism is not used. * PD-separated HSTU execution is not supported yet. * KV-cache-based or paged HSTU attention is not supported yet. * request_stage = 1 is not supported. * Each recommendation prompt contains at least one context/candidate pair. These limitations can be addressed in follow-up work after the basic HSTU execution path and serving interface are established.

signals.title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Isolate tiering shutdown failures
signals.text: # [Bugfix][KV Offload] Continue tier cleanup after shutdown failures ## Purpose `TieringOffloadingManager.shutdown()` tears down secondary tiers before the CPU primary tier. Previously, an ordinary exception from one secondary tier immediately aborted the loop, skipping all later secondary tiers and the primary tier. The primary tier owns the memoryview and `SharedOffloadRegion` cleanup for the scheduler-side mmap. This change makes normal shutdown follow the same best-effort resource-ownership policy already used for tiering initialization cleanup: every secondary tier is attempted in configuration order, then the primary tier is attempted regardless of earlier ordinary exceptions. Failures remain observable through `logger.exception`, including the secondary tier index, configured tier type, and implementation class. The change intentionally does not catch `BaseException`, retry shutdown calls, or change scheduler and backend behavior. This reduces the graceful-shutdown risk that a secondary teardown exception prevents the primary mmap owner from releasing its resources. It does not address `SIGKILL`, process crashes, or a shutdown call that blocks forever. The most relevant in-tree failure surface is P2P teardown, which releases NIXL and ZMQ resources and can surface ordinary backend exceptions. The same is true for externally configured secondary tiers. File-system and object tiers handle most cleanup errors internally; a blocked lookup or I/O thread is a hang rather than an exception and is outside this change's scope. ## Why this is not a duplicate The duplicate-work search found no open PR that implements per-secondary-tier failure isolation in `TieringOffloadingManager.shutdown()`. This is distinct from #51622, which centralizes cleanup ordering for the CPU worker's GPU-to-CPU and CPU-to-GPU handlers. This change covers the scheduler-side tiering manager and ensures secondary-tier failure cannot skip the primary tier's mmap cleanup. ## Test Plan ```bash .venv/bin/python -m compileall -q \ vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py uvx --from pre-commit pre-commit run --files \ vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py \ PR_DESCRIPTION.md git diff --check ``` ## Test Result - `compileall`: passed. - `pre-commit`: all applicable hooks passed. - `git diff --check`: passed. - Model evaluation: not applicable; this only changes shutdown cleanup control flow. ## AI Assistance AI assistance was used for repository inspection, implementation, and this PR description. The human submitter must review every changed line and run the validation they consider appropriate before submitting.

signals.title: [ROCm][Perf] Enable fused KDA decode on gfx942 (MI325X)
signals.text: ## Purpose PR #50654 added the fused Kimi-K3 KDA decode kernel (`csrc/libtorch_stable/kimi_k3/fused_kda_decode_kernel_rocm.cu`), but gated it to gfx950 (MI355X) in two places, so it never activates on gfx942 (MI325X): - **Build gate** — `CMakeLists.txt` filtered the HIP source to `gfx950` only, so the kernel was not compiled and `VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_DECODE` (and therefore `torch.ops._C.fused_kda_decode`) was never defined on a gfx942-only build. - **Runtime gate** — `is_fused_kda_decode_supported()` in `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_decode.py` ended with `return on_gfx950()`. This change extends both gates to gfx942 as well, so MI325X can take the fused decode path instead of falling back to the three-launch Triton path. The kernel body is unchanged. It uses only CDNA-common primitives — wave64, DPP row/quad permutes (`quad_perm`, `row_half_mirror`, `row_mirror`), `__builtin_nontemporal_load/store`, and bf16 intrinsics — with no MFMA / FP8 / gfx950-only paths, so no source-level changes are required for gfx942. LDS use is ~2.8 KiB/block and register pressure ~130 VGPR, both well within CDNA3 limits. ## Changes - `CMakeLists.txt`: HIP arch filter `gfx950` -> `gfx942|gfx950` (and comment). - `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_decode.py`: gate `on_gfx950()` -> `on_gfx950() or on_gfx942()`. - `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_decode.py`: extend the module skip guard from gfx950 to gfx942 / gfx950 so the correctness suite runs on MI325X. All other backends and the CUDA path are unchanged; the shape/dtype/head-count guards in `is_fused_kda_decode_supported()` are unchanged. ## Performance The kernel-level win is large, but the end-to-end win on MI325X is currently small: the Kimi-K3 decode step is dominated by the MXFP4 MoE (int4) and the MLA attention plus the TP8 collectives, which dwarf the KDA linear-attention block. The fusion removes ~66 us of per-layer kernel time (mostly launch overhead), but that is a small fraction of today's total per-token cost. It should become more visible once #50817 (MXFP4 MoE Triton a16w4 for gfx942) lands and shrinks the dominant MoE cost — the fixed KDA saving then represents a larger share of a smaller decode step. ### End-to-end (tp8, 256-in / 256-out, max-concurrency 4) | Metric | Triton fallback | Fused KDA | Delta | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Mean TPOT (ms) | 425.95 | 422.66 | -0.77% | | P99 TPOT (ms) | 427.64 | 424.19 | -0.81% | | Output tok/s | 9.29 | 9.36 | +0.75% | | Mean TTFT (ms) | 1577.24 | 1574.03 | -0.20% (flat) | TTFT is unchanged, as expected for a decode-only kernel. ### Per-layer kernel sequence (torch profiler medians, us) Baseline runs the KDA decode as ~16 separate kernels per layer — the conv1d update, the recurrent delta-rule step, and the gated output RMSNorm decomposed into a chain of launch-overhead-bound (~4 us floor) elementwise ops. Fused collapses all of them into a single kernel: | # | Baseline kernel | us | Fused kernel | us | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | _causal_conv1d_update_kernel | 5.01 | kda_decode_fusion_kernel<true, 12, true, true, true> | 7.77 | | 2 | fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode_kernel | 6.45 | | | | 3 | __amd_rocclr_copyBuffer | 4.37 | | | | 4 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.41 | | | | 5 | pow (tensor, scalar) | 4.41 | | | | 6 | reduce Mean | 5.01 | | | | 7 | add | 4.45 | | | | 8 | rsqrt | 4.37 | | | | 9 | mul | 4.21 | | | | 10 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.17 | | | | 11 | mul | 4.21 | | | | 12 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.45 | | | | 13 | sigmoid | 5.05 | | | | 14 | mul | 4.33 | | | | 15 | float32->bfloat16 copy | 4.49 | | | | 16 | __amd_rocclr_copyBuffer | 4.57 | | | | | **total (16 kernels)** | **~73.96** | **total (1 kernel)** | **7.77** | ~9.5x less kernel time for the KDA decode block (~74 -> 7.8 us/layer). The `12` template arg is 12 heads/rank (96 KDA heads at TP8). Across the model's KDA layers (~69 per the kernel header) that is ~4.6 ms/token of raw kernel time removed, in the same ballpark as the ~3.3 ms/token TPOT drop measured above (the remainder overlaps with other work). ## Not a duplicate - `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "KDA decode gfx942"` - `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "fused_kda_decode MI325"` ## Test Plan Run on an MI325X (gfx942) box after building with gfx942 in the arch list: 1. Build compiles the kernel and registers the op: `python -c "import torch, vllm; print(hasattr(torch.ops._C, 'fused_kda_decode'))"` -> expect `True`. 2. Kernel correctness: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_decode.py -v` 3. Model accuracy (output-affecting change) — serve Kimi-K3 on MI325X and run gsm8k, compared against the Triton fallback path: `make gsm8k` 4. Decode latency / throughput before vs after (fused vs Triton fallback): `make bench-kda-mi325` ## Test Result - Op registered: **True** on the gfx942 build (`hasattr(torch.ops._C, "fused_kda_decode")`); the fused kernel appears in the trace (see Performance). - Latency/throughput: **-0.77% mean TPOT**, +0.75% output tok/s - gsm8k (fused vs Triton): **parity** — both 1.00 exact_match on flexible-extract and strict-match (5-shot, limit=100, stderr 0). The fused kernel matches the Triton fallback exactly. - `test_amd_kda_decode.py`: **12/12 passed** on MI325X (gfx942) — fused output matches the Triton reference across heads {12, 24, 96} x tokens {1, 7, 128}, plus the null-slot, no-output-norm, and padding edge cases. ## Checklist - [x] Compiles for gfx942 (kernel present in the .so with gfx942 codegen) - [x] `test_amd_kda_decode.py` passes on MI325X (12/12) - [x] gsm8k parity with the Triton path - [x] AI assistance used (see below) ## AI assistance This change was drafted with AI assistance (Claude). A human must review every line and run the build, tests, and eval on MI325X hardware before merge; the correctness and accuracy results above are not yet filled in.

signals.title: [Bugfix][Ray] Strip brackets from IPv6 node IP for MessageQueue connect_ip
signals.text: ## Purpose On IPv6-only clusters, `ray.util.get_node_ip_address()` can return an IPv6 address wrapped in brackets (e.g. `[fe80::1]`; a documented Ray behavior). `RayExecutorV2` passed this value straight into `MessageQueue(connect_ip=...)` at two call sites: - `RayWorkerProc._init_message_queues` (`worker_response_mq`) - `RayExecutorV2._init_executor` (`rpc_broadcast_mq`) Inside `MessageQueue`, the branch that enables IPv6 is guarded by `is_valid_ipv6_address(connect_ip)`, which is backed by `ipaddress.IPv6Address(...)`. That parser **rejects the bracketed form**: ``` ::1 -> valid [::1] -> INVALID <- what Ray returns fe80::1 -> valid [fe80::1] -> INVALID <- what Ray returns ``` Consequently `remote_addr_ipv6` stayed `False`, the ZMQ socket never had `IPV6` enabled, and the subsequent `bind`/`connect` to the bracketed address failed. The exported `Handle` also carried `remote_addr_ipv6=False`, so remote readers connected without IPv6 support and failed too. ## Fix Normalize the Ray node IP by stripping brackets before handing it to `MessageQueue`. `MessageQueue` then re-brackets the bare address itself (its existing `connect_ip = f"[{connect_ip}]"` path). This keeps the "connect_ip is a bare address" contract that `shm_broadcast` already assumes. IPv4 and already-bare IPv6 addresses are unaffected — `.strip("[]")` only removes leading/trailing brackets, which never appear in an IPv4 address. ## Why this is not a duplicate - No open PR or issue addresses bracketed-IPv6 `connect_ip` in `RayExecutorV2` (searched `get_node_ip_address`, `connect_ip ipv6`, `ray_executor_v2 ipv6`). - #50969 also touches `ray_executor_v2.py`, but it fixes the **TCPStore port bind TOCTOU race** (`_select_tcpstore_port` / `distributed_init_method`). It does not touch the `MessageQueue` `connect_ip` values and is an orthogonal change. - #18986 (closed) concerned data-parallel IPv6 host recognition, a different code path. ## Test Plan / Results Behavior of the normalization + downstream validity check, verified locally: ``` '[fe80::1]' -> 'fe80::1' is_valid_ipv6=True 'fe80::1' -> 'fe80::1' is_valid_ipv6=True '[::1]' -> '::1' is_valid_ipv6=True '::1' -> '::1' is_valid_ipv6=True '10.0.0.1' -> '10.0.0.1' is_valid_ipv6=False (unchanged) '127.0.0.1' -> '127.0.0.1' is_valid_ipv6=False (unchanged) ``` Lint (pre-commit) on the changed file: ```bash pre-commit run ruff-check --files vllm/v1/executor/ray_executor_v2.py # Passed pre-commit run ruff-format --files vllm/v1/executor/ray_executor_v2.py # Passed ``` Model evaluation is not applicable: this change only affects startup address normalization for the control-plane MessageQueue and does not alter model execution or outputs. ## AI disclosure AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation, and drafting. The human submitter has reviewed every changed line and can defend the change and tests end-to-end.

signals.title: [LoRA] Avoid false target matches for unsupported module types
signals.text: LoRA target matching previously relied only on module-name suffixes. This can produce false matches when modules with the same suffix have different runtime types. This behavior was reported in [this Gemma 4 LoRA test](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42662#issuecomment-4830505389). The vision tower emitted warnings for modules such as: - `vision_tower.encoder.layers.0.self_attn.o_proj` - `vision_tower.encoder.layers.0.mlp.down_proj` These modules are `Gemma4ClippableLinear` containers and cannot be wrapped directly. However, LoRA was successfully loaded into their inner linear layers: - `vision_tower.encoder.layers.0.self_attn.o_proj.linear` - `vision_tower.encoder.layers.0.mlp.down_proj.linear` The warnings were therefore false alarms caused by suffix-only matching. This PR passes the runtime module instance to `is_supported_lora_module` and checks both the module-name suffix and its actual type. Supported inner linear layers continue to receive LoRA, while unsupported container modules with the same suffix are skipped. ## Purpose ## Test Plan ## Test Result --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [Kernel][Model] Add manual CUDA RoPE KV-cache fusion for Llama
signals.text: ## Purpose Address the NVIDIA CUDA/Llama portion of #43503 and advance the manual-fusion migration described in #43224. This change adds a stable CUDA operation that writes rotary-embedded Q into a caller-owned output and writes rotary-embedded K plus V directly into the paged KV cache. Llama invokes it explicitly before the existing attention PIECEWISE split. On the supported non-DCP FlashAttention decoder path, attention consumes Q plus cached K/V, so raw K/V are no longer forwarded after the update. Unsupported rotary, attention, cache, quantization, DCP, and sharing cases keep the existing RoPE/cache-update/attention sequence. ROCm keeps the existing `RopeKVCacheFusionPass`; CUDA uses the model-visible call site and no longer registers that pass. This overlaps #43355 but is materially different from its current pass-owned Step 1. This PR includes the manual Llama owner requested by #43503, caller-owned-Q and cache-only-K/V dataflow, separate RoPE/cache token domains, RoPE-only behavior without slot metadata, NHD/HND stride support, and production graph and serving qualification. The implementation is independent: #43355 is not in this branch's ancestry, its code is not incorporated here, and the semantic oracle and CUDA implementation predate discovery of that PR. #43355 was inspected only to make the required duplicate-work comparison explicit. The dynamic qualification below was collected from the same source patch before its conflict-free rebase, at `faade21ae` on vLLM base `63a9a5010`. The submitted commit is based on `cdc4824a2`; it has the same source patch under stable patch-id, and range-diff shows only the subsequently authorized DCO trailer. The intervening KV-packing change leaves ordinary FlashAttention on the identity `customize_spec`, so the supported request-time path is unchanged. ## Test Plan - Compare the native operation with the incumbent path across MHA/GQA/MQA, NeoX/interleaved, full/partial RoPE, NHD/HND, short and negative slot mapping, FP16/BF16, and FP8 cache cases. - Exercise missing-slot fallback and CUDA/ROCm pass registration. - Compile real `VllmBackend` graph composition with the manual node before attention. - Run Compute Sanitizer memcheck, racecheck, and synccheck over the focused launches. - Exercise the V2 PIECEWISE CUDA Graph route and a paired fixed TinyLlama serving A/B. - Run targeted Ruff, formatting, Typos, Markdown, SPDX, import, CUDA-policy, and diff checks. ## Test Result - The focused pytest selection completed with 6 passed; the shape and layout coverage is listed in the test plan above. - Memcheck reported 0 errors; racecheck reported 0 hazards, errors, or warnings; synccheck reported 0 errors. - The CUDA Graph route recorded 22 fused calls during capture and 0 during 63 request replays; fused and unfused output tokens matched. - On an RTX 5090 with driver 595.71.05, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, and CUDA 13.0, BF16 TinyLlama with 64 output tokens completed two balanced rounds with two warmups and five samples per arm. Paired `unfused/fused` ratios were 1.0505 and 1.0237 (median 1.0371); aggregate medians were 211.634 ms fused and 221.877 ms unfused. - Retained longer operator controls measured about 1.50x at TinyLlama's head-64 shape and 1.57--1.62x across head-128 decode cases. A current-main benchmark CLI smoke also completed successfully. This PR includes non-trivial assistance from OpenAI Codex. I reviewed every changed line, validated the behavior end to end, and take responsibility for the contribution. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose and related issues are described. - [x] The test plan includes the commands and scenarios run. - [x] The test and model-evaluation results are reported. - [x] The design documentation is updated. </details>
