signal.title: [Refactor] Simplify B12X linear kernels and warmup
signal.text: ## Summary - consolidate the B12X scaled-MM linear implementations and tests - replace per-format model scans with shared warmup units - simplify internal B12X lifecycle checks - add a DGX Spark nightly job for the B12X linear, warmup, and block-FP8 tests This is a refactor only; no kernel selection or supported-format change is intended. ## Duplicate work No open PR duplicates this change. Related open B12X PRs cover attention or MoE, not the linear refactor. ## Testing - `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' PYTHONPATH=. /home/mgoin/code/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/kernels/test_b12x_linear.py tests/model_executor/test_b12x_warmup.py tests/kernels/quantization/test_block_fp8.py -k b12x -q` — 35 passed, 4 hardware tests skipped - parsed and checked the new Buildkite job definition - changed-file pre-commit hooks — passed - `git diff --check` — passed The four real block-FP8 cases require SM12x hardware and are covered by the new DGX Spark nightly job. No model evaluation was run because this refactor does not change model outputs, accuracy, or serving behavior. AI assistance from OpenAI Codex was used. This is a draft; the human submitter must review every changed line and understand and defend the change before marking it ready.

signal.title: [Model][Perf] Enable fused KDA decode for Ling-3.0 (H=32)
signal.text: > [!IMPORTANT] > This PR is intentionally a Draft. Tensorizer compatibility and human > verification remain before it is marked Ready. ## Summary Ling-3.0-flash has 35 KDA layers and 32 local heads at TP=1, but the NVIDIA fused KDA decode kernel did not support H=32. This PR adds that specialization and enables it for `BailingMoeV3KimiDeltaAttention`, combining the convolution update, recurrent KDA update, and gated RMSNorm into one decode kernel. Unsupported configurations continue to use the existing implementation. I searched open vLLM issues and PRs for Ling/Bailing, KDA decode, and H=32 CUDA fusion; none implements this specialization together with the Bailing integration. ## Implementation - Add H=32 validation and dispatch to the existing stable-ABI CUDA kernel. - Share fused-path eligibility checks between Kimi-K3 and Bailing. - Add a separate Bailing fused-decode op. Prefill, speculative decoding, and unsupported configurations retain the original path. - Refresh the kernel-layout convolution and norm-weight buffers after loading and layerwise reload. - Fix full-CUDA-graph NULL-row handling for both the existing H=12/24/48/96 specializations and the new H=32 path: padded rows produce zero output and no longer write concurrently to reserved slot 0. ## Validation The same test suites pass on both tested architectures: | GPU | `test_kda.py` | `test_bailing_moe_v3.py` | | --- | ---: | ---: | | RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120) | 54 passed | 6 passed | | NVIDIA H20 (sm90) | 54 passed | 6 passed | ```bash cd /root/r23/vllm-main PYTHONPATH=/root/r23/runtime_overlay:/root/r23/vllm-main \ /root/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py PYTHONPATH=/root/r23/runtime_overlay:/root/r23/vllm-main \ /root/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/models/test_bailing_moe_v3.py /root/vllm/.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ csrc/libtorch_stable/kimi_k3/fused_kda_decode_kernel.cu \ vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/kda_decode.py \ vllm/model_executor/models/bailing_moe_v3.py \ vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kda.py \ tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py \ tests/models/test_bailing_moe_v3.py # all hooks passed ``` The tests cover H=32 correctness, repeated state updates, eager/CUDA-graph replay, padded rows, and post-load buffer refresh. On H20, an FP64 operator oracle also showed lower numerical error for the fused H=32 path in the tested synthetic cases (B=1-128): output RMS error was `6.7e-5`-`8.8e-5` versus `1.37e-4`-`1.74e-4` for the fallback, and final recurrent-state max error after 64 decode steps was `4.28e-8` versus `4.66e-4`. This is kernel-level numerical evidence, not a model-quality or universal equivalence claim. ### Model evaluation GSM8K was evaluated on the full FP4 checkpoint using 500 fixed questions with 5-shot greedy decoding on the RTX PRO 6000: | Arm | Correct | Accuracy | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Base | 465 / 500 | 93.0% | | Fused | 461 / 500 | 92.2% | The exact two-sided McNemar result is `p=0.424`. This run does not detect a statistically significant difference, but it does not establish equivalence. Both arms used the same UE8M0-to-FP32 scale-loading workaround, which is orthogonal to this diff. ## Performance Each cell is an independent within-device patched-fallback-to-fused comparison. Both platforms used a balanced six-process schedule with 3 warmups and 15 samples per slot and a fixed 64-token decode workload. | Mode | RTX PRO 6000 (sm120) | NVIDIA H20 (sm90) | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Eager / B1 | **-25.717% (1.346x)** | **-24.820% (1.330x)** | | FULL CG / B1 | **-4.246% (1.044x)** | **-4.215% (1.044x)** | | FULL CG / B8 | **-6.113% (1.065x)** | **-8.039% (1.087x)** | All 30/30 paired wall-time samples improved in every case on both GPUs. The H20 run used a 12-layer random-weight proxy with 10 KDA layers while preserving Ling's production KDA geometry (H=32, head dimension 128, convolution width 4). It validates the sm90 path and performance direction, but is not an absolute cross-GPU or model-quality comparison. On H20, the fused kernel replaced a measured 13-launch convolution/recurrent/ norm subset with one launch and was 1.41-2.39x faster under CUDA Graph and 1.56-8.61x faster in eager mode for B=1-256. The NULL-row fix also affects existing H=12/24/48/96 paths. H20 testing found no measurable overhead without padding; at B=128 with 25%, 50%, and 75% padding, H=48/H=96 kernel latency improved by about 1.31x, 2.35-2.38x, and 4.58-4.95x respectively. ## Scope and Draft status - This is decode-only; there is no prefill or TTFT performance claim. - The Bailing fast path requires TP=1/local H=32, head dimension 128, convolution width 4, BF16 activation/state, and no speculative tokens. - Unsupported configurations retain the original path. - Before Ready, native `TensorizerLoader` round trips and old artifacts missing the new shadow buffers need a safe refresh or fallback. - The human submitter must review every changed line and verify the reported tests and results before marking the PR Ready. ## AI assistance disclosure OpenAI Codex/GPT models assisted with code review, refactoring, test and benchmark development, result analysis, and drafting this description. **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>**

signal.title: [Kernel] ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs for faster Mamba2 speculative decode
signal.text: ## Background This is the third sub-PR split from the larger ReplaySSM draft PR (#47576), which contains the complete Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet implementation for both standard and speculative decode. The first sub-PR, Mamba2 standard decode (#48018), landed as `866fea2b9`, so this PR is based directly on `main` and adds Mamba2 speculative decode. ReplaySSM caches recent SSM inputs instead of writing the recurrent state back to HBM on every step. It is a collaboration between Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA, and the full derivation and figures are in the [blog post](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/). AI assistance was used for parts of this work, and the authors have reviewed every changed line. ## Core concept To roll back rejected drafts, vLLM's native Mamba2 spec path keeps a separate recurrent state snapshot for every draft token, so a step with `T = 1 + num_speculative_tokens` tokens writes `T` full `(nheads, head_dim, dstate)` states and reads one back. Cost grows linearly in `T`, which is why the native path can fall below plain standard decode at serving batch. ReplaySSM replaces the snapshots with one checkpoint state plus a small circular buffer of the per-step SSM inputs (`x`, `dt`, `B`). This changes three things: - Rollback is a cursor move. - Verification is parallel. Every draft output is computed from the same checkpoint in one GEMM, which removes the length-`T` serial recurrence. - Traffic is flat in `T`. The full state is materialized only on a periodic flush. In most of the steps (non-flush steps), no state is store back to HBM. The table below is the measured per-step DRAM traffic at bs256, Nemotron-3-Super-120B geometry, fp32 state, cold L2. Baseline traffic scales with `T`; ReplaySSM does not. | T | baseline GB | ReplaySSM non-flush GB | ReplaySSM flush GB | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 2 | 3.18 | 1.18 | 2.21 | | 4 | 5.35 | 1.20 | 2.23 | | 6 | 7.53 | 1.22 | 2.26 | | 8 | 9.73 | 1.23 | 2.30 | ## What this PR adds Everything is behind a flag. With ReplaySSM disabled, the decode path is unchanged. - The Mamba2 cached spec kernel `selective_state_update_replayssm_spec`, its device-side cursor helpers `commit_replayssm_spec` and `reset_replayssm_spec_cursors`, and their hardware-keyed launch configs in `replayssm_config.py`. - One new config flag, `--use-replayssm-spec`. It reuses `--replayssm-buffer-len` from #48018 for the history block `B` (default 16). It requires speculative decoding, `--mamba-cache-mode none` and the Triton mamba backend, and is mutually exclusive with `--use-replayssm`. - Integration. The Mamba2 mixer dispatches to the kernel under the flag, the metadata builder owns the block-keyed ring cursors, and the state-shape and state-dtype calculators size the `post_conv_cache` and `dt_cache` ring on the paged state. The conv path reuses vLLM's `causal_conv1d_update` unchanged, with rollback handled by its existing `num_accepted_tokens` shift. - A throughput benchmark, `benchmarks/replayssm/e2e_spec_decode_throughput.py`, which runs standard decode, native spec and ReplaySSM spec on GSM8K in separate subprocesses. ## Design notes ### When the ring flushes `B` is the maximum history the ring carries into a verify step (default 16). A verify step consumes a whole window at once, so the flush rule is `history + T > B`: flush whenever the next window would not fit. That guarantees every verify step has room for a full `T`-draft window, so a window never truncates. The ring holds `L = B + T` logical slots, rounded up to `next_pow2(L)` so wraparound indexing is a bit mask rather than a modulo. ### Paged cache layout The ring caches and the checkpoint live inside the paged KV block, appended as two extra tensors on the baseline `(conv, ssm)` state, for four tensors total. They stay live across decode steps, so they must sit in HBM between launches, and appending them onto the paged state reuses vLLM's per-request block allocation and block-table indexing directly. Only `x` and `B` are cached, while `C` is read from the conv output each step. `dt` is always stored in fp32; the state checkpoint follows `mamba_ssm_cache_dtype` and the input ring follows the activation dtype. Only the small per-block cursors live outside the page: `write_pos` (committed history offset), `post_origin` (the window's circular base) and `is_flush`, all shaped `(num_gpu_blocks,)` and indexed by physical block id. One design difference from #48018 (feedback welcome): Standard decode caches x, dt, and B as three head-major tensors, while speculative decode caches dt together with a single token-major post_conv_cache. Although the layouts differ, they represent the same three logical caches. The launcher simply slices post_conv_cache into x and B views, which the kernel receives as separate strided pointers. The layout is chosen based on how the cache is written. Standard decode appends one token at a time after the tensors have already been split, so storing separate head-major tensors is natural. Speculative decode, on the other hand, scatters an entire T-token window from causal_conv1d_update, whose output is packed in channel-last order. Keeping the cache in that layout turns the scatter into a simple strided copy instead of requiring a transpose into three differently shaped tensors. ### CUDA graphs and continuous batching The number of accepted tokens is only known after the step's forward and sampling, so `commit_replayssm_spec` runs at the *next* build and does two jobs at once: it commits the previous step's acceptance (`write_pos += num_accepted`, or advances `post_origin` on a flush) and decides this step's `is_flush`. Folding it into the next build rather than issuing a separate post-forward launch keeps every cursor update on-device, so there is no device-to-host sync on `num_accepted_tokens`. Every step issues both a verify launch and a flush launch, each compiled for its single role with `is_flush` as a compile-time constant, and every row early-exits from the launch that does not apply to it. Which rows flush is routed on-device by the flags. ### Entering decode A request's ring must start empty on its first verify step, including when it lands on a recycled block. The builder derives that from `replayssm_decode_base`, the context length recorded at admission by #48018: a row resets when `num_computed == decode_base`. Because `decode_base` is re-anchored when a request is readmitted, a preempted and recomputed request re-fires the reset and does not inherit its old cursors. One row needs more care. A final single-token prompt chunk is reclassified as a decode (full-cudagraph dispatch is shape-based, so leaving it a prefill lets a decode graph replay against a stale cursor), which puts it one token short of `decode_base`. Those rows reset the ring and are forced to flush in the same step. Without the forced flush they would append a token to a freshly emptied ring without advancing the checkpoint, and the next step's reset would drop it. ## Results Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B on one B300, TP1, fp32 SSM state, `B=16`, MTP drafter, greedy GSM8K with `ignore_eos`, CUDA graphs on. `T = 1 + num_speculative_tokens`. Produced with `benchmarks/replayssm/e2e_spec_decode_throughput.py`. ### End-to-end throughput ReplaySSM spec over native spec, NVFP4 checkpoint: | bs | T=2 | T=4 | T=6 | T=8 | |---:|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0.88x | 1.04x | 1.05x | 1.17x | | 32 | 1.15x | 1.13x | 1.03x | 1.38x | | 128 | 1.24x | 1.29x | 1.48x | 1.90x | | 256 | 1.34x | 1.77x | 1.91x | 2.09x | | 512 | 1.78x | 1.85x | 2.11x | 2.34x | ReplaySSM spec over standard (no-spec) decode: | bs | T=2 | T=4 | T=6 | T=8 | |---:|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 1.36x | 1.88x | 1.89x | 1.81x | | 32 | 1.52x | 1.85x | 1.74x | 1.73x | | 128 | 1.67x | 1.92x | 1.92x | 1.64x | | 256 | 1.88x | 2.13x | 1.97x | 1.73x | | 512 | 2.11x | 2.16x | 2.12x | 1.83x | Compared with native spec decoding, ReplaySSM speedup grow with `T` since native spec decoding stores `T` state snapshots per step. Compared with standard decode, ReplaySSM provides 1.8x to 2.2x speedup across all batch sizes (acceptance provides the gain even at small batch.) ### Acceptance length At bs256, `B=16`: | T | native spec | ReplaySSM | |---:|---:|---:| | 2 | 1.95 | 1.95 | | 4 | 3.43 | 3.44 | | 6 | 4.24 | 4.20 | | 8 | 4.40 | 4.44 | ### Kernel-level Isolated per-kernel latency on the Super-120B geometry, fp32 state, cold L2, `ncu` at base clock. The baseline is `_selective_scan_update_kernel` at its swept-best config, with its shipped default config in parentheses (no tuned config JSON ships for B300, so the engine actually runs the default). Baseline microseconds at bs256, growing linearly in `T`: | T | tuned (default) | |---:|---| | 2 | 611 (960) | | 4 | 1110 (1690) | | 6 | 1620 (2450) | | 8 | 2140 (3270) | ReplaySSM remains nearly flat at bs256: the verify kernel is 264 to 314 us across T=2 to 8, the flush kernel 678 to 707 us, and the fused scatter 21 to 29 us. Amortizing over the exact flush cadence, and taking the worst-case acceptance `a = T` at every step, gives the speedup against the tuned baseline: | T | bs 32 | bs 128 | bs 256 | bs 512 | |---:|---|---|---|---| | 2 | 1.17x | 1.53x | 1.59x | 1.67x | | 4 | 1.84x | 2.21x | 2.33x | 2.41x | | 6 | 2.30x | 2.76x | 2.86x | 2.95x | | 8 | 2.98x | 3.54x | 3.75x | 3.86x | Small batch is not the target regime: the SSM kernel is latency-bound there, and in a hybrid model the step is dominated by the MLP layers. ### Serving capacity Native spec holds `1 + num_speculative_tokens` states per request for rollback. ReplaySSM holds one checkpoint plus the small input ring, so more requests fit in the same HBM. Maximum decode concurrency at `max_model_len=2048`, `(B, T) = (16, 4)`, B300: | native spec | ReplaySSM | ratio | |---:|---:|---:| | 211.7 | 649.7 | 3.07x | These are worst-case caps at the full request length. Beyond this point, throughput saturates. ## Tests Per-step kernel correctness is covered by `tests/kernels/mamba/test_replayssm_spec_decode_mamba2.py`. A `T`-window verify step is checked against decoding the same window one token at a time, over multi-flush sequences, across three state and activation precision combinations, the production model geometries (small, tiny, Nemotron-Nano-4B, Super-120B, Ultra-550B), `B` in {16, 32} and `T` in {2, 4, 6, 8}. It covers rollback across a flush, continuous batching with per-row cursors and null-padded slots, and the builder's `bc_pre` scratch shape. Non-flush checkpoints are asserted bit-exact, since a non-flush step won't touch the state. A "teeth" case corrupts one history slot and asserts the output changes, so the history is provably being read. Metadata builder unit tests are in `tests/v1/attention/test_replayssm_spec_metadata_builder.py`. The cursor logic is the riskiest new code, so it is covered without a model: commit advances `write_pos` by the accepted count, a flush advances `post_origin` past committed history and restarts `write_pos`, the early-flush rule fires exactly one window before the ring would overflow, rejected drafts and zero-accept rows commit nothing, a first decode resets a recycled block, a resumed request re-anchors after preemption, a steady-state row is left alone, a mixed batch resets only the entering rows, and null-padded rows are skipped. Two cases pin the parts that a captured graph depends on: the per-row scratch widens to the padded batch and stays the persistent buffer, and the block-keyed cursors are passed through whole. One case covers the forced flush for a final single-token prompt chunk, and one asserts the builder rejects a page that is not the four-tensor spec layout. Engine-level parity lives in `tests/v1/e2e/test_replayssm_decode.py`, which compares native spec against ReplaySSM spec with greedy decode and `check_logprobs_close` on Nemotron-3-Nano-4B with an ngram drafter. Results: the kernel file is 149 passed and the builder file is 14 passed. Engine parity passes. The pre-existing suites (standard-decode kernel, prefill/decode equivalence, standard metadata builder, block-table update) still pass unchanged at 164 passed together with the new builder file. ``` pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_replayssm_spec_decode_mamba2.py \ tests/v1/attention/test_replayssm_spec_metadata_builder.py \ tests/v1/e2e/test_replayssm_decode.py -q ``` ## Model evaluation (GSM8K) Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-FP8 on one B300, TP1, MTP drafter at T=4, fp32 SSM state, model-card sampling (temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95), thinking on, N=1319. | config | accuracy | acceptance | |---|---:|---:| | standard (no spec) | 95.91 | n/a | | native spec | 96.59 | 3.09 | | ReplaySSM spec | 95.68 | 3.09 | Thinking remains enabled because `enable_thinking=False` significantly degrades this checkpoint. ## Duplicate check No open PR addresses ReplaySSM Mamba2 speculative decode. This PR is split from the large draft PR [#47576](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47576), which stays open as the full design, and builds on the Mamba2 standard-decode sub-PR [#48018](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48018). The GDN standard-decode sub-PR [#48792](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48792) is a sibling and does not overlap with the files modified here. The related prior ReplaySSM PRs we are aware of cover standard decode only: - [#43102](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43102) and [#43439](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43439), earlier PRs from our collaborator on the same ReplaySSM effort. This is the newer, more complete version. - [#46239](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46239), opened by another contributor based on our original fork. We have since made substantial changes, intend to land the feature ourselves, and have notified the author. ## Out of scope - Prefix caching. Rejected by the validator; `--mamba-cache-mode none` is required. The align-mode support added for standard decode in #48018 is untouched. - P/D disaggregation and KV connectors. Rejected by the validator. - Stochastic rounding. Rejected by the validator. - Kernel performance optimization for low-precision state (e.g., FP16). Planned for a follow-up PR. - Speculative decode for GDN, which will land in a later sub-PR.

signal.title: [Frontend][Core] Add release_kv_cache_memory() API
signal.text: ## Motivation Sleep level 2 releases KV cache memory, but it also discards model weights. This is unnecessarily expensive when a framework only needs temporary GPU headroom while keeping the same model instance resident. One concrete use case is model weight update in RL training. The workaround in [verl#7373](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pull/7373) uses `sleep(level=2)` followed by `wake_up(tags=["weights"])` before updating the standalone model. Releasing only the KV cache reduces peak GPU memory and can avoid OOM during the update, without discarding and remapping weights. ## Summary This PR adds `release_kv_cache_memory()` as a dedicated KV-only partial-sleep operation. It discards KV cache allocations, keeps model weights resident, and pauses scheduling until the released memory is restored with the existing `wake_up()` API. ## Implementation ### Call flow The offline and server entry points converge on the same engine path: ```text LLM.release_kv_cache_memory() -> LLMEngine ---------\ -> EngineCore POST /release_kv_cache_memory -> EngineClient ------/ | v Executor.discard(("kv_cache",)) | v Worker -> SleepModeBackend | v CuMem/XPU allocator.discard(tags) ``` `EngineCore` first pauses the scheduler and clears the prefix cache. Depending on the selected pause mode, it either handles existing requests immediately or waits for in-flight requests to finish before asking all workers to discard KV cache allocations. The scheduler remains paused after release; a discard failure also fails closed instead of resuming scheduling with potentially partially unmapped memory. At allocator level, only mapped allocations tagged `kv_cache` are unmapped and released, without a CPU backup. Per-allocation mapping state prevents duplicate unmap or map operations when release, sleep, and wake-up calls are mixed. ### Interaction with sleep levels `release_kv_cache_memory()` is treated as a KV-only partial sleep. A later `sleep(1)` or `sleep(2)` can upgrade that state to a full sleep: | Current state | Operation | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | Fully awake | `release_kv_cache_memory()` | KV cache discarded, weights resident, scheduler paused | | KV-only sleeping | `sleep(1)` | Weights offloaded, KV cache remains discarded | | KV-only sleeping | `sleep(2)` | Weights discarded, KV cache remains discarded | | KV-only sleeping | `wake_up(["kv_cache"])` | KV cache remapped and scheduling resumed | | Full sleep | `wake_up(["kv_cache"])` | Only KV cache remapped; weights remain sleeping and scheduling stays paused | | Full sleep | `wake_up()` | All allocations restored and scheduling resumed | The executor tracks the exact internal state with `sleeping_tags`. Scheduling is resumed only after no sleeping tags remain. ### Logging and observability This PR reuses the existing sleep-state logger instead of adding a dedicated `kv_cache_released` Prometheus state. After KV release, the existing metrics report `awake=0`, `weights_offloaded=0`, and `discard_all=0`: the engine is not available for scheduling, but it is not in sleep level 1 or 2. The precise resource state remains available internally through `sleeping_tags`. There is currently no requirement to monitor KV-only release separately. If that becomes useful, a dedicated Prometheus state and its transition logic can be added in a follow-up change. ## Scope The public API intentionally supports only KV cache release. Existing sleep levels already cover the other current cases: - `sleep(1)` offloads weights and discards KV cache memory. - `sleep(2)` discards all managed GPU memory. A generic public tag API would also need to define whether each tag is discarded or offloaded, increasing the API surface and overlapping with existing sleep semantics. More fine-grained public memory management can be discussed when a concrete additional use case appears; the internal `discard(tags)` path remains extensible. ## Related work - [vLLM#42658](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42658) explores generic tag-level sleep management. This PR instead provides a smaller, explicit end-to-end API for the known KV-only use case. - [vLLM#46438](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46438) contains related allocator-level selective-discard work. - [verl#7373](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pull/7373) demonstrates the downstream model-update use case and its current sleep/wake workaround. This PR does not duplicate the generic public API proposed in #42658; its scope and semantics are intentionally narrower. ## Tests ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/executor/test_executor.py::test_discard_records_sleep_state_after_worker_failure \ tests/v1/executor/test_executor.py::test_sleep_after_kv_cache_discard \ tests/v1/engine/test_sleep_lifecycle.py \ -q -o addopts='' ``` Result: `5 passed`. GPU-dependent end-to-end coverage is also included for offline `LLM.release_kv_cache_memory()` and the development server endpoint and metrics. ```bash pre-commit run ``` Result: passed. Model evaluation is not applicable because this change does not affect model outputs or accuracy. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to review the implementation and draft this description. The submitter reviewed the resulting changes and test scope.

signal.title: [Bugfix] Return 4xx for client-caused errors in /detokenize
signal.text: ## Purpose `POST /detokenize` wraps `create_detokenize` in a blanket `except Exception` that reports every failure as HTTP 500. Its sibling `POST /tokenize` in the same file has no such wrapper, so its exceptions reach the global exception handlers registered by `init_exception_handler`, which map client-caused errors to 4xx (`VLLMValidationError` to 400, `VLLMNotFoundError` to 404, raw `ValueError`/`TypeError`/`OverflowError` to 400) and keep genuine server errors at 500. The two endpoints therefore disagree on identical client errors: | error raised by the serving layer | /tokenize | /detokenize before | /detokenize after | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `VLLMValidationError` | 400 | 500 | 400 | | `VLLMNotFoundError` | 404 | 500 | 404 | | `ValueError` | 400 | 500 | 400 | | `RuntimeError` (real server bug) | 500 | 500 | 500 | `create_detokenize` can surface client-caused errors in practice, for example through `_maybe_get_adapters` (bad LoRA adapter name) and `renderer.tokenize_prompt_async`. This is the same class of bug fixed for the Anthropic entrypoint in #52246: client-caused errors must be 4xx, never 500. The fix removes the wrapper so `/detokenize` takes the exact shape of `/tokenize`. Genuine server errors still return 500 through the global `Exception` safety-net handler, as the last table row shows. ### Why the `OverflowError` special case is dropped rather than kept The old code re-raised `OverflowError` as a `RequestValidationError`. Dropping it does not change the status code: - vLLM's `validation_exception_handler` returns 400 for `RequestValidationError`. - The global `OverflowError` fallback (`create_error_response`) also returns 400. Only the error body changes: the response now has the platform-standard shape (`type: "BadRequestError"` with the raw exception message) that `/tokenize` and every other endpoint produce, instead of a wrapped `1 validation error: ...` message with `type: "Bad Request"`. Fast tokenizers do raise `OverflowError` for out-of-range token ids, so the path is real, and the regression test pins its 400. ### Scope Other blanket `except Exception` handlers under `vllm/entrypoints/` are left alone deliberately: `serve/dev`, `serve/elastic_ep`, and `serve/fault_tolerance` are admin/dev endpoints rather than client-input surfaces, and `cohere/api_router.py` is annotated `# noqa: BLE001 - report as 500 for parity`, a deliberate choice. The `mode="before"` validator hardening from #52528 is already complete repo-wide, so nothing to do there. A search of open PRs for detokenize and tokenize router work found no overlapping PR. ## Test Plan New `TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses` in `tests/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/test_serving_tokenization.py`, mirroring `TestClientErrorResponses` from #52246. It builds the real router plus the real global exception handlers, mocks `ServingTokenization`, and asserts: - `VLLMValidationError` returns 400 with `param` propagated - `VLLMNotFoundError` returns 404 - `ValueError` returns 400 - `OverflowError` returns 400 (pins the status code of the removed special case) - `RuntimeError` still returns 500 - `/tokenize` and `/detokenize` return the same status for the same client error ```bash pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/test_serving_tokenization.py pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/exception_handling/ ``` ## Test Result New tests against the old handler (fix reverted): 6 failed, all 4xx cases came back as 500. ```text FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_vllm_validation_error_returns_bad_request FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_vllm_not_found_error_returns_not_found FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_value_error_returns_bad_request FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_overflow_error_returns_bad_request FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_server_error_still_returns_internal_server_error FAILED ...::TestDetokenizeClientErrorResponses::test_tokenize_and_detokenize_agree_on_client_errors 6 failed, 2 deselected ``` With the fix: ```text tests/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/test_serving_tokenization.py: 8 passed tests/entrypoints/serve/exception_handling/: 39 passed ``` Live server check (`vllm serve HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct` on the CPU backend): ```text POST /tokenize {"prompt": "Hello world"} -> 200 POST /detokenize {"tokens": [9906, 1917]} -> 200 POST /detokenize {"tokens": [4611686018427387904]} -> 400 {"error": {"message": "out of range integral type conversion attempted", "type": "BadRequestError", ...}} POST /detokenize {"model": "no-such-model", ...} -> 404 NotFoundError ``` The third case is the real OverflowError path: a token id inside the protocol's int64 bound but beyond the fast tokenizer's range keeps its 400 through the global handler. `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean on both changed files, and mypy (CI configuration via `tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`) reports no issues. This change was developed with AI assistance; I reviewed and tested every line.

signal.title: [Kimi-K3][AMD] Return KDA and MLA projection outputs directly
signal.text: ## Purpose Kimi-K3's AMD attention paths copied each output projection into a caller-owned buffer even though the projection already returns a tensor with the required shape, dtype, layout, and lifetime. This PR removes that redundant post-projection allocation and copy from both attention families: - 69 KDA layers - 24 MLA layers - 93 post-attention-projection copies per model step in total The functionality from #50847 is now folded into this PR. #50654 is separate and complementary: it optimizes the earlier KDA recurrent/conv/RMSNorm path, while this PR removes the later copy after the output projection. ## Implementation - Return KDA output-projection storage directly from both the shared KDA implementation and the dedicated full-rank Kimi-K3 implementation selected by current `main`. - Return MLA output-projection storage directly. - Use one return-value contract in `KimiDecoderLayer` for KDA and MLA. - Preserve attention arithmetic, state updates, normalization, projection, tensor-parallel communication, and HIP-graph replay behavior. ## Validation ```text Targeted ownership tests: 3 passed Ruff 0.14.0 check: passed Ruff 0.14.0 format check: passed git diff --check: passed DCO: passed ``` The tests cover KDA dispatch ownership, the concrete full-rank Kimi-K3 KDA forward path, and MLA dispatch ownership. In each case, the returned tensor is the exact projection tensor and has the same `data_ptr()`. ## Fixed-cohort decode A/B ### Setup ```text GPU: 8 x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950) Parallelism: TP8 Model: Kimi-K3, BF16 activations / MXFP4 weights Decode: non-speculative Prefix caching: enabled Prompt: 63,911-token shared prefix + 4,089-token suffix Output: 1,024 tokens per request, ignore EOS Concurrency: C16 and C24 fixed cohorts HIP graph: FULL, capture sizes 1/16/24 Sampling: greedy, seed 42 Runs: 1 warmup + 3 measured runs per concurrency and variant Success rate: 240/240 measured requests ``` Both variants used image `localhost/kimi-pp8-upstream-clean` (vLLM `beca88e59`, AITER `99733dc00`). The baseline was the unmodified image. The candidate mounted only this PR's AMD runtime files from `43d81ba3e`. The relevant AMD Kimi-K3 files in the image are identical to the rebased `main` baseline before this PR. ### Results Means over three measured runs. TPOT and ITL are end-to-end serving metrics, not the reviewer's pure-GPU trace period. | Cohort | Metric | Baseline | Combined PR | Delta | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | C16 | Mean TPOT | 73.141 ms | 72.428 ms | **-0.713 ms (-0.97%)** | | C16 | Median ITL | 70.488 ms | 70.186 ms | **-0.302 ms** | | C16 | Output throughput | 193.575 tok/s | 195.555 tok/s | **+1.02%** | | C24 | Mean TPOT | 74.958 ms | 74.457 ms | **-0.501 ms (-0.67%)** | | C24 | Median ITL | 71.311 ms | 70.916 ms | **-0.396 ms** | | C24 | Output throughput | 278.245 tok/s | 280.452 tok/s | **+0.79%** | Mean-TPOT standard deviation across the three runs was 0.184 ms / 0.348 ms for baseline C16/C24 and 0.019 ms / 0.122 ms for candidate C16/C24. ### Interpretation The reviewer's trace found that the complete 93-copy group costs approximately 0.495 ms at C16 and 0.563 ms at C24. The combined A/B removes all 93 copies and measures a 0.713 ms C16 and 0.501 ms C24 TPOT reduction. C24 closely matches the trace-derived removable cost. C16 is modestly larger, which is plausible because returning projection storage directly also changes allocator and lifetime behavior; the baseline's run-to-run variance is also higher. The absolute TPOT values should not be compared directly with the reviewer's 32.82/35.98 ms pure-GPU periods because TPOT includes serving and scheduling overhead. The A/B delta is the relevant same-harness comparison. ## Scope summary ```text #50592: remove 69 KDA + 24 MLA post-projection copies #50847: functionality absorbed by this PR #50654: separate earlier KDA recurrent-output/fusion optimization ```

signal.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
signal.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. - https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8 The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight. To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Bugfix] Fix DeepSeek V4 mHC broadcast buffer for weight sync
signal.text: ## Purpose Fix Stale broadcast weights after refit. finalize_mhc_broadcast_weights() rebound layer.hc_attn_fn_broadcast to a freshly-allocated tensor on every call. CUDA graphs captured against the original tensor's address keep replaying with the old pointer, so a weight refit (repeat load_weights() after capture, e.g. RL weight sync) left captured graphs reading stale broadcast weights. Fixed by allocating only when the buffer is None and otherwise copy_()-ing in place, keeping the address stable. ## Test Plan Two unit tests added to tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py: 1. test_deepseek_v4_mhc_broadcast_finalize_sums_hc_streams — first finalize allocates the buffer with the stream-summed values. 2. test_deepseek_v4_mhc_broadcast_refit_refreshes_in_place — after mutating hc_attn_fn and re-finalizing, the buffer is the same tensor object with updated values (the refit contract). pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py -k mhc_broadcast -v pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py -k "hc_head_tilelang or mhc_broadcast" End to end tests on verl side with DSV4 training ## Test Result - -k mhc_broadcast: 2 passed. - Combined with the tilelang hc_head kernel tests (which flip torch.set_default_device to CUDA earlier in the file): 10 passed. - Full file collects all 53 tests cleanly. - Mutation check: with the model.py fix reverted to HEAD, the refit test fails on the buffer-identity assertion and the sums test still passes — the pair pins both the pre-existing semantics and the new in-place contract. - End to end tests on verl side with DSV4 training returned to normal training inference mismatch. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [X] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [X] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [X] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signal.title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Rewind store cursor at both block_ids.clear() sites
signal.text: ## Summary `OffloadingConnector` kills the engine with `AssertionError` in `_build_store_jobs`. Likely the underlying cause of #52170. Updated to cover **both** sites where the invariant breaks. ## The invariant `_build_store_jobs` compares a plain slice against a **strided** one: ```python offload_keys = group_state.offload_keys[start_chunk_idx:num_chunks] offload_block_ids = group_state.block_ids[ start_chunk_idx * bpc + bpc - 1 : num_chunks * bpc : bpc] assert len(offload_keys) == len(offload_block_ids) ``` The strided slice needs `len(block_ids) >= num_chunks * blocks_per_chunk`. `num_chunks` comes from token counts; `block_ids` comes from what the scheduler has supplied. Anything that empties `block_ids` without rewinding `next_stored_chunk_idx` breaks it. `block_ids` is cleared in **two** places. `next_stored_chunk_idx` is rewound in **neither** — the only reset today is in `reset_cache()`. ### Site 1 — `_update_req_states`, resumed after preemption ```python if preempted: for group_state in req_status.group_states: group_state.block_ids.clear() # cursor left stale ``` The list cannot be reconstituted, because of what `yield_req_data` supplies: ```python for req_data in scheduler_output.scheduled_new_reqs: yield req_data.req_id, req_data.block_ids, False # FULL list yield from zip(cached_reqs.req_ids, cached_reqs.new_block_ids, # DELTA only (r in cached_reqs.resumed_req_ids for r in cached_reqs.req_ids)) ``` `preempted` is `req_id in resumed_req_ids`, and resumed requests arrive on the **cached** path, which carries only that step's newly-allocated blocks. ### Site 2 — `get_num_new_matched_tokens`, lookup path ```python for group_state in req_status.group_states: group_state.block_ids.clear() # cursor left stale ``` then, further down, the only post-lookup cursor write: ```python # Skip prefix-hit chunks for block-level policy; for # request-level, next_stored_chunk_idx stays at 0 so all # chunks (including hits) are offloaded. if req_status.offloading_context.policy == OffloadPolicy.BLOCK_LEVEL: group_state.next_stored_chunk_idx = num_chunks ``` `BLOCK_LEVEL` is fine — it overwrites the cursor. **`REQUEST_LEVEL` relies on "stays at 0", which the code never enforces**; it is only true on a request's first pass. This function re-enters — the in-flight-transfer branch returns `None` and asks the scheduler to query again — so a second call clears `block_ids` with a cursor that has already advanced. ## Fix Rewind `next_stored_chunk_idx` to 0 alongside each clear, matching what `reset_cache()` already does (*"Reset store progress so active requests re-offload from chunk 0"*). At site 2 this makes the existing comment true rather than aspirational; `BLOCK_LEVEL` still overwrites it immediately after. Cost is re-storing chunks that may already be in the host cache — stores are keyed by block hash, so redundant work rather than incorrect state. Clamping `num_chunks` to what `block_ids` supports would also silence the assert, but leaves the cursor and the list describing different things, which is what the assert exists to catch. ## Why it needs load to reproduce Site 1 requires preemption — enough concurrent long requests that the scheduler evicts a running one. Startup, smoke tests and idle soaks never preempt. That matches #52170 (30 concurrent multi-turn conversations, 160K first prompts, prefix caching on). ## Status Draft, and I want to be straight about the evidence: this is traced from source and explains the stack trace, the timing and the load-dependence, but **I have not reproduced the assert against a patched build**. My own repro attempts did not even reach preemption — the scheduler reported `preempted_requests=0` throughout, because the load used short outputs, so requests never grew into a full pool. Reproducing site 1 needs sustained concurrency with *long generations*, not just long prompts. Opening as a draft so the analysis is on #52170, which has no diagnosis yet. Related: #49118 (closed) fixed a different trigger for the same assert — aborting a queued, never-scheduled request.

signal.title: Fix weight tying
signal.text: Fixes #51063. vLLM decides whether to tie `lm_head` purely from `tie_word_embeddings` and never looks at the checkpoint, so a config claiming tied weights against a checkpoint with a real `lm_head` silently discards it and generates gibberish. `ModelConfig.maybe_untie_word_embeddings` now checks the safetensors metadata and builds the model untied so the head loads; after loading, `torch.equal` re-ties it if it was just a redundant copy (as in `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`) or warns and keeps it if it genuinely differs. This matches `PreTrainedModel.tie_weights`. The reverse case, untied config with no head in the checkpoint, now ties and warns instead of leaving the head uninitialised. That makes the per-model workarounds redundant. `AutoWeightsLoader` now skips weights whose target parameter aliases one already loaded, which removes ~50 hand-rolled `lm_head` skips and also covers the ~20 models that tie with no skip at all. Tying itself is now expressed one way. `self.lm_head = self.lm_head.tie_weights(self.model.embed_tokens)` is the only form that dispatches through `quant_method.tie_weights`, so the other two are converted to it: - `self.lm_head.weight = self.model.embed_tokens.weight` (33 sites) bypassed the quant method entirely, so it was wrong for quant methods that repack. The `ParallelLMHead` already exists at that point, so this is a one-line swap with no structural change. - `self.lm_head = self.model.embed_tokens` (23 sites) built no `ParallelLMHead` at all in the tied branch. These now always build one and tie it. Two consequences worth review: a transient vocab x hidden allocation, and the quant config is now consulted for the `lm_head` prefix where it previously never was. - Five models hardcoded tying with `assert config.tie_word_embeddings` (`gemma`, `gemma2`, `commandr`, `cohere2_moe`, `mpt`). Untying at config time would trip these, so the asserts are dropped and an untied config keeps using the embeddings exactly as it does today. Those five still have no real `lm_head`, so they cannot honour one in a checkpoint; left for a follow-up. So `AutoWeightsLoader` now skips weights whose target parameter aliases one already loaded. That removes ~50 hand-rolled `lm_head` skips and also covers the ~20 models that tie with no skip at all.

signal.title: [Perf][Kernel] Adopt PTX 9.4 `ldmatrix.s8.s4` (hardware INT4→INT8 expanding load) in W4A8-INT8 paths
signal.text: ## Summary PTX ISA 9.4 (CUDA 13.4.0 Developer Preview) exposes a new `ldmatrix` variant that performs **in-flight sign extension of packed INT4 to INT8 during the shared-memory matrix load**: ``` ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n16.{x1,x2,x4}{.shared{::cta}}.s8.s4 r, [p]; ``` Source data is densely packed signed 4-bit elements; the hardware expands them to signed 8-bit values in the destination fragment. This can eliminate the register-level INT4→INT8 unpack sequences (`lop3`/`prmt` bit tricks and PRMT LUTs) in our W4A8-INT8 kernels, and potentially the dequant-oriented weight interleaving in repack. Doc: PTX ISA 9.4, §9.7.16.5.15 (`ldmatrix`), https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/developer-preview/13.4/parallel-thread-execution/index.html ## Hardware verification (already done) Verified with `ptxas`/`nvdisasm` from CUDA 13.4.0 preview (`V13.4.46`), no GPU required: - `ptxas` accepts the instruction for **sm_90a, sm_100a/f, sm_103a, sm_107a/f, sm_110f, sm_120f, sm_121a** (PTX targets per doc: `sm_90a, sm_100f, sm_110f, sm_120f`). - SASS is a **single LDSM instruction** on every architecture — no unpack sequence is generated. The encoding is bit-identical across all seven targets (opcode `0x783b` = LDSM, modifier `0x9000/0x9100/0x9200` for x1/x2/x4; cf. `LDSM.16.M88` = `0x0000`, `LDSM.U4x16P64TO8.M816` = `0xa800`, `LDSM.U6x16P32TO8.M816` = `0xb000`). - Notably **Hopper (sm_90a) is supported** — the datapath appears to have existed in silicon since GH100; PTX 9.4 merely exposes it. Existing H100/H200 fleets benefit immediately. - `nvdisasm` 13.4 does not yet print a mnemonic for this modifier (hex only); expect this to be fixed in the GA release. ## Affected code paths (vLLM @ `76bf55240`, 2026-07-23) ### 1. Marlin W4A8-INT8 — replaceable (bit-exact) - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/dequant.h:494` — `dequant<int32_t, kU4B8>`: unpacks two nibbles per pass with `(q & 0x0F0F0F0F | 0x80808080) - 0x08080808) ^ 0x80808080`, i.e. u4-with-bias-8 → s8. - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/marlin_template.h:945` — `frag_b_quant` is loaded from shared memory with plain 128-bit loads over Marlin's dequant-interleaved layout, then dequanted at `marlin_template.h:1163` (`dequant_data`). - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/gptq_marlin_repack.cu` — repack currently bakes in the dequant interleave. **Equivalence:** for `kU4B8`, stored nibble `v ∈ [0,15]` yields output `v − 8`. Storing `s4 = v XOR 0x8` at repack time (free) makes `sign_extend(s4) == v − 8` **bit-exact**. The ALU sequence (≈6 ops per 32-bit word × 2 fragments) disappears, and the B-fragment interleave in repack can be dropped in favor of the canonical 8-bit `ldmatrix` tile layout. ### 2. Machete W4A8-INT8 — replaceable (bit-exact) - `csrc/libtorch_stable/cutlass_extensions/vllm_numeric_conversion.cuh:213` — `NumericArrayConverter<int8_t, vllm_uint4b8_t>` implements the identical `[-8..7]` mapping via a PRMT LUT (`lut_4bit_to_8bit_convert`, line 158). Used by the Machete mainloop's register-transform stage. - Replacement means moving the conversion out of the CUTLASS transform pipeline into the smem→rmem copy atom; requires a new copy atom + prepacked-layout adjustment in `machete_prepacked_layout.cuh` rather than a converter swap. Larger change; track separately as phase 2. ### 3. Marlin W4A8-INT8 with runtime zero-point — partially replaceable - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/dequant.h:570` — `sub_zp_and_dequant<int32_t, kU4>` (asymmetric AWQ-style zp, see #24722). Pure sign extension can't absorb a runtime zp, but `ldmatrix.s8.s4` + one packed s8 correction add (`zp − 8` per group) still beats the current mask/sub/xor sequence. Lower priority. ### 4. Out of scope - `cutlass_w4a8/` (W4A8-**FP8**, `MmaType = e4m3`): target type is FP8, not covered by this instruction. - `moe/moe_wna16_utils.h`, AWQ/GPTQ FP16 paths: dequant target is FP16/BF16. ## Proposed plan - [ ] **Phase 0 — layout verification**: confirm the `m8n16.s8.s4` output fragment layout matches `mma.m16n8k32.s8` operand-B fragments (the `m8n16`/`m16n16` 8-bit ldmatrix shapes were introduced in PTX 8.6 for exactly this pairing; verify the s4 source packing order within each 8-byte row against our repack output). Only `m8n16` is available for `.s8.s4` (no `.trans`), so B must be stored K-major in smem. - [ ] **Phase 1 — Marlin symmetric path (`kU4B8`)**: - repack: store `v XOR 0x8` nibbles, drop dequant interleave for the `is_a_8bit && !has_zp` configuration; - kernel: replace `frag_b_quant` plain loads + `dequant` with `ldmatrix.m8n16.x4.s8.s4`, guarded by `__CUDA_ARCH_FAMILY_SPECIFIC__` / arch macros for {90a, 100f, 110f, 120f} and `CUDA >= 13.4`; - keep the existing lop3 path as fallback for sm_80/86/89 and older toolkits. - **No on-disk/checkpoint format change**: repack runs at weight-loading time (`process_weights_after_loading` → `ops.gptq_marlin_repack`); both transforms live inside the repack kernel and only affect the in-GPU-memory layout. - The in-memory Marlin layout becomes kernel-variant-dependent (ldmatrix layout vs legacy interleave). Repack must take a layout-variant flag driven by the same arch/toolkit predicate as kernel selection; if repacked-weight caching across processes is ever introduced, the layout needs a version tag. - [ ] **Phase 1.5 — benchmark**: microbench LDSM-expand vs LDS+lop3 (MIO-pipe pressure vs ALU pressure; note Marlin is often ALU-bound in the dequant stage at high occupancy), plus end-to-end gptq W4A8-INT8 throughput on H100/H200, B200, RTX 5090. - [ ] **Phase 2 — Machete**: smem→rmem copy atom using `ldmatrix.s8.s4`, prepacked layout update. - [ ] **Phase 3 — zp path**: evaluate `ldmatrix.s8.s4` + packed correction add for `sub_zp_and_dequant`. ## Caveats - CUDA 13.4 is currently a **Developer Preview**; land behind a build-time gate and revisit at GA. Instruction availability/targets could still shift (precedent: a→f promotions between 8.6 and 8.8). - `nvdisasm` cannot yet name the instruction; debugging SASS requires reading hex until tooling catches up. - Ada (sm_89) and Ampere keep the existing path permanently — the instruction is sm_90+ only. ## References - PTX ISA 9.4 release notes: "Adds support for `.s8.s4` types for `ldmatrix` instruction for `.m8n16` shape" — targets `sm_90a, sm_100f, sm_110f, sm_120f`. - Existing sub-byte ldmatrix formats (`.b6x16_p32`, `.b4x16_p64`, unsigned, padded) introduced in PTX 8.6 for the f8f6f4 MMA path — the new `.s8.s4` differs in being **densely packed** and **sign-extending**. - #24722 (Marlin W4A8-INT8 dequant tricks this would supersede on sm_90+).

signal.title: [Bugfix] Pick the DeepSeek V4 eager cudagraph region per model runner
signal.text: #51430 narrowed the DeepSeek V4 eager cudagraph region, which corrupts MRV1 output, and #51768 responded by defaulting the model to MRV2 and rejecting MRV1 + PIECEWISE. That default costs ROCm, where MRV1 is still the faster runner for this model. Choose the region from the runner instead: MRV1 wraps the whole attention body in `_prepare_and_attn_eager`, restoring the pre-#51430 region it needs, while MRV2 keeps the narrow region and its shorter TTFT. The nested `_sparse_indexer_and_attn` break runs inline, since `add_eager` clears `_capturing` first. MRV1 + PIECEWISE is then correct on every platform, so drop the rejection. CUDA still defaults to MRV2; ROCm defaults to MRV1 until MRV2 is competitive there. Claude was used to help.

signal.title: [KV Offloading] Back-pressure detection and remediation
signal.text: ## Purpose Add back-pressure detection to the KV cache tiering offloading manager. When a secondary tier (disk, shared storage, P2P) becomes slow, the manager detects saturation via store completion latency and stops cascading new stores to that tier until it recovers. This prevents unbounded job pileup from degrading serving latency. See associated RFC; https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50031 ### Design - **Detection**: An exponential moving average (EMA) of store completion latency is tracked per secondary tier. When the EMA exceeds a high-water mark (1.0s), the tier is marked as under pressure. Pressure clears when the EMA drops below a low-water mark (0.5s). The hysteresis band prevents oscillation. - **Response**: Stores to pressured tiers are silently dropped — blocks remain in the CPU primary tier subject to normal LRU eviction. Loads from pressured tiers continue normally. - **Observability**: Two new Prometheus metrics per tier: - `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_backpressure_active` (gauge) — 1 when pressure is active - `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_backpressure_stores_dropped` (counter) — number of dropped stores ### Changes - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/backpressure.py`: Add abstract `BackpressureDetector` and `BackpressurePolicy` APIs. Implement subclasses for EMA and store skipping. - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py`: Add `BackpressureState` dataclass and per-tier tracking. Update `_process_finished_jobs()` to feed the EMA on store completions. Gate store cascades in both `complete_store()` (global tiers) and `_cascade_to_request_level_tiers()` behind pressure checks. Report metrics in `get_stats()`. Reset state in `reset_cache()`. - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`: Add `submit_time` field to `JobMetadata` for latency measurement. Add `BACKPRESSURE_ACTIVE` and `BACKPRESSURE_STORES_DROPPED` metric keys. - `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py`: New test suite (12 tests). ### Test plan The test suite uses a `DelayedSecondaryTierManager` that holds completed jobs until explicitly released, allowing precise control over apparent store latency. It exercises: 1. **EMA updates on store completion** — EMA starts at 0 while jobs are in-flight, updates to `alpha * latency` after a fast completion. 2. **Pressure activates above high water** — Slow store (5x threshold) flips `is_under_pressure` to True. 3. **Pressure clears below low water** — Repeated fast completions decay EMA below low-water mark, deactivating pressure. 4. **Hysteresis prevents oscillation** — Mid-range EMA (between low/high water) does not toggle pressure in either direction. 5. **Stores skipped under pressure** — Blocks land in primary but are not cascaded to the secondary tier. 6. **Stores resume after pressure clears** — After clearing pressure, the next store cascades normally. 7. **Dropped store count tracked** — `stores_dropped` increments correctly per skipped cascade. 8. **Metrics reported via get_stats** — Prometheus gauge and counter appear in reduced stats with correct values; dropped count resets after collection. 9. **Metrics gauge zero when no pressure** — Backpressure gauge reports 0 when inactive. 10. **Reset cache clears backpressure** — `reset_cache()` zeros EMA and clears pressure state. 11. **Request-level tier respects backpressure** — Request-level cascades (via `prepare_store`) also skip pressured tiers. 12. **Loads continue under pressure** — Lookups still return RETRY and initiate promotion; only stores are suppressed. ```bash pytest -sv tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py ``` Note: portions of this PR are generated with claude. cc @varun-sundar-rabindranath

signal.title: [Test] Add a prefix-caching x tool-calling gate
signal.text: ## Purpose Agentic deployments run prefix caching and tool calling together — repeated system prompts and tool definitions are exactly the prefix a cache is meant to reuse — yet no test exercises the combination: the per-parser tests never boot an engine, and the tool-calling e2e tests never enable prefix caching. A regression that only appears when the cache engages is invisible today. Adds `tests/tool_use/test_prefix_cache_tool_calling.py`, which boots the same tool-calling server with prefix caching off and on and asserts (1) a well-formed, schema-conformant tool call in both configurations, and (2) that under the caching configuration the cache was *actually exercised* (`vllm:prefix_cache_queries` and `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` non-zero, and zero in the control arm). Assertion 2 keeps the gate honest: a cache that never engaged would pass while proving nothing. Test-only; requires a GPU and a small model, so it suits a nightly or opt-in tier rather than a blocking gate. ## Test Plan Run on 1 GPU: `pytest tests/tool_use/test_prefix_cache_tool_calling.py -v` ## Test Result | Run | Result | |---|---| | As filed (GB200, recent dev build, Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct) | 3 passed, 1 skipped (control-arm skip by design) | | Planted defect — caching arm secretly booted with caching disabled | exactly 1 failed: the cache-engagement assertion; tool-calling assertions stayed green | Counter helper probed against 6 synthetic expositions (with/without `_total`, multi-engine labels summed, `_created` ignored, absent series -> 0, trailing timestamp not misread): 6/6. ruff 0.14.0 (`check` + `format --check`) clean. signal.title: [Attention][MLA] FlashMLA sparse: DCP on the fp8_ds_mla mixed-batch path + MTP
signal.text: DCP support for the `FLASHMLA_SPARSE` backend on the `fp8_ds_mla` KV path, including MTP spec decode under full cudagraphs. `fp8_ds_mla` is what the backend selector picks on Hopper for DSA models with small per-rank head counts (GLM-5.2 / DeepSeek-V3.2 at TP4/DCP4), and this path previously refused DCP outright. Earlier revisions stacked on #46076 and carried the sparse-indexer DCP machinery (global top-k merge, `--dcp-sparse-indexer-mode`); all of that has since landed in main via #46076 and its follow-ups, so the PR is now backend-side only: +234/−34 across `flashmla_sparse.py`, `flashmla.py` and one test file. (#45426 was our earlier standalone version with its own indexer; this supersedes it and reuses the upstream merge machinery instead.) ## Changes `flashmla_sparse.py`: - Opt the backend into the shared DCP decode merge (`can_return_lse_for_decode`): the fp8 mixed-batch kernel now returns decode LSE, sliced together with the head padding and reshaped to the `(tokens, heads)` layout the reducer consumes. - Under DCP the indexer emits global token ids: keep this rank's shard and convert to local `fp8_ds_mla` slots via `triton_filter_and_convert_dcp_index` with `compact_valid_to_front=False` — the scattered `-1`s stay in place and the fp8 kernel masks them natively, skipping the per-call front-pack. Rows where this rank owns none of the selected tokens get `(0, -inf)`, the identity of the cross-rank LSE merge, so they drop out of the reduce. - Allow varlen decode under DCP (`supports_dcp_with_varlen` when `cp_kv_cache_interleave_size == 1`): causality comes from the indexer's top-k indices, not kernel metadata. This is what makes MTP + DCP work under full cudagraphs. - Fail-closed guards instead of silent corruption: `ag_rs` comm backend only; fp8 mixed-batch path only (the split prefill/decode path returns LSE for decode tokens only, and the bf16 sparse path is rejected under DCP); a head-envelope guard rejecting configs where local and DCP-gathered head counts pad to different fp8 decode kernel envelopes (e.g. 128 q-heads at TP8/DCP8). `flashmla.py` (dense FlashMLA decode): flatten the kernel's `[batch, heads, seq_len]` LSE to `[tokens, heads]` for the DCP reducer — matters under spec decode, where `seq_len > 1`. Tests: `test_fp8_dcp_head_envelope_guard` in `test_sparse_mla_backends.py`, parametrized over local head counts × DCP world sizes, both accepting and rejecting cases. ## Testing 4×H200, GLM-5.2-NVFP4, TP4/DCP4/EP + MTP, `fp8_ds_mla`, current rebase: - `test_sparse_mla_backends.py` + `test_indexer_dcp_localize.py`: 140 passed / 0 failed (SM90). - Full cudagraph capture clean; exact needle recovery at 198k context across all ranks. - Warm decode 78 tok/s at batch 1, 854 aggregate at batch 32 (786k context window). - dcp=1/2/4 byte-identical on long (>2048-tok) contexts in earlier revisions of the same merge path. The branch has also been soaking continuously since mid-July on a production 4×H200 GLM-5.2-NVFP4 deployment (TP4/DCP4/EP + MTP) via nightly-based images carrying this PR. Related fixes in the surrounding DCP infra that this path exposed were split out and handled separately: #48379 (fp8_ds_mla boot on main, merged), #50823 (block-table width under DCP, merged), #50883 (offload block-size scaling under DCP, open). AI assistance (Claude) was used; every line reviewed by the submitter, tests run by the submitter. <details> <summary>History: pre-rebase description (union indexer mode, perf vs #45426) — superseded</summary> Earlier revisions added an opt-in `--dcp-sparse-indexer-mode {exact,union}` on top of #46076's global top-k merge, motivated by a ~30% batch-1 decode regression of the exact merge vs our standalone indexer (#45426): 52.0 → 36.4 tok/s warm at batch 1, with union recovering to 43.5 and a follow-up localizer opt to 50.7. After the indexer machinery landed upstream in its final form, the flag and the indexer-side changes were dropped from this PR; the numbers above no longer describe the current diff. </details>

signal.title: [KVConnector] Decouple store retention from HBM retention
signal.text: ## Purpose This PR decouples Mooncake Store retention from local HBM prefix-cache retention. For hybrid KV-cache layouts, local residency and remote persistence serve different purposes. Local retention controls what must stay in HBM to continue execution, while store retention controls what can be reused by future shared-prefix requests. This distinction matters for sliding-window style cache groups. To keep only the latest replayable sliding-window tail in HBM, users may set: ```bash VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL=0 ``` ## Design The change is intentionally small: MooncakeStoreWorker now initializes MooncakeStoreCoordinator with retention_interval=None. This keeps the existing local retention behavior unchanged, while allowing Mooncake Store to persist reusable sliding-window checkpoints independently. This matches the direction described in the DeepSeek-V4 inference framework: hybrid attention introduces heterogeneous KV entries with different cache sizes and policies, and on-disk SWA KV storage is managed through full caching, periodic checkpointing, or zero caching depending on the storage/computation tradeoff. ## Tests ```bash pytest -q signal.title: [Feature]: split local/external prefix-cache hits in prompt_tokens_details  #52137
signal.text: ## Purpose This PR adds full support for exposing **local vs external prefix‑cache hits** across the OpenAI chat and completion endpoints. vLLM already tracks `num_local_cached_tokens` and `num_external_cached_tokens` internally, but only the summed `cached_tokens` reached the serving layer. This PR completes the data plumbing so users can see the full breakdown in both streaming and non‑streaming responses. This resolves the feature request to expose distributed prefix‑cache source information for observability, debugging, and pricing use cases. ### Summary of changes **Engine / Core** - Added `num_local_cached_tokens` and `num_external_cached_tokens` to `RequestState`. - Forwarded both fields from `prefill_stats` in `OutputProcessor`. - Added the same fields to `RequestOutput` so offline `LLM().generate()` users receive them. **OpenAI Protocol** - Extended `PromptTokenUsageInfo` with `local_cached_tokens` and `external_cached_tokens`. - Fixed docstring placement so `multimodal_tokens` retains its documentation and new fields have their own. **Chat Endpoint** - Added support for both fields in streaming and non‑streaming paths. - Updated `_make_prompt_tokens_details` to make new parameters optional, preserving existing test calls. **Completion Endpoint** - Added streaming support: capture local/external cached tokens on first iteration and populate them in the final usage chunk. - Added non‑streaming support in `request_output_to_completion_response`. **Tests** - Added streaming + non‑streaming tests for both chat and completion endpoints. - Reused existing mock helpers instead of introducing new ones. - Added invariant checks: `cached_tokens == local_cached_tokens + external_cached_tokens`. - Generalized `_collect_metrics_stream_chunks` to accept a `RequestOutput`. --- Tests added: - Chat: streaming + non‑streaming breakdown tests, helper‑level tests, invariant checks. - Completion: streaming + non‑streaming breakdown tests, invariant checks. All new fields behave correctly across: - streaming and non‑streaming - chat and completion - offline `LLM().generate()` - OpenAI protocol responses --- ## Test Result - **Chat tests:** 37 passed - **Completion tests:** 27 passed - **ruff check + format:** clean A teardown error from `torch.accelerator.empty_cache()` occurs due to CPU‑only Windows environment and is unrelated to the changes. signal.title: [CPU][MLA] Fix prefill backend selection so MLA runs end-to-end on CPU
signal.text: ## Purpose Make DeepSeek-V2-Lite run end-to-end on CPU when MLA is enabled, including the contextful prefill path needed by external KV reloads (for example LMCache). This is the missing follow-up to #49453: that PR brought up the CPU MLA decode path and the basic CPU MLA backend plumbing, but it still left CPU MLA unable to run real external-hit prefill flows. ## Why #49453 was insufficient #49453 added the following pieces: - `CPUMLABackend` / `CPUMLAImpl` under `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/` - CPU MLA decode via `torch.ops._C.mla_decode_kvcache` - CPU MLA KV-cache writes via the PyTorch fallback path - CPU platform plumbing (`block_size=16`, disable chunked prefill / prefix caching for MLA) - ARM correctness fixes in the CPU C++ code That was enough to make the CPU MLA decode path exist, but not enough to make a DeepSeek MLA model actually run through the full prefill lifecycle. The remaining gaps were: 1. CPU MLA prefill was still mis-routed to a GPU-oriented backend instead of a CPU-native one. 2. The CPU MLA prefill backend only handled the "new tokens only" path. It did not implement: - `return_softmax_lse=True` for suffix prefill - `run_prefill_context_chunk(...)` for prefill rows that already have context 3. The shared MLA layer still assumed the custom cache gather op `_C_cache_ops.gather_and_maybe_dequant_cache` existed, but that op is not available on CPU. 4. After fixing the above, the context/suffix merge still fell through to the Triton merge kernel, which is not usable in this CPU environment. 5. The UT added in #49453 did not exercise this failure mode. It covered backend selection and the cold/no-context CPU MLA path, but it never created a prefill row with `num_computed_tokens > 0`, so it never executed the LMCache-style external-hit/contextful prefill path. Because LMCache / KV connectors create prefill rows with `num_computed_tokens > 0`, they necessarily exercise the contextful MLA prefill path. That is why #49453 could merge while still failing for DeepSeek-V2-Lite + CPU + LMCache. ## What this PR adds 1. A CPU-native MLA prefill backend, `CPUSDPAMLAPrefillBackend` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/prefill/cpu_sdpa.py`). 2. CPU support for contextful MLA prefill in that backend: - `run_prefill_new_tokens(..., return_softmax_lse=True)` - `run_prefill_context_chunk(...)` 3. A CPU fallback for MLA context KV gather in `vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py`, avoiding the missing `_C_cache_ops.gather_and_maybe_dequant_cache` dependency. 4. A pure PyTorch CPU fallback for `merge_attn_states(...)` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/merge_attn_states.py`, so prefix/suffix partial results can be merged without Triton. 5. Stronger CPU MLA tests, including an end-to-end external-KV-hit smoke test using `ExampleConnector` with `dummy` weights and token-id prompts, so it does not need to load real model weights and does not depend on tokenizer initialization. ## Why this is not duplicate work This PR is not duplicating #49453. #49453 brought up the CPU MLA backend and made the decode path possible, but it left CPU MLA prefill incomplete and did not cover the external-hit/contextful prefill path at all. This PR closes the remaining CPU MLA correctness gaps so DeepSeek-V2-Lite can run through cold prefill, external KV reload, and prefix/suffix merge on CPU. I also checked current open PRs for overlapping work before proceeding. I did not find an open PR that fixes this CPU MLA contextful prefill path. ## Tests Added / updated coverage in `tests/v1/attention/test_cpu_mla_backend.py`: - `test_kv_cache_cpu_write` Verifies the CPU MLA KV-cache write path still stores MLA latent KV rows in the layout expected by the CPU decode kernel. - `test_cpu_mla_prefill_backend_selected` Verifies CPU MLA prefill selects the CPU backend. - `test_cpu_mla_prefill_new_tokens` Verifies the CPU SDPA MLA prefill backend matches a reference ragged causal attention implementation, including `return_softmax_lse=True`. - `test_cpu_mla_prefill_context_chunk` Verifies the CPU SDPA MLA backend correctly handles prefill context chunks and returns the expected per-head LSEs. ## Verification ### 1. Targeted pytest coverage Ran: ```bash /Users/mbl/projects/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/attention/test_cpu_mla_backend.py -v ``` Result: ```text 5 passed in 17.85s ``` ### 2. Local shell e2e: CPU TP=2 + LMCache + no prefix cache This validation uses: - `load_format="dummy"` so no real model weights are loaded - `hf_overrides` to shrink DeepSeek-V2-Lite to 2 layers / 4 routed experts - `skip_tokenizer_init=True` plus token-id prompts so the offline path does not depend on tokenizer startup - `tensor_parallel_size=2` - `LMCacheMPConnector` - `--no-enable-prefix-caching` On this single-NUMA local machine I also had to set `VLLM_CPU_SIM_MULTI_NUMA=1`, otherwise CPU worker autobinding refused to launch two local workers. I also had to set `gpu_memory_utilization=0.25`, because on the CPU backend that flag controls the fraction of system memory reserved per worker. On my local machine, TCP port `6555` and LMCache's default HTTP port `8080` were already in use, so the verified run below uses `6556` and `18080`. Started LMCache: ```bash source ~/.venv-lmcache/bin/activate lmcache server \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 6556 \ --chunk-size 256 \ --l1-size-gb 4 \ --eviction-policy LRU \ --max-workers 2 \ --http-port 18080 ``` Started vLLM: ```bash source ~/.venv-lmcache/bin/activate VLLM_HOST_IP=127.0.0.1 \ VLLM_LOOPBACK_IP=127.0.0.1 \ VLLM_CPU_SIM_MULTI_NUMA=1 \ vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite \ --load-format dummy \ --trust-remote-code \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --max-model-len 1024 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.25 \ --block-size 64 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --port 8024 \ --hf-overrides '{"num_hidden_layers":2,"n_routed_experts":4,"first_k_dense_replace":0,"num_experts_per_tok":2}' \ --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_connector_module_path":"lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"127.0.0.1","lmcache.mp.port":6556,"lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode":"lmcache_driven"}}' ``` Prepared a prompt with 300 token so LMCache has at least one full 256-token chunk to store and later reload: Sent the first request to warm/store KV: ```bash curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8024/v1/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite", "prompt": "Attention mechanisms are the foundational building block of the Transformer architecture, and understanding them requires tracing their motivation back to the limitations of recurrent and convolutional models. Before Transformers, sequence-to-sequence tasks were dominated by recurrent neural networks that processed tokens one step at a time, which made parallelization across sequence length impossible and caused information from early tokens to degrade as it was carried through many recurrent transitions. Convolutional networks offered some parallelization but still struggled to relate positions that were far apart unless the network was made very deep. The self-attention layer solves this by letting every token attend to every other token directly, so the path length between any two positions is always exactly one step regardless of how long the sequence is. Concretely, each input token is mapped to a query, a key, and a value vector through learned linear projections, and the output for a given token is a weighted sum of the value vectors of all tokens, where the weights come from the dot product between its query and the keys of others, scaled by the square root of the key dimension and passed through a softmax. Multi-head attention extends this idea by running several attention operations in parallel with different projected subspaces, allowing the model to attend to different kinds of relationships simultaneously, such as syntax at one head and coreference at another. Positional encodings are added to the token embeddings because attention itself is permutation invariant and would otherwise be blind to word order, and the original paper used fixed sinusoidal functions while later variants learned the positions directly. The encoder stack applies self-attention followed by a feed-forward network with residual connections and layer normalization, while the decoder inserts an additional masked attention sub-layer so that predictions for a position can only depend on earlier positions and never on future ones. Training such models at scale revealed that depth, data, and compute matter enormously, and that careful learning rate schedules with warmup prevent the early instability that raw Adam often shows on these architectures. Beyond machine translation where the Transformer first proved itself, attention became the substrate for large language models, vision transformers that treat image patches like tokens, and multimodal systems that align text and pixels in a shared space. Researchers have since studied the inductive biases of attention, its sample efficiency relative to convolutions, and the ways in which it can fail on rare patterns or long-range dependencies that exceed the effective context actually used during training. Efficient variants such as sparse attention, linear attention, and low-rank approximations try to reduce the quadratic cost of attending over the full sequence so that models can handle documents with tens of thousands of tokens without running out of memory. In practice, the choice of attention variant is a tradeoff between quality, speed, and the hardware available, and production systems frequently combine multiple tricks such as fused kernels,Flash style exact attention, and KV caching so that decoding new tokens reuses previously computed key and value vectors instead of recomputing them. This caching is exactly why serving engines care so deeply about memory layout and transfer, because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch size and quickly becomes the dominant memory consumer during long conversations. When you reason about deploying these models, you should think about how the prompt length, the number of concurrent requests, and the chosen block size all interact to determine how many blocks of KV cache fit in a given device, and how connectors that move that cache between processes or machines can smooth out load spikes. The deeper point is that attention is not just a mathematical operation but an architectural choice with system level consequences, and the cleanest mental model is to always ask what each token is allowed to look at, how that view is paid for in compute and memory, and where the resulting state is stored and moved as the sequence grows.", "max_tokens": 8, "temperature": 0 }' ``` Sent the second
