signal.title: [Bugfix][Kernel] Hoist tensor-descriptor build out of unified-attention TD ti…
signal.text: ## Summary Part of the TD adoption strategy proposed in #42545. `USE_TD`'s K/V tile loader rebuilt the tensor descriptor every tile iteration, since the descriptor's `base` baked in the per-tile physical block index. That forces a `tensormap_create` per iteration, which the pipeliner can't predicate: - On Hopper (sm_90), this only compiles at `num_stages=1`, costing roughly 50% throughput vs the raw-pointer default. - On sm_100/sm_120, it fails to compile at all: `'ttng.tensormap_create' op pipeliner doesn't know how to predicate this op`. ## Fix Move the loop-invariant `kv_head_idx` into the descriptor base and build one descriptor per K/V cache before the tile loop, addressing the per-tile physical block via a `load()` coordinate instead. This makes the descriptor loop-invariant, restoring `num_stages > 1` compilation on Hopper and fixing the sm_100/sm_120 compile failure outright. The hoisted 3D descriptor also needs a registered scratch allocator on sm_100/sm_120 (`Kernel requires a runtime memory allocation, but no allocator was set` otherwise). Wired up `set_triton_allocator()`, matching the existing pattern in `fused_moe` / GDN / LoRA's TD paths, cached per device to avoid a redundant call on every forward pass. ## Testing ### Correctness ``` pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention.py -k use_td ``` `290 passed` on H100/H200. ### Throughput `vllm bench throughput`, Qwen3-4B bf16, TRITON_ATTN, H100/H200: | Workload | in/out | raw ptr | TD hoisted | hoisted/raw | |---|---|---|---|---| | prefill_heavy | 2048/128 | 17.57 req/s | 15.85 req/s | 0.90x | | decode_heavy | 128/1024 | TBD | TBD | TBD | | balanced | 1024/256 | 28.25 req/s | 25.13 req/s | 0.89x | Repro: ``` COMMON="--model Qwen/Qwen3-4B --dtype bfloat16 --attention-config '{\"backend\":\"TRITON_ATTN\"}' --max-model-len 4096 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --seed 42" VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD=0 vllm bench throughput $COMMON --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2048 --random-output-len 128 --num-prompts 200 VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD=1 vllm bench throughput $COMMON --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2048 --random-output-len 128 --num-prompts 200 ``` B200 (sm_100), same model/backend/workloads: | Workload | in/out | raw ptr | TD hoisted | hoisted/raw | |---|---|---|---|---| | prefill_heavy | 2048/128 | 26.01 req/s | 22.05 req/s | 0.85x | | decode_heavy | 128/1024 | 23.25 req/s | 17.98 req/s | 0.77x | | balanced | 1024/256 | 40.22 req/s | 32.34 req/s | 0.80x | Correctness on B200: `290 passed` as well, same suite. --- Note : triton-lang/triton#10281 (still open/unmerged upstream) fixes the underlying pipeliner predication issue directly. Tested whether that changes anything here, on stock Triton and on #10281's own Triton build, across all three architectures: | GPU | raw pointer | hoisted TD | hoisted/raw | |---|---|---|---| | H200 (sm_90) | 29.35 [27.27, 29.36] | 26.20 [25.02, 26.26] | 0.893x | | B200 (sm_100) | 44.61 [41.87, 44.62] | 33.87 [32.73, 34.19] | 0.759x | Matches the baseline above, on SM120 hoisted TD still beats loop-local by 2.0%-16.7% even with #10281's fix, reaching 98.7%-99.7% of raw-pointer. --- cc: joint effort with @oonyshch @BabyDrangoner,coauthored the repro and root cause on H200/b200

signal.title: [Frontend] Add --sleep-idle-ttl auto-sleep and wake-on-request
signal.text: ## Purpose Sleep mode today is orchestrated entirely from outside: the dev-mode `/sleep` and `/wake_up` endpoints work well for RLHF flows, but anyone who wants an engine to release GPU memory when idle has to run an external controller that tracks activity, drains requests, and holds traffic during wake-up. This PR makes that a first-class server capability. With `--sleep-idle-ttl <seconds>` (requires `--enable-sleep-mode`), the API server puts the engine to sleep after the configured idle period and wakes it automatically when the next inference request arrives, holding the request until wake-up completes. `--sleep-idle-level` selects level 1 or 2; level-2 wake follows the documented sequence (wake weights, `reload_weights`, wake KV cache). Only inference endpoints reset the idle timer or trigger wake, so health probes and `/metrics` never keep the engine awake. Engines slept manually through the dev `/sleep` endpoint are never auto-woken, preserving existing RLHF semantics. In-flight tracking is a pure ASGI middleware, so streaming responses hold the engine awake until the last byte. The feature is rejected at startup with multiple API server processes, since each process only observes its own traffic. ## Test Plan Unit tests mock the engine client and cover sleep-after-TTL, in-flight blocking, timer reset, level-2 wake ordering, single-flight wake under concurrency, external sleep/wake interplay, and endpoint classification: ``` pytest tests/entrypoints/openai/test_idle_sleep.py -v ``` End to end: served `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` on one H100 with `--enable-sleep-mode --sleep-idle-ttl 60`, then exercised warm request, idle window, 30 s of `/health` and `/metrics` probes while asleep, and a wake-on-request cycle. ## Test Result All 19 unit tests pass; `pre-commit` (including mypy) is clean. On the H100: the engine slept 65 s after the last request (TTL 60 s plus 5 s poll granularity), GPU memory dropped from 73.9 GiB to 1.4 GiB while asleep, probes never woke it, and the first request after sleep returned HTTP 200 in 0.66 s end to end with the in-server wake taking 0.30 s. Repeated sleep/wake cycles were clean across three rounds. Docs updated in `docs/features/sleep_mode.md`.

signal.title: [Model][Generative Recommendation] Add HSTU model support to vLLM
signal.text: ## Purpose This PR adds HSTU-based generative recommendation model support to vLLM. HSTU is a ranking model architecture designed for generative recommendation. Unlike traditional language models, HSTU does not autoregressively generate text tokens. Instead, it synchronously computes ranking scores for all candidate items in a request. The goal of this change is to enable generative recommendation models to reuse the existing vLLM and large-model serving ecosystem, including: - Hugging Face model and configuration loading. - vLLM model registration. - GPU model execution. - Attention backend selection. - Optimized CUDA operators. - Request batching and scheduling. - Asynchronous output handling. - CUDA Graph execution. - Future distributed inference and online serving infrastructure. Generative recommendation and large language models have several common characteristics. Both can be represented as sequence models, use embedding layers and transformer-style computation, and benefit from optimized attention kernels, GPU batching, asynchronous execution, and production-level model serving infrastructure. By integrating HSTU into vLLM, generative recommendation models can reuse the existing large-model ecosystem instead of maintaining an independent inference stack. ## Inference Paradigm Although HSTU and large language models share several model and runtime components, their inference semantics are different. | Aspect | Large language model | Generative recommendation model | | --- | --- | --- | | Decode behavior | Autoregressively generates one token at a time | Synchronously computes scores for all candidates in a request | | Model output | Vocabulary logits for the next token | One ranking score for each candidate item | | Sampling | Requires token sampling and token ID generation | Does not generate a sampled token | | Request progress | Continues until the requested number of tokens is generated | Completes after all candidate scores are returned | | Output format | Usually `[num_tokens, vocab_size]` | Packed candidate-score output | | Scheduler signal | Uses sampled token IDs to update request state | Uses candidate scores to complete the request | The default vLLM generation path is designed around language-model execution: 1. Run the model forward pass. 2. Produce vocabulary logits. 3. Invoke the token sampler. 4. Generate token IDs. 5. Update the request state. 6. Continue decoding until the request is finished. This flow cannot be directly reused for HSTU because HSTU produces candidate ranking scores rather than vocabulary logits. Passing HSTU outputs through the normal sampler would incorrectly interpret candidate scores as vocabulary logits and could produce invalid token IDs. Therefore, this PR adds a score-only execution path: 1. Run the HSTU forward pass. 2. Extract the score corresponding to each candidate item. 3. Convert candidate IDs and scores into `LogprobsTensors`. 4. Return the scores through `prompt_logprobs_dict`. 5. Skip the standard token sampler. 6. Skip generated-token state updates. 7. Complete the request after all candidate scores are returned. The scheduler is also updated to support score-only recommendation requests. A request can be completed after candidate scores are produced even when no `new_token_ids` are returned. ## Implementation Overview This PR contains five main categories of changes. ### 1. Model Structure and Model Registration Files: - `vllm/model_executor/models/hstu.py` - `vllm/model_executor/models/registry.py` - `tests/models/registry.py` Changes: - Add the HSTU model implementation. - Add HSTU embedding layers, transformer blocks, normalization layers, and prediction heads. - Register the HSTU model with vLLM. - Support Hugging Face HSTU model loading. - Add HSTU to the model registry test data. - Add model registration and model import coverage. ### 2. Model Configuration and Configuration Registration Files: - `vllm/transformers_utils/config.py` - `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/__init__.py` - `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/hstu.py` Changes: - Add HSTU-specific configuration classes. - Support HSTU model and task configuration fields. - Support `model_type = "hstu"`. - Convert HSTU configuration data from Hugging Face configuration files into the vLLM configuration representation. - Preserve compatibility with the existing vLLM configuration loading flow. ### 3. Model Operators and Operator Registration Files: - `vllm/v1/attention/backends/hstu_attn.py` - `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py` - `vllm/v1/attention/selector.py` Changes: - Add the HSTU attention backend. - Integrate the external HSTU variable-length attention operator. - Register the HSTU attention backend with vLLM. - Automatically select `HSTU_ATTN` for HSTU or generative recommendation models when no explicit backend is configured. - Preserve explicit attention backend configuration as the highest-priority option. - Validate unsupported attention combinations and return clear errors. - Pass per-request context and candidate metadata to the HSTU attention implementation. Automatic backend selection is only applied when the user has not explicitly selected an attention backend. This preserves the existing backend override behavior. ### 4. Model Runner V1 Adaptation File: - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` Changes: - Add generative recommendation metadata collection. - Add HSTU candidate score extraction. - Pass HSTU metadata through the forward context. - Bypass the standard token sampler for HSTU requests. - Return candidate scores through the prompt-logprobs output path. - Add recommendation-specific request completion handling. - Preserve the existing execution path for non-HSTU models. ### 5. Model Runner V2 Adaptation Files: - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/gr_state.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/async_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` Changes: - Add `GRState` for request-scoped generative recommendation state. - Store user IDs, candidate count, prompt token IDs, and request stage. - Move candidate score extraction from the Model Runner into `GRState`. - Convert packed HSTU outputs into `LogprobsTensors`. - Add asynchronous score output handling. - Return candidate scores through `prompt_logprobs_dict`. - Skip token sampling and token-state updates for HSTU requests. - Complete score-only requests in the scheduler when candidate scores are available. - Preserve the one-token early-return behavior required by generative recommendation inputs. ## Test Plan ### 1. Environment Setup The operator is installed inside the following NVIDIA PyTorch container:`nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.06-py3` Install the required system dependency:`apt update && apt install -y libxcb1` ### 2.HSTU Operator Installation and Validation The HSTU attention operator is provided by the NVIDIA `recsys-examples` repository. Clone the recsys-examples repository:`git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/recsys-examples.git && cd recsys-examples/corelib/hstu` For H20 and other Hopper-based devices, enter the corresponding device directory before compiling: `cd hopper` Install the HSTU operator:`Install the HSTU operator:` After the compilation completes successfully, validate the operator installation with: `python vllm/tests/models/generativemodel/test_hstu_op.py` ### 3.vLLM Installation Clone the vLLM repository:`git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git && cd vllm` Install the current vLLM source with CUDA support:`VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cuda pip install -v -e .` ### 4. HSTU Model Inference: After the HSTU changes are included in vLLM, run:`python vllm/tests/models/generativemodel/test_hstu.py` This test validates: * HSTU model loading. * HSTU configuration loading. * HSTU model registration. * HSTU attention backend initialization. * HSTU forward execution. * Candidate score extraction. * Candidate ID and score formatting. * Score-only execution without token sampling. * Recommendation request completion. * Model Runner integration. * CUDA Graph execution. ### 5. Model Registry and Hugging Face Loading Run the model registry tests:`pytest -q tests/models/test_registry.py -k HSTUForCausalLM` This validates that: * HSTUForCausalLM is registered. * The HSTU model class can be imported. * Hugging Face model metadata is available. * The HSTU configuration can be loaded. * The vLLM model registry can resolve the HSTU model. ## Test Result ### HSTU Operator The test returned like: ```text Input q shape: torch.Size([40, 4096]) Output shape: torch.Size([40, 4096]) Run success ``` ### HSTU Model Inference The test returned candidate IDs and their corresponding ranking scores. A truncated example of the output is: ```text Request 0: 12676:0.6602 47052:0.5078 45082:0.4336 79131:0.3984 34671:0.4844 5695:0.4570 95647:0.1777 60217:0.5273 70284:0.4258 16361:0.4238 Request 1: 8023:0.4863 24460:0.6094 ... ``` Each line follows the format:`Each line follows the format:` The output confirms that HSTU synchronously computes the scores of all candidates for a request and returns the scores through the generative recommendation output path. The test also confirms that: * HSTU outputs are not passed through the standard vocabulary sampler. * No artificial generated token IDs are produced. * Requests complete after candidate scores are returned. * Candidate scores are returned through prompt_logprobs_dict. * Both Model Runner V1 and Model Runner V2 execution paths are supported. * The HSTU attention backend is initialized and executed successfully. * CUDA Graph execution works in the validated CUDA environment. ### Model Registration and Hugging Face Loading The model registration and Hugging Face loading tests passed. HSTUForCausalLM can be resolved and imported through the vLLM model registry, and the HSTU configuration can be loaded from the Hugging Face model configuration. ### Scheduler and Score-Only Execution The scheduler validation passed for score-only recommendation requests. A recommendation request is correctly completed after candidate scores are produced, even when no new_token_ids are returned. The standard token sampling path is skipped for HSTU requests, and no regular language-model token state update is performed. ### Attention Backend Selection When no explicit attention backend is configured, the HSTU model automatically selects HSTU_ATTN. When an explicit attention backend is configured, the user-provided backend remains authoritative and is not overridden by the HSTU automatic selection logic. ### Current Scope and Limitations This initial integration focuses on bringing HSTU into the vLLM model and serving ecosystem. The current implementation assumes: * Prompt lengths are consistent across users. * Candidate lengths are consistent across users. * HSTU and non-HSTU requests are not mixed in the same batch. * Candidate scores are produced during an unchunked prefill. * Pipeline parallelism is not used. * PD-separated HSTU execution is not supported yet. * KV-cache-based or paged HSTU attention is not supported yet. * request_stage = 1 is not supported. * Each recommendation prompt contains at least one context/candidate pair. These limitations can be addressed in follow-up work after the basic HSTU execution path and serving interface are established.

signal.title: [Bugfix] Fix speculative decoding for short_conv (LFM2) models
signal.text: ## Purpose Supersedes #44296 (rebased onto main with the original commit and authorship preserved — thanks @Tonoken3); that PR has had failing pre-commit since opening and merge conflicts since July 6 with no author activity, so this revives it to make the merge cheap. Speculative decoding (ngram, EAGLE-3, any method) on `short_conv` (LFM2 / LFM2.5) targets silently corrupts output at the first rejected token: attention KV rolls back, but the conv sliding window retains rejected-token activations. `mamba2` / GDN already handle this via the spec-aware `causal_conv1d_update` path; `short_conv` was never wired in: 1. `MambaStateShapeCalculator.short_conv_state_shape` sizes the conv state `conv_kernel - 1` (no `num_spec`), so there is no room to roll the window back (mirror: `mamba2_state_shape` adds `num_spec`). 2. `GPUModelRunner._build_attn_group_metadata` never injects `num_accepted_tokens` for `ShortConvAttentionMetadataBuilder`, so the layer never sees the accepted-token counts. Changes vs #44296: rebased onto current main, fixed the mypy failure that blocked its pre-commit (`assert state_indices_tensor_d is not None`), added a regression test for the spec-widened conv state shape. ## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR #44296 is this fix (red CI + conflicts + stale for 8 weeks; original commit and authorship preserved here). #50146 bundles a rebase of the same target-side fix with 6 further drafter-side changes across 9 files and depends on other open PRs; this PR is the minimal, independently mergeable target-side correctness fix for released models. ## Test plan - `pre-commit run` (incl. mypy-3.10): pass. - New `tests/kernels/mamba/test_short_conv_state_shape.py`: pass. - E2E (we are the model vendor — Liquid AI serving team; LFM2.5-230M fine-tune + trained EAGLE-3 drafter with ~0.9/step acceptance, ROCm MI325X, v0.26.0 + this patch): without the fix, low-concurrency spec decode diverges after the first rejection (doubled/fused tokens, occasionally flipped outputs; under default cudagraphs it degrades to garbage from ~token 2). With it, `--enforce-eager`, `PIECEWISE`, and default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` all produce identical, correct output on fixed-seed content probes. AI assistance was used to rebase, fix, and validate this change; I reviewed every changed line and am accountable for it.

signal.title: [ROCm] Enable shared-expert multi-stream overlap on ROCm
signal.text: # [ROCm] Enable shared-expert multi-stream overlap on ROCm ## What this PR does 1. `current_platform.is_cuda()` -> `is_cuda_alike()` in `SharedExperts._determine_shared_experts_order`, so ROCm can take the `MULTI_STREAM_OVERLAPPED` path. Today the aux stream is allocated on ROCm and never used, and the shared expert always runs serially with the routed experts. ## Dependencies **This must land on top of #52033.** The flip on its own is not safe on a tree that predates #48223: it enables the aux stream over the old raw `wait_stream` fork/join, and Kimi-K3 at TP=8 dies during warmup on all 8 ranks. #48111 already flagged the one-liner as insufficient. #52033 supplies the event-based fork/join, launch-before-dispatch, and the input clone — and it contains this same `is_cuda_alike()` flip, so **if #52033 lands as written this PR is fully subsumed and should simply be closed.** **It also needs #50618** (`[ROCm][Bugfix] Fix wvSplitK OOB reads on strided activations`), for the reason below. The defect is in `csrc/rocm/skinny_gemms.cu`. `wvSplitK` bounds its LDS activation preload by `Kap * N` (**stride** × rows) instead of `(N-1)*Kap + K`. For a dense, offset-0 tensor those are equal, so the bug is invisible. For a **strided view of a wider buffer it over-reads by exactly `storage_offset` elements**. Kimi-K3's KDA fuses several outputs into one row and hands the 128-element `f_a` slice to `f_b_proj`; at TP=8 that view is `stride=(6288,1)`, `storage_offset=6144`, so the preload runs **12,288 bytes past the end of the parent allocation**. Whether those bytes are mapped is a matter of allocator layout. Enabling the aux stream adds a second per-stream allocator pool, which moves that tensor to the tail of a 2 MiB segment — which is why an unrelated feature appeared to cause a memory fault, and why the fault addresses are 2 MiB-aligned (`0x…200000`, `0x…600000`). Single-variable arms on 8× MI355X, Kimi-K3 TP=8, boot-only, ladder `1,2,4,8`: | arm | result | |---|---| | overlap off (control) | clean | | overlap on | **fault** | | + ROCm/aiter#4715 (capture-safe split-K workspace) | fault | | + fresh `torch.cuda.Event` per call | fault | | + `AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3` (rules out kernel co-residency) | fault | | + shared-expert output into a main-stream static buffer | fault | | + aux-stream drain before capture | fault | | + shared-expert GEMMs moved back to the main stream | fault | | `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM=0` | **clean** | | only `wvSplitK`/`LLMM1` disabled, `wvSplitKrc` left on | **clean** | ### One caveat about #52033's `dp_size > 1` gate #52033 gates the ROCm overlap behind `self._moe_config.moe_parallel_config.dp_size > 1`, on the basis that "only DPA deployments benefit". **Every number below is TP=8 / DP=1**, i.e. exactly the configuration that gate excludes, and the overlap is a solid win there. If the gate lands as written, TP deployments get none of this by default. I did not touch the gate in this PR, because it does not exist in `main` — it arrives with #52033. For measurement I bypassed it locally with an env escape hatch: ```python if not current_platform.is_rocm(): return True +if envs.VLLM_ROCM_FORCE_SHARED_EXPERTS_STREAM: + return True return self._moe_config.moe_parallel_config.dp_size > 1 ``` The right place to settle this is #52033 itself. My suggestion there would be to either relax the heuristic now that there is TP data, or keep it but make it overridable, so TP users are not silently opted out. ## Superseded results (2026-08-13) — kept for the record, do not cite Kimi-K3 MXFP4, 8x MI355X, TP=8, EP=1, DSpark MTP (`num_speculative_tokens=2`), kv-cache fp8, `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, capture ladder `seq 1..60`, floor 61. Median generation throughput, matched request load per pair, zero faults in every arm: | conc | baseline | overlap | delta | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 86.40 tok/s | 98.40 | **+13.9%** | | 4 | 266.10 tok/s | 295.15 | **+10.9%** | | 8 | 462.00 tok/s | 498.70 | **+7.9%** | Control: with the patch applied but the overlap forced never to fire, throughput returns to baseline (93.90 vs 93.30 on an earlier config), so the gain is the overlap and not the restructuring.

signal.title: [Model] Register model capabilities directly
signal.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 MD018 MD041 --> ## Purpose #7168 moved model inspection into a subprocess so model imports and CUDA initialization stay out of the parent. #9208 changed its result transport, #9233 consolidated capability checks into one child per implementation, #23558 cached the result, and #46567 fixed package-submodule invalidation. #51746 added an explicit cache-preparation command. In a follow-up conversation, Simon and I agreed to close that approach because users were unlikely to pre-bake and re-check entries, and to study the subprocess inspection path from first principles. On a fresh cache, vLLM still launches that child once for each lazy implementation before the cache can help. The existing extractor derives 22 capability fields from the model class, including its bases, flags, and method signatures. It does not need weights or an initialized engine. This PR makes that same typed result an optional part of lazy model registration. For 320 of the 325 unique built-in implementations, `inspect_model_cls()` now returns the declaration before source lookup, cache access, model import, or child launch. The five dependency-bound implementations keep runtime inspection. Existing two-argument plugins also keep the current cache-backed subprocess path. ## Measured A Linux CUDA acceptance run on one NVIDIA RTX 4090 Laptop GPU (driver 595.71.05, Torch 2.13.0+cu132, CUDA runtime 13.2) compared every direct declaration with a fresh legacy subprocess inspection, n=1 per implementation. All 320 declarations matched across all 22 field values and runtime types. Parent CUDA remained uninitialized. The focused Qwen mechanism screen used five fresh processes per arm and an empty ModelInfo cache for every process: | Fresh Qwen lookup | Legacy path | Direct declaration | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Inspection child processes | 1 | 0 | | ModelInfo cache files written | 1 | 0 | | Median `inspect_model_cls()` time | 4.6166 s | 5.154 microseconds | | Median outer process time | 8.3860 s | 3.7417 s | The two arms ran sequentially, so these are descriptive mechanism measurements, not an end-to-end serving benchmark or a causal performance comparison. ## The fix `ModelInfo` is a public, frozen, keyword-only declaration with the same 22 typed fields produced by the existing extractor. A plugin can opt into the direct path at its existing registration site: ```python from vllm import ModelInfo, ModelRegistry ModelRegistry.register_model( "MyModelForCausalLM", "my_plugin.models:MyModelForCausalLM", model_info=ModelInfo( architecture="MyModelForCausalLM", is_text_generation_model=True, supports_pp=True, ), ) ``` Rather than store 320 copies of 22 fields, the built-in catalog maps each exact `(module, class)` implementation pair to one of 55 shared sparse profiles, then materializes the architecture name. Aliases therefore share the implementation declaration. Import-time validation rejects duplicate entries, overlap with the dynamic set, and any catalog drift from the live registry. The integration point is the existing built-in registry comprehension, which now passes `model_info=_get_builtin_model_info(mod_relname, cls_name)`. No model class or model runner changes. The five dependency-bound implementations remain explicit dynamic entries. When a registration omits `model_info`, the old fallback still runs. Cache entries now validate schema version, vLLM version, model-module hash, extractor hash, field names, and field types. Source discovery walks module specs with `PathFinder` without executing package parents. A declaration still does not bypass platform, dependency, or implementation-loading checks. ## Verification - The supported local registry suite passed with 365 passed, 18 skipped, and 2 deselected. The unfiltered file has two environment-only failures because this environment lacks optional `timm` for `HCXVisionForCausalLM` and `KananaVForConditionalGeneration`. - The branch collects 385 registry cases versus 392 at its tested upstream base. It adds one test function and no new test file. - Ruff, scoped mypy, the import-light probe, and `git diff --check` passed. All nine commits carry DCO signoffs. H200 and MI300 registry CI remain the cross-platform acceptance gate. This PR changes metadata discovery, not model implementations, sampling, or output semantics. ## Test plan ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/models/test_registry.py \ --deselect='tests/models/test_registry.py::test_registry_imports[HCXVisionForCausalLM]' \ --deselect='tests/models/test_registry.py::test_registry_imports[KananaVForConditionalGeneration]' .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/models/test_registry.py::test_model_info_declaration_contract \ tests/models/test_registry.py::test_registry_inspects_builtin_without_import_or_cuda \ tests/models/test_registry.py::test_lazy_model_info_fallback_is_typed \ tests/models/test_registry.py::test_lazy_model_info_source_lookup_does_not_import_parent ``` AI assistance was used. I take responsibility for the implementation, compatibility boundary, and measurements.

signal.title: [Feature] Initial support for fault tolerant ep using scale-down
signal.text: ## Purpose This PR adds **scale-down** and **auto-recovery** support to the vLLM fault tolerance (FT) framework for DP+EP MoE deployments (external LB mode). The existing FT framework (`--enable-fault-tolerance`) supports `retry` — reinitializing the DP process group after a transient fault where all ranks survive. When a DP rank permanently dies (hardware failure, OOM kill, etc.), `retry` alone is insufficient: the dead rank's expert slots become unreachable and EPLB placement tables reference non-existent slots. This PR introduces two complementary capabilities: 1. **Scale-down** (`POST /fault_tolerance/apply` with `instruction: "scale_down"`): Removes dead DP ranks, masks the corresponding EP ranks at the all2all kernel level, redistributes orphaned logical experts onto surviving ranks using EPLB redundant slots, selectively reloads only reassigned expert weights from disk, rebuilds the DP Gloo group over the surviving slots, and resumes inference — all without a full restart. 2. **Auto-recovery** (`--fault-tolerance-config='{"auto_recovery": true}'`): Lets the engine self-heal without external orchestrator commands. On fault, the engine queries the all2all mask from its workers and unions it cluster-wide via the DP store: if no new dead ranks are detected (transient fault), it auto-retries; otherwise it derives the dead DP ranks from the EP mask and auto-scales-down. ### Design - **Slots model: EP topology unchanged** From vLLM's point of view, a removed rank remains as an empty slot: `parallel_config.data_parallel_size` / `data_parallel_rank` stay frozen at their initial values and DP rank ids never change, so there is exactly one coordinate system (original) and no densification anywhere. `removed_dp_ranks` is always in original coordinates and is cumulative-safe — it may include ranks removed by earlier rounds; the engine applies only the increment. Likewise the all2all kernel keeps the original EP world size with dead EP ranks masked via `update_mask()` (both `deepep_low_latency` and `nixl_ep`), which avoids model re-init, graph recompile, and CUDA graph re-capture. Only the rebuilt Gloo `cpu_group` uses dense internal ranks over `sorted(alive)`, computed at reinit time and never written back to config. - **EPLB is disabled after scale-down and re-enabled by a future scale-up.** Post-scale-down the EP/EPLB groups still span the original EP world size, so dynamic rebalancing would attempt collectives with dead ranks; EPLB async rebalancing is therefore suppressed (`eep_eplb_suppressed`) until a scale-up restores the slots. - **Failed recovery is retryable.** The engine commits the topology change (`data_parallel_master_ip`, cumulative dead set) only after the Gloo group reinit succeeds, so a failed attempt leaves a consistent state that can be re-dispatched. Invalid commands (own-rank removal, fully stale removal, <1 survivor) are rejected up front with an observable `ft_error` — the orchestrator re-reads status and re-issues. - **The orchestrator can pass an explicit `request_id` to identify the recovery round.** All engines in one round share the same `request_id`, which namespaces that round's coordination keys in the DP store so concurrent or stale rounds cannot cross-talk. When empty, it falls back to the engine's local reinit epoch. - **Auto-recovery rejects external commands while it is in progress.** A `_recovery_lock` serializes auto-recovery (busy-loop thread) against external commands (input-sockets thread); a command arriving during an ongoing recovery is rejected with a recorded `ft_error`, keeping a single recovery driver per engine at any time. ### Implementation Notes - **TP sibling lockstep barrier (TP > 1).** `_synchronize_dp_ranks` (v1) and `sync_cudagraph_and_dp_padding` (v2) run a per-step Gloo barrier over the TP CPU group when FT is enabled and `tp_size > 1`, preventing intra-TP deadlock: a sibling whose peer stopped arriving fails on the host within `cpu_distributed_timeout_seconds`, never leaving an orphaned TP collective (e.g. fused allreduce kernels without timeout) running on its device stream. The TP CPU group is rebuilt during worker `retry`. - **nixl_ep dispatcher sync.** After masking, each MoE layer's cached `num_dispatchers` is rewritten to the nixl_ep kernel's `active_rank_bound` (highest surviving EP rank + 1); the kernel sizes combine output by `active_rank_bound` and asserts the width matches. DeepEP-LL keeps a fixed num_ranks-wide layout and needs no sync. - **Dead-column neutralization.** Under the slots model the DP allreduce tensors keep their original width and a dead rank's column stays 0 after the SUM allreduce, which is not neutral for min/`all(==1)` aggregations. After the allreduce, each rank locally fills dead columns (from `get_dp_group().dead_dp_ranks`) with aggregate-neutral values. - **EPLB async state reset.** A new `ft_reset_epoch` on the EPLB state lets the async worker detect a recovery and abandon in-flight transfers instead of applying stale results; the async thread survives exceptions when FT is enabled. - **Side-stream mask query.** Worker `query_mask` runs on a separate CUDA stream so a poisoned main stream cannot block the mask read that auto-recovery and status reporting depend on. ### Known limitations - `scale_down` requires EPLB with `num_redundant_experts > 0`. - Requires an FT-capable all2all backend (`deepep_low_latency` or `nixl_ep`) and external LB mode with one engine per API server. - EPLB dynamic rebalancing stays suppressed after scale-down (lifted by a future `scale_up`). - Recovery is not guaranteed for faults occurring at certain stages (e.g. mid weight-transfer in EPLB). - Auto-recovery cannot self-heal the death of DP rank 0 (the coordination TCPStore master is hosted by rank 0); the engine fails closed and waits for an external `scale_down` command with `dp_store_port`/`dp_master_ip`. ## Test Plan E2E tests live in `tests/v1/fault_tolerance/test_fault_tolerance_e2e.py` (gated on `has_nixl_ep`): 1. `test_injected_fault_retry_recovers_all_ranks` (DP=2) — injected fault, all ranks UNHEALTHY, `retry`, all ranks HEALTHY and serving. 2. `test_scale_down_removes_dead_rank_and_recovers` (DP=4, EPLB with 32 redundant experts) — SIGKILL rank 1's worker; survivors go UNHEALTHY, victim's engine goes DEAD and rejects `retry` with a recorded `ft_error`; `scale_down(removed_dp_ranks=[1])` to all survivors; all survivors return to HEALTHY and serve completions. Manual cluster validation (external LB, 4 independent API servers, one engine each): - Model: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (MoE, 64 logical experts), `--data-parallel-size 4 --tensor-parallel-size 2` (EP world size 8), `--enable-expert-parallel`, `--all2all-backend nixl_ep`, `--enable-eplb` with 64 redundant experts (async), `--enable-fault-tolerance`, `--cpu-distributed-timeout-seconds 30`, `engine_recovery_timeout_sec=500`. - Drive baseline inference on all ranks; kill one worker of DP rank 1 (TP1 sibling) during active inference; verify survivors detect the fault and go UNHEALTHY while the victim's engine goes DEAD; send `scale_down(removed_dp_ranks=[1])` to the 3 survivors; verify expert redistribution + weight reload, Gloo group rebuilt over the surviving slots (original rank coordinates unchanged), all survivors HEALTHY and serving. ## Test Results Manual scale-down validation (2026-08-12, config above): **PASSED**. This run exercises the TP=2 single-worker-kill scenario end to end. Sanitized full log (host IP / GPU model / local paths redacted) attached. | Phase | Observation | Timestamp | |---|---|---| | Cluster ready | 4 ranks (DP=4 × TP=2, EP world 8) initialized, serving baseline traffic | 17:49:24 – 17:50:48 | | Fault injected | One worker of DP rank 1 (TP1 sibling, EP rank 3) killed during active inference | 17:50:48 | | First survivor-side error | Survivors' TP1 workers hit gloo `Connection reset by peer` on the per-TP-rank DP group | 17:50:48 | | Victim DEAD | Engine 1's executor shut down its remaining worker; busy loop cancelled → status DEAD; its API server stays up and keeps answering `/fault_tolerance/status` | 17:50:57 | | Survivors UNHEALTHY | Engines 0/2/3 raise from the nixl_ep kernel timeout with mask `[0,0,1,1,0,0,0,0]` (EP ranks 2,3 = DP rank 1, both TP workers) | 17:51:18 | | scale_down dispatched | `POST /fault_tolerance/apply` `removed_dp_ranks=[1]` → 202 on R0/R2/R3 | ~17:51:44 | | Expert redistribution | 257 (layer, expert) pairs reloaded from disk per worker (652–733 tensors); `num_dispatchers` synced to `active_rank_bound=8` | 17:51:45 | | Scale-down complete | Gloo DP group rebuilt 4→3 (dense group ranks R0→0, R2→1, R3→2; original `data_parallel_rank` frozen); Engines 0/2/3 → HEALTHY, `cumulative dead_dp_ranks=[1]` | 17:51:45 | | Post-recovery inference | All 3 survivors resume serving `/v1/chat/completions` with HTTP 200 | 17:51:45 – 17:52:07 | Key observations: - Recovery itself (mask replay + redistribution + weight reload + group reinit) completes in ~1s once dispatched; end-to-end latency is dominated by fault detection (immediate for the TP1 siblings via gloo connection-reset; ~30s for the surviving engines via the nixl_ep kernel timeout). - No hangs, no orphaned TP collectives — the TP sibling lockstep barrier keeps survivor device streams clean. E2E pytest: ``` .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/fault_tolerance/test_fault_tolerance_e2e.py -v -s ``` <!-- TODO: paste CI result once the fault-tolerance e2e step runs --> - **AI assistance**: this change was developed with AI assistance (kimi-k3); every changed line was reviewed by the human submitter. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. - [ ] (Optional) Release notes update. </details>

signal.title: [Bug]: FP8 block-scaled weights fail on sm120 (RTX 5090) — DeepGEMM "Unknown SF transformation" during process_weights_after_loading
signal.text: ### Your current environment <details> <summary>Environment</summary> ``` vLLM: 0.26.1rc1.dev608+g99a10304d (docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:muse-glimmer) GPU: 2x NVIDIA RTX 5090 (sm120 / device capability 12.0), PCIe Platform: Linux x86_64, CUDA 12.x Model: RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-FP8-block (compressed-tensors, block-scaled FP8 weights) ``` </details> ### 🐛 Describe the bug FP8 block-scaled weights (`compressed-tensors` w8a8) fail to load on sm120 with a DeepGEMM assertion. It happens in `process_weights_after_loading` — during weight loading, before any inference — so the engine never starts: ``` RuntimeError: Assertion error (/workspace/.deps/deepgemm-src/csrc/apis/layout.hpp:60): Unknown SF transformation ``` Full call chain (both TP workers fail identically): ``` compressed_tensors_w8a8_fp8.py:169 process_weights_after_loading -> kernels/linear/scaled_mm/deep_gemm.py:96 process_weights_after_loading -> quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py:1138 deepgemm_post_process_fp8_weight_block -> quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py:1077 deepgemm_post_process_weight_scale_block -> utils/deep_gemm.py:494 transform_sf_into_required_layout -> _transform_sf_into_required_layout_impl -> deepgemm csrc/apis/layout.hpp:60 "Unknown SF transformation" ``` The reason this is reached rather than skipped is that vLLM treats sm120 as a supported DeepGEMM target. `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py` gates on capability family 100 **or** 120 in two places (lines 42-43 and 79-80), and `is_deep_gemm_supported()` documents "only Hopper and Blackwell GPUs are supported" — so consumer Blackwell selects the DeepGEMM path, and then DeepGEMM's own layout transform rejects the scale-factor layout it is handed. Either the SF transform needs an sm120 case, or the capability-family-120 gate should exclude this path for block-scaled FP8 weights. ### Reproduction ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:muse-glimmer \ --model RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-FP8-block \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88 --max-model-len 131072 ``` Fails ~75 s in, at weight loading, reproducibly. ### Workaround `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` (plus `VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0`) makes the same command work. With that set the model loads and serves normally on 2x RTX 5090 — 177.6 tok/s decode with DFlash speculative decoding, 663,458-token KV cache — so only the DeepGEMM SF-layout path appears to be affected, not FP8 on sm120 in general. I have not tested whether NVFP4 or non-block-scaled FP8 checkpoints hit the same transform on this hardware; the NVFP4 variant of the same model loads fine with DeepGEMM left at its default.

signal.title: [Bugfix][MoE] Preserve unquantized weight storage on ROCm
signal.text: ## Summary - Preserve unquantized MoE parameter storage during ROCm post-load padding by copying the padded view into existing storage instead of rebinding `.data`. - Return directly after AITER unquantized MoE `shuffle_weights()` so the AITER runtime layout is not forced through an extra `.contiguous()` conversion. - Add a ROCm MoE weight replay test covering both AITER and TRITON backends. ## Motivation In RL-style serving and training loops, external weight updates can trigger `process_weights_after_loading()` more than once after model initialization. Reassigning `param.data` in that path can replace the underlying parameter storage. That is unsafe once CUDA graphs or runtime kernels have captured parameter storage addresses, and can leave later rollouts reading stale or invalid storage. We observed this as a training-time rollout corruption issue after weight updates: generated responses became invalid, and reward/score collapsed to 0. Preserving the existing parameter storage with `.copy_()` keeps captured addresses stable while still applying the padded layout. For AITER unquantized MoE, `shuffle_weights()` already returns the runtime layout consumed by AITER. In local Qwen3.5-35B GRPO measurements, avoiding the final contiguous conversion for AITER was slightly faster after normalizing rollout generation time by response length. ## Replay test The new `tests/rocm/test_moe_weight_replay.py` test constructs a Qwen3.5 MoE LLM with sleep mode and CUDA graphs, generates a deterministic greedy response, runs level-2 sleep/wake, then replays checkpoint-format weights through a framework-agnostic load-then-post-load helper: 1. stream checkpoint-format weights into `model.load_weights(...)` in buckets; 2. call `process_weights_after_loading(...)` once after all buckets are loaded; 3. verify the ROCm MoE padding branch was actually exercised; 4. verify MoE `w13_weight` / `w2_weight` parameter storage addresses do not change; 5. verify greedy token IDs are deterministic after replay. This covers both AITER and TRITON MoE backends as first-class correctness cases. ## Local validation Static/lightweight checks in the PR checkout: - `python3 -m py_compile tests/rocm/test_moe_weight_replay.py vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/unquantized_fused_moe_method.py vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/unquantized.py` - `python3 -m ruff check tests/rocm/test_moe_weight_replay.py vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/unquantized_fused_moe_method.py vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/oracle/unquantized.py` - `python3 -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_unquantized_backend_selection.py tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_weight_loading_padded.py` - 38 passed, 2 skipped Heavy replay validation with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and tensor parallel size 2: - pre-fix AITER: failed as expected; the test entered the ROCm padding branch and detected MoE parameter `data_ptr` changes. - pre-fix TRITON: failed as expected; the test entered the ROCm padding branch and detected MoE parameter `data_ptr` changes. - fixed AITER: passed. - fixed TRITON: passed. ## Benchmark note Local 10-step Qwen3.5-35B GRPO runs kept score/reward normal with zero aborted responses. Normalized rollout timing for AITER was slightly better without the final contiguous conversion: about 22.95 ms/token vs 23.11 ms/token.

signal.title: [ROCm][Perf] Use AITER tuned GEMM for the MoE router gate
signal.text: ## Purpose The MoE gate linear layer was set to use a bf16×bf16→fp32 GEMM on tier 5 for faster performance, but it is conditioned on Hopper and Blackwell. This enables it for AITER when the underlying tuned GEMM shapes exist. ### Trace comparison On the CPU side, the gate previously performed two operations: a conversion of its input to fp32, followed by the multiply. AITER was already invoked, but with fp32 operands it found no tuned kernel and fell through to `aten::linear` → `aten::matmul` → `aten::mm`. The input now remains in bf16, AITER dispatches a tuned kernel directly, and the cast is moved after the GEMM, where it applies only to the small output. The GPU stream shows the same change. The `add_rmsnorm_quant` kernel on the left is unaffected by this PR and serves as a scale reference between the two panels. ## Test Plan `tests/kernels/test_rocm_aiter_router_gemm.py`, skipped unless ROCm and AITER tuned GEMM are available. It verifies agreement with an fp64 reference, top-k expert selection, and equivalence with the `F.linear` fallback it replaces, across three router shapes and M from 1 to 128. End-to-end throughput, latency and accuracy were measured on MI355X against an otherwise identical build. ## Test Result 81/81 kernel tests pass on gfx950 with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`. MI355X, TP4, geomean over a 16-point concurrency sweep (ISL 1024/8192, OSL 1024): **TPOT -3.05%, output throughput +3.10%**. Accuracy is unchanged within one standard error: gsm8k strict-match 0.9515 against 0.9500 baseline, RULER niah_single_2 0.876 against 0.860. `ruff check` and `ruff format` are clean. ## Model-level signal.title: [ROCm][Perf] Skip redundant sparse index remap on non-indexer layers
signal.text: ## Summary With cross-layer index sharing, only some attention layers update the shared top-k buffer. The old path still remapped that buffer on every layer. This PR runs the remap only when the layer owns an indexer. For GLM-5.2 with `index_topk_freq = 4`, this reduces remaps from 78 to 21 per forward pass. ## Safety - Layer 0 always owns an indexer, so the shared output is initialized before reuse. - Non-indexer layers do not change the inputs to the remap. - The default `index_topk_freq = 1` path is unchanged. - Speculative decoding still remaps on every layer. ## Results MI355X, TP=4, rank 0, same serving workload: | remap kernel | before | after | change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | launches | 139,378 | 37,254 | **-73.3%** | | GPU time | 2,392.1 ms | 645.7 ms | **-73.0%** | | launches per layer | 1.000 | 0.269 | matches 21/78 | The red box below is a redundant remap on a layer with no indexer. signal.title: [ROCm][Perf] Skip cleaning sparse prefill MQA logits
signal.text: ## Summary The sparse prefill path creates the MQA-logits buffer with `torch.full(..., -inf)`. This launches an FP32 fill before every logits kernel. This PR passes `clean_logits=False` to AITER, so the buffer uses `torch.empty` and the fill is removed. ## Safety The only consumer is `top_k_per_row_prefill`. It reads each row only inside `[cu_seqlen_ks, cu_seqlen_ke)`. Its vectorized path also guards the final partial load, so padding values are never read. The top-k result is unchanged. ## Results MI355X, TP=4, rank 0, comparable before/after captures: | metric | before | after | |---|---:|---:| | FP32 fill launches | 18,162 | **0** | | FP32 fill GPU time | 1,250.2 ms | **0 ms** | | MQA-logits launches | 18,108 | 17,930 | The removed fill was **0.89% of total GPU kernel time**. In the sample below it takes 74.6 µs and is fully serialized before the logits kernel. ![Before: FP32 fill before MQA logits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amd-sriram/vllm/ce9490285bbd8099e2d37c5aec8b3d24b7a20785/figures/fig_pr4_before.png) ![After: fill removed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amd-sriram/vllm/ce9490285bbd8099e2d37c5aec8b3d24b7a20785/figures/fig_pr4_after.png) ## Model-level e2e results ### Test conditions | | | |---|---| | Hardware | MI355X (gfx950), TP=4 | | Model | `amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4`, fp8 KV cache | | Stack | vLLM `69715823`, AITER `4a1cc77`, flydsl `0.3.0` | | Server | `--async-scheduling --max-num-seqs 256 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --block-size 64 --no-enable-prefix-caching`, `index_topk_freq=4` | | Env | `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_SPARSE_INDEXER=1`, `AITER_USE_FLYDSL_MOE_SORTING=1`, `VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4` | | Perf | `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, `--ignore-eos --request-rate inf`, ISL 1024 and 8192, OSL 1024, concurrency 1-256 (16 points) | | Accuracy | `lm_eval` gsm8k 5-shot chat template with thinking enabled, `max_gen_toks=8192`; signal.title: Support CUTLASS W4A8 MoE with DeepEP low latency
signal.text: ## Summary This PR adds CUTLASS W4A8 MoE support for DeepEP low-latency dispatch. The existing CUTLASS W4A8 MoE path assumes flat routed-token inputs. DeepEP low-latency dispatch produces padded batched-expert tensors and carries the real routed-row count separately. This PR adds a batched CUTLASS W4A8 experts implementation for that activation format while preserving the existing native ABI. Key changes: - add `CutlassBatchedExpertsW4A8Fp8` for DeepEP low-latency `BatchedExperts`; - select the batched W4A8 backend only when DeepEP low-latency is enabled; - build W4A8 batched metadata in Python using physical expert offsets and SwapAB problem shapes; - keep `csrc` and `_custom_ops.py` unchanged so existing wheels can reuse the native extension; - add targeted workspace, metadata, backend-selection, two-GEMM, and 8-rank DeepEP integration coverage. ## Validation This has been validated internally with our MiniMax-M3-W4AFP8 model based on vLLM v0.26.0 image. We have not yet found a convenient public W4A8 MoE checkpoint that selects this CUDA CUTLASS backend, so public model-level validation is still pending. We will consider adding public-model coverage in a follow-up once a suitable checkpoint or fixture is available. ## Notes This PR is intended as initial support for the CUTLASS W4A8 + DeepEP low-latency path. Internally, we have also made additional optimizations to CUTLASS + DeepEP low latency that improved decode performance by over 30%. Those changes are not included here and can be proposed in a separate PR.

signal.title: [XPU] Support sequence parallelism for block fp8 on XPU
signal.text: ## Purpose Enable sequence parallelism (SP) support on XPU for the block-quant W8A8 FP8 model SP is enabled with: ```json {"pass_config":{"enable_sp":true},"use_inductor_graph_partition":true} ``` ## Test Plan Model: `RedHatAI/Qwen3-32B-FP8-block` (dense, block-quant W8A8 FP8, `weight_block_size=[128,128]`), tp=4, `--linear-backend xpu`. ### Server (one of the three, per case) ```bash # sp_on VLLM_XPU_FUSED_MOE_USE_REF=1 VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \ python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-32B-FP8-block --port 8072 --host 0.0.0.0 \ --trust-remote-code --gpu-memory-util=0.9 --max-num-batched-tokens=8192 \ --max-model-len=6000 --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 64 \ --linear-backend xpu -tp=4 \ --compilation-config '{"pass_config":{"enable_sp":true},"use_inductor_graph_partition":true}' # sp_off VLLM_XPU_FUSED_MOE_USE_REF=1 VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \ python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-32B-FP8-block --port 8072 --host 0.0.0.0 \ --trust-remote-code --gpu-memory-util=0.9 --max-num-batched-tokens=8192 \ --max-model-len=6000 --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 64 \ --linear-backend xpu -tp=4 # eager VLLM_XPU_FUSED_MOE_USE_REF=1 VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \ python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-32B-FP8-block --port 8072 --host 0.0.0.0 \ --trust-remote-code --gpu-memory-util=0.9 --max-num-batched-tokens=8192 \ --max-model-len=6000 --no-enable-prefix-caching --block-size 64 \ --linear-backend xpu -tp=4 --enforce-eager ``` ### Client (bench serve, run twice per case; signal.title: [Feature]: support affinity settings in helm chart
signal.text: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch ### Problem This issue concerns [chart-helm](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/examples/online_serving/chart-helm). This Helm Chart does not support configuring `affinity` for Deployment/Pod. Currently, the following use cases are not supported: - The case where users want to specify `podAffinity` - The case where users want to specify `podAntiAffinity` - The case where users want to specify generic `nodeAffinity` (Currently, the specific `nodeAffinity` is created by `gpuModels` in `values.yaml`.) - The case where users do not want to explicitly pin GPU product labels (Currently, it is mandatory to pin this by `gpuModels` in `values.yaml`.) ### Expected behavior The chart should allow users to provide generic `affinity` block via `values.yaml`, mapped directly to Deployment's `spec.template.spec.affinity`. This would make it possible to specify `podAffinity`, `podAntiAffinity`, and `nodeAffinity` that is not limited to the one pinning GPU product labels. ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signal.title: [Bugfix] Clamp block table indices in align mode to prevent OOB gather
signal.text: In mamba_cache_mode='align' with speculative decoding, sequences with seq_len near max_model_len caused indices_to_gather to exceed the block table column count, triggering a CUDA device-side assert in torch.gather. Fixes #42084 ## Purpose Fix an out-of-bounds `torch.gather` in `mamba_get_block_table_tensor` when `mamba_cache_mode='align'` is used together with speculative decoding and a large `max_model_len`. In `align` mode the Mamba block table has shape `(#requests, cdiv(max_model_len, block_size))` — one column per block over the full context window, with **no** extra speculative columns appended. When computing the gather indices: ```python start_indices = (seq_lens - 1) // kv_cache_spec.block_size offsets = torch.arange(1 + kv_cache_spec.num_speculative_blocks, ...) indices_to_gather = (start_indices.unsqueeze(1) + offsets).to(torch.int64) ``` for a sequence with `seq_len` near `max_model_len`, `start_indices` is at or near the last valid column. Adding `num_speculative_blocks` (which is `num_speculative_tokens` when using a draft model) then pushes `indices_to_gather` past the end of the block table, triggering: ``` torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered ``` This crashes the entire EngineCore process, killing all in-flight requests. **Fix:** add a single upper-bound clamp on `indices_to_gather` before the gather call, mirroring the identical `.clip(max=block_table.shape[1] - 1)` pattern already used in `make_local_attention_virtual_batches` (line 452 in the same file): ```python indices_to_gather.clamp_(max=block_table.shape[1] - 1) ``` Fixes #42084 ## Test Plan New CPU-only regression test added to `tests/v1/attention/test_mamba_update_block_table.py`: ```bash pytest tests/v1/attention/test_mamba_update_block_table.py::test_mamba_get_block_table_tensor_align_mode_oob_clamp -v ``` The test constructs a block table sized for `align` mode (`cdiv(max_model_len, block_size)` columns, no speculative tail), then calls `mamba_get_block_table_tensor` with `seq_lens` near `max_model_len` and `num_speculative_blocks=2`. Without the fix the test raises an index error; with the fix it passes and verifies the output shape and value bounds. ## Test Result **Before fix:** ``` IndexError: index out of bounds ``` **After fix:** ``` PASSED tests/v1/attention/test_mamba_update_block_table.py::test_mamba_get_block_table_tensor_align_mode_oob_clamp ``` --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signal.title: [RFC]:  Unify the Tensor Type for Device-Pointer Storage to `torch.uint64`
signal.text: ### Motivation. In vLLM, several kernels accept `Tensor` objects whose elements are not ordinary numeric values but raw device pointers (i.e., `data_ptr()` of other tensors). These pointer tensors are used for batch memory copies, grouped operations (e.g., MoE where each expert has its own pointer array), attention block-table lookups, and cross-GPU IPC workspaces. Device pointers are semantically unsigned 64-bit values (`CUdeviceptr` / `uintptr_t`). However, the current vLLM codebase exhibits three inconsistent storage practices, one of which is clearly problematic: 1. **Unconditional use of `torch.int64`** — problematic. Assigning an unsigned address (`data_ptr()`) to a `torch.int64` tensor triggers `ValueError: Overflow when unpacking long long` when the address exceeds `2^63-1`. This has been actually triggered on XPU for encoder-cache CPU offload [descriptor_buffers.py](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/ec_connector/cpu/worker/descriptor_buffers.py#L32) and Mamba speculative decoding state batch copy ([mamba_utils.py#L649](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py#L649)), with workaround PRs ([#49532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49532), [#50552](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50552)) that keep `int64` + bit-reinterpretation. The cross-GPU IPC workspace ([lamport_workspace.py#L210](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/minimax_rms_norm/lamport_workspace.py#L210)) carries the same latent risk. 2. **Platform-dependent branching (`int64` / `uint64`)** — currently works but is fragile. `swap_blocks_batch` uses `int64` for CUDA/ROCm and `uint64` for XPU [(`cache_kernels.cu#L86`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/libtorch_stable/cache_kernels.cu#L86) [(`_custom_ops.py#L2831`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/_custom_ops.py#L2831). The KV-cache CPU offload [(`gpu_worker.py#L153`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/gpu_worker.py#L153) avoids the assignment pitfall only because it uses a `.numpy()` view, not because the branching logic is inherently safe. This approach forces every new call site to remember the correct dtype per platform — high maintenance cost and error-prone. 3. **Unconditional use of `torch.uint64`** — currently fine and already adopted in attention block-table pointer lookup [(`block_table.py#L82`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py#L82), LoRA batch Triton kernels [(`triton_ops/utils.py#L54`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/utils.py#L54), and KV-cache offload copy parameters [(`cuda_mem_ops.py#L111`)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/cuda_mem_ops.py#L111). However, these work only because they currently construct the tensor in one go and do not perform element-wise assignment; if such assignment is introduced later, the same overflow error will reappear. Three unrelated modules (encoder-cache offload, Mamba speculative decoding, and Lamport workspace) have been hit — or are being hit — by the same problem at different times by different developers. This clearly indicates a **convention-level** issue, not a single code bug. The codebase currently lacks an explicit, copyable example; `int64` and `uint64` examples are almost evenly split, leaving new code to the author's personal judgment. ### Proposed Change. ### Goal Establish a clear vLLM-wide convention: **all tensors that store device pointers must use `torch.uint64`**. Specifically: - Remove all platform-based dtype branches — no special casing for CUDA/ROCm vs. XPU. - Align the low-level kernels (CUDA / Triton) that receive pointer arrays to expect `uint64` data, matching the upper layer. ### Prerequisite ⚠️ PyTorch currently does not support scalar assignment to `uint64` tensors (e.g., `t[0] = 2**63 + 5` raises `ValueError: Overflow when unpacking long long`), even when the tensor itself is of type `uint64`. This issue is platform-independent (occurs on CUDA, ROCm, and XPU alike). The upstream PyTorch issue ([pytorch/pytorch#191458](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191458)) and its fix PR ([#191604](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191604)) are not yet merged. Until that fix lands, vLLM must adopt **workarounds** for assigning to `uint64` pointer tensors: - Use `.numpy()` views for element-wise assignment (see [`gpu_worker.py#L301-L303`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/gpu_worker.py#L301-L303)). ### Task List The following tasks can be implemented in separate PRs, gradually moving toward the unified type: - [ ] **Encoder-cache CPU offload** Change the dtype in [`descriptor_buffers.py#L32`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/ec_connector/cpu/worker/descriptor_buffers.py#L32) and [`worker/__init__.py#L112`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/ec_connector/cpu/worker/__init__.py#L112) to `uint64`, and align with [#49532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49532). - [ ] **Mamba speculative decoding state batch copy** Change the dtype in [`mamba_utils.py#L649`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py#L649) and [#L732](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py#L732) to `uint64`, and align with [#50552](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50552). - [ ] **Cross-GPU IPC workspace** Modify [`lamport_workspace.py#L210`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/minimax_rms_norm/lamport_workspace.py#L210) and its consuming kernels to use `uint64`. - [ ] **Unify `swap_blocks_batch`** Remove the platform branch for CUDA/ROCm vs. XPU, and update [`cache_kernels.cu#L86`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/csrc/libtorch_stable/cache_kernels.cu#L86), [`_custom_ops.py#L2831`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/_custom_ops.py#L2831), and [`gpu_worker.py::_new_descriptor_buffers#L153`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/gpu_worker.py#L153) to consistently use `uint64`. - [x] **Upstream PyTorch fix** Advocate for merging [pytorch/pytorch#191604](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191604) (or an equivalent) to fix the `uint64` scalar assignment overflow. Until then, provide a shared **workaround helper** (e.g., `assign_uint64`) for vLLM modules to reuse, avoiding direct `__setitem__` operations. ### Alternatives Considered - **Keep status quo with platform branches**: Rejected — requires every new call site to remember platform-specific dtype, high maintenance cost, and the latent overflow risk remains. - **Use `torch.int64` everywhere with bit-reinterpretation**: Rejected — workaround PRs ([#49532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49532), [#50552](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50552)) already exist but are fragile and do not solve the root cause. - **Use a custom wrapper type**: Rejected — adds unnecessary complexity and does not align with PyTorch tensor semantics. ### Backward Compatibility This change is backward compatible for existing `uint64` usages. For `int64` usages, callers that currently rely on signed interpretation may need to adjust. However, since these tensors store raw pointers, the signed interpretation is semantically incorrect; no valid use case should depend on it. ### Performance Impact No performance impact is expected. The dtype change does not affect kernel execution efficiency; it only affects tensor construction and assignment paths. ## Related Links - [pytorch/pytorch#191458](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191458) - [pytorch/pytorch#191604](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191604) - [vLLM PR #36423](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36423) - [vLLM PR #49532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49532) - [vLLM PR #50552](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50552)

signal.title: [Bugfix][Model][CI/Build] Fix CUDA graph capture in GLM-OCR / GLM4-MoE-Lite MTP layers
signal.text: ## Purpose FIX #48749 `GlmOcrMultiTokenPredictorLayer.forward` and `Glm4MoeLiteMultiTokenPredictorLayer.forward` mask the position-0 embedding with an in-place boolean-mask assignment: ```python inputs_embeds[positions[0] == 0] = 0 # glm_ocr_mtp.py inputs_embeds[positions == 0] = 0 # glm4_moe_lite_mtp.py ``` A boolean-mask `index_put_` calls `nonzero()`, whose output shape is data-dependent, so it synchronizes device to host to size the allocation. That is not allowed inside an active CUDA graph capture, and the V2 model runner captures the MTP prefill graph (`speculator.capture()` -> `prefill_cudagraph_manager.capture()`), so engine startup fails: ``` File "vllm/model_executor/models/glm_ocr_mtp.py", line 87, in forward inputs_embeds[positions[0] == 0] = 0 torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: operation not permitted when stream is capturing ``` It was reported on A100-SXM4-80GB in #48749. The equivalent capture-safe form is already used by the other two MTP implementations: - `vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_mtp.py:113` - `vllm/model_executor/models/glm4_moe_mtp.py:113` both of which read `inputs_embeds = torch.where(positions.unsqueeze(-1) == 0, 0, inputs_embeds)`. This PR applies the same form to the two remaining implementations. GLM-OCR keeps `positions[0]` because it is an MRoPE model, where `positions` has shape `(3, seq_len)`. Duplicate-work checks were performed before opening: no open PR references #48749 or touches `glm_ocr_mtp.py`. #39483 and #43747 fix different code paths that surface the same CUDA error. Related: #49869 fixes an unrelated GLM-OCR MTP weight-loading regression (#49856). On main as of 3ee2df303 with the HF checkpoint, startup fails there before reaching graph capture, so that patch was applied locally to reproduce this crash. The crash fixed here reproduces with no local patches on v0.25.1. The two fixes are independent and can merge in either order. ## Test Plan Adds a GLM-OCR entry to `tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/mtp/test_mtp.py`, covering engine startup and CUDA graph capture with MTP for this model. **The entry will fail in CI until #49869 lands**, because GLM-OCR MTP weights fail to load (#49856) and the engine dies before reaching graph capture. It was run locally with that patch applied, before and after the fix: ``` pytest "tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/mtp/test_mtp.py::test_mtp_correctness[glm_ocr]" ``` ## Test Result | Environment | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | 3ee2df303, RTX 2080 Ti (sm75), torch 2.13.0+cu130, #49869 applied locally so MTP weights load | e2e test fails: `cudaErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported` at `glm_ocr_mtp.py:87` while capturing prefill FULL graphs | e2e test passes; `exact text matches=100/100` | | 0.25.1, Tesla T4 (sm75), CUDA 12.9, `num_speculative_tokens: 3` | engine dies during startup capture (traceback in #48749) | starts; captures prefill 51/51 PIECEWISE and 49/49 FULL, decode 35/35 FULL; serves; OCRs a document block correctly | pre-commit: all hooks passed on the three changed files. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate the stream-capture failure, implement this change, run validation, and prepare this PR. A human reviewed the changed lines and ran the unit tests above.

signal.title: fix: avoid overlapping stores in XPU KV cache kernel
signal.text: ## Summary Fix overlapping stores in the DeepSeek V4 XPU qnorm/RoPE KV kernel. The KV branch previously performed a bulk store across all 512 KV elements before separately storing the rotated RoPE region. These stores overlap in the RoPE region and can result in nondeterministic KV cache contents. The bulk store is now masked to `NOPE_DIM`, matching the existing Q-branch pattern: ```python tl.store(kv_out_base + offs, kv_full, mask=offs < NOPE_DIM)
signal.author: AbarnaaSree

signal.title: [Bug] XPU qnorm/rope kernel: overlapping stores in one program corrupt the KV cache nondeterministically
signal.text: **File:** `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/xpu/xpu_qnorm_rope_kv_fp8_insert.py` **Confirmed present in v0.27.1** (tag `6e448d0ea9bf`) and on `main`. ## Summary In the KV branch, the kernel stores all 512 elements of `kv` — RoPE region included, still unrotated — and then overwrites that region with the rotated values at stride-2 addresses: ```python # lines 93-94 kv_full = tl.load(kv_base + offs) tl.store(kv_out_base + offs, kv_full) # writes the unrotated rope region ... # lines 106-107 tl.store(kv_out_base + even_offs, new_even) # overwrites it, stride-2 addresses tl.store(kv_out_base + odd_offs, new_odd) ``` Two stores to the same addresses within one program, with different lane-to-address mappings and no ordering between them. Nothing guarantees the rotated store wins. ## Evidence On MTT S5000 (MUSA), 4096 tokens × 64 heads, compared against FlagGems' fused kernel, which is byte-exact against the pure-torch reference on the same inputs: - **30 tokens** of 4096 have a cache RoPE region that differs - **29 of those 30** hold values exactly equal to the **unrotated** `kv` — i.e. the bulk store landed last - the remaining one is partially overwritten, consistent with a lane-granular race - a **second run on identical inputs gives 29, not 30** — nondeterministic Concretely, token 96: the cache holds `[1.023, 0.262, -1.516, -0.277]`, exactly the raw `kv` values, where the correct rotated values are `[-0.441, 0.961, 1.531, -0.132]`. ## Fix One line, and it is also cheaper — mask the bulk copy so the overlap never exists: ```python tl.store(kv_out_base + offs, kv_full, mask=offs < NOPE_DIM) ``` This skips 64 redundant stores per KV token as well. With it applied, output is byte-identical to the reference. ## Note XPU scheduling may simply never expose this, but the ordering assumption does not hold on any backend. We found it because MUSA schedules differently.

signal.title: [Bugfix][Mamba] Fix overlapping state copy race
signal.text: [PR #30877](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/30877) introduced generic Mamba state copies, and [PR #40172](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40172) added the fused GPU copy. A speculative-decode convolution-state shift can copy within the same physical block with overlapping source and destination ranges. Parallel memcpy-style loads/stores do not provide memmove ordering, which explains the intermittent [AMD CI failure](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/11556/list?sid=019fbc8d-6c5e-4172-83cb-f45a49946645&tab=output). This version is rebased over [PR #49436](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49436): - Temporal state copies retain #49436's 3D grid and 16-way tiled copy. - DS convolution copies use stable row-to-lane ownership while iterating tokens low to high. - SD convolution copies retain `_memcpy_u64_tiled(..., NUM_TILES=1)` for distinct physical blocks and exact self-copies, and use an ordered token copy only for a true same-physical-block left overlap. - Conv copies remain single-CTA (`tile_idx > 0` returns), so no grid-wide barrier is assumed or required. - The generic fallback is unchanged. MRv1 and MRv2 already share this fused copy kernel for the relevant hybrid/speculative/aligned path; routing every MRv1 configuration through the MRv2 lifecycle would break unsupported/custom state layouts such as ReplaySSM and would not cover the CPU fallback. - Existing overlap assertions derive expected values from untouched snapshots. The broad Python-vs-fused golden uses disjoint pages so the generic memcpy helper is not treated as a memmove oracle. ## Validation - `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -s tests/v1/worker/test_mamba_utils.py`: **37 passed** - `uvx pre-commit run --files vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py tests/v1/worker/test_mamba_utils.py`: **passed** - The original failing revision reproduced locally on MI355; the rebased implementation passed the same snapshot checks. - Qwen3.5-0.8B MTP checks across 8×MI355, MRv1/MRv2, SD/DS, and batch 1/8 produced matching output hashes. A counterbalanced device-kernel benchmark on MI355 covered both runners, SD/DS, same-page and distinct-page copies, and batch 1/8. For a 24-layer Qwen3.5-shaped state copy: | Path | Batch | Result vs current main | |---|---:|---:| | SD same-page, MRv1 | 1 / 8 | +14.7 µs / +1.1% | | SD same-page, MRv2 | 1 / 8 | +18.0 µs / +1.2% | | SD distinct-page, both runners | 1 / 8 | -2.5% / +1.7–1.8% | | DS, both runners and mappings | 1 / 8 | 95.5–98.5% lower latency | The SD same-page cost is the overlap-safe ordering; the common distinct-page path retains the tiled memcpy. MRv1 and MRv2 copy-kernel latency is effectively equivalent because they already execute the same fused mechanism. This PR was developed with assistance from OpenAI Codex.

signal.title: [XPU][MoE] Enable MoE kernel unit tests on Intel XPU
signal.text: This PR enables three MoE kernel unit-test files on Intel XPU using the proven dual-HW pattern from PRs #42736 and #43307: * tests/kernels/moe/test_count_expert_num_tokens.py * tests/kernels/moe/test_batched_moe.py * tests/kernels/moe/test_triton_moe_no_act_mul.py The pattern is: * Replace hardcoded `device="cuda"` with `device=current_platform.device_type`. * Add a module-level `pytestmark` that skips when neither a CUDA-alike nor an XPU platform is available. * Scope fp8/cap-89 gates to `current_platform.is_cuda()` so XPU runs the bf16 path that it already supports. Two infrastructure fixes were required to unblock the tests on XPU: 1. `tests/conftest.py`: extend the `workspace_init` fixture so it initializes the workspace manager on XPU in addition to CUDA. The CUDA branch is untouched. 2. `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/fused_batched_moe.py`: guard two call sites of `torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` with `current_platform.is_cuda_alike() and ...`. On CUDA/ROCm this short-circuits to the original behavior (the second operand is the only side effect). On XPU the old code raised `RuntimeError: Tried to instantiate dummy base class _cuda_isCurrentStreamCapturing` because the symbol is a torch dummy stub when CUDA is unavailable. Validation on Intel B70 (XPU): * test_count_expert_num_tokens.py: 146 passed * test_batched_moe.py: 384 passed, 384 skipped, 0 failed * test_triton_moe_no_act_mul.py: 74 passed Total: 604 passed, 384 skipped, 0 failed. CUDA behavior is preserved: * `current_platform.device_type` on CUDA hosts equals `"cuda"`. * The new module-level `pytestmark`s evaluate identically to the old per-test skip conditions on CUDA. * The two production guards reduce to the original boolean on CUDA/ROCm because `is_cuda_alike()` is True there. ### Note on the 384 skipped cases in `test_batched_moe.py` The skips are **platform-independent** and are produced by the test's own pre-existing parameter-validity guards — they are not XPU-specific and skip identically on CUDA/ROCm. The `@pytest.mark.parametrize` decorators form a full cartesian product over `(per_act_token_quant, block_shape, dtype, ...)`, and the test then prunes the combinations that are meaningless or illegal: * `if (per_act_token_quant or block_shape is not None) and not use_fp8_w8a8:` → skip quantization/blocking knobs on a non-fp8 dtype. * `if per_act_token_quant and block_shape is not None:` → skip the illegal per-act-token **and** block-quant combination. The only `current_platform.is_cuda()`-conditioned skip is the Triton `fp8e4nv` arch-`<89` guard, which simply never triggers off-CUDA. As a result **both the bf16 and the fp8 (`float8_e4m3fn`) kernel paths actually execute and pass on XPU** — of the 384 fp8-dtype cases, the valid ones run (the skipped ones are the invalid combos above), so no real XPU coverage is hidden behind the skip count. These guards are left untouched to preserve identical behavior across CUDA/ROCm/XPU. ## Purpose ## Test Plan ## Test Result --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>
